vice-president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am particularly pleased with the debate on this subject. many of you know that i consider the fight against trafficking in human beings to be one of my personal priorities, which, in my view, must not only be visible but also have concrete and important results. as you know, i proposed a commission communication on this subject last october, along the lines suggested by the rapporteur, mrs prets: an integrated approach to the development of a european action plan to combat trafficking in human beings firmly and decisively. last december, following that communication, the council of ministers for justice and home affairs agreed to the proposal and adopted an action plan. the latter refers specifically to the best practices, common standards and procedures for combating and preventing trafficking in human beings. today, with this report, which i share and particularly appreciate, parliament is playing its own essential political role - and certainly a necessary one - by paying particular attention to women and children, that is to say, to the categories which in my view are most exposed to this very form of slavery, which europe has a duty to combat. i would say that it is a moral duty, not just an institutional and legal one, to abolish this form of slavery. this moral duty, as the report suggests, requires an integrated approach based on the principle of absolute respect for the dignity of every child, every woman, every man and every human being in general. this is not a legal or bureaucratic basis but our fundamental principles, based on the rules of the treaties, the european charter of rights and, if i may say so, also on morality. although the european union is already implementing policies in this area, these need to be strengthened. i am referring, for example, to a policy to strengthen the principle of equality between the sexes in order to prevent women from being marginalised in the world of work and relegated to more humble jobs, a policy which will certainly promote an improvement in the level of culture necessary to eliminate demand at the root. here's another important point: unfortunately, demand is a component of exploitation. if there were no demand, if there were fewer customers or if users who were prepared to cooperate with exploiters were drastically eliminated, the phenomenon would undoubtedly take on much less dramatic dimensions. i understand why the rapporteur has chosen not to put the issue of prostitution at the centre of the report under consideration. however, i personally believe - and i emphasize this personally - that we must also tackle the problem of how to discourage the customers, who are consciously using exploited and trafficked girls, with a firm hand. no one can ignore these dramatic conditions. this is a very sensitive subject, which we cannot discuss today, but which will have to be discussed. the present degree of harmonisation is limited. the member states have different laws and although there is a framework decision specifically dealing with trafficking in human beings, the exploitation of children, the horrendous paedophilia and child pornography, there is still little harmonisation in practice. i agree with the rapporteur that little has been done for the victims of human trafficking, who cannot be helped only when they decide to cooperate with the police authorities. they must also be helped to reintegrate into society! a child who has suffered the horror of pornography and pedophilia cannot be helped only by cooperating with the police and revealing the names of his exploiters but needs constant assistance throughout his life, because the consequences of the damage he has suffered will likely be indelible. the commission has worked to ensure that the approach to european legislation is based on the broad lines laid down by the united nations in the convention on the rights of the child. i am pleased to note that the council also shares this approach and is therefore in favour of extending all forms of protection to children under the age of 18. there is no such thing as a child that is too narrow: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the rights of children under 18 years of age are protected. i also share another aspect of the report, when it stresses the links between the strictly criminal matter of trafficking in human beings and illegal immigration, as well as the issue of social protection and the need for a union foreign policy aimed at introducing - and we are doing so in all international relations - a clear reference to trafficking in human beings as one of the priority objectives for the european union. in short, those who negotiate with the union and wish to establish close relations at international level must be aware that the european union cannot tolerate the large flows and the exploitation of women and children and, in general, of human beings. to do all this, a database is needed. i agree with you on this one: we are in fact working on it, even technically. i am working closely with europol to improve their database so that we can build a real european statistical system that provides reliable data in the future. we often ignore the real extent of the phenomenon and this is unacceptable. europe will have a reliable database and statistical system, and at the same time i intend not only to respond to parliament's call but also to propose a number of concrete initiatives which, on the basis of the action plan approved in december, will translate into concrete action our desire to decisively eradicate trafficking in human beings, especially children and women.

mr president, mr mandelson, five lessons from hong kong. first, our negotiating method is flawed. a year before the summit, we are making agricultural concessions by re-founding the cap. the result is that when you come to the negotiating table, no matter how talented you are - and it's immense - you have no choice but to cross the agricultural red line. secondly, hong kong confirms the seattle and cancun. agriculture, despite its 5% share, is europe's rich comparative advantage, otherwise why would it be at the heart of the war waged by brazil, for example, at each of the summits? thirdly, the apparently generous reduction in customs duties for developing countries in the name of market access is criticized by those same countries, such as mexico, which have understood that the customs gift is not made to the poor but to northern companies producing for the poor, such as bangladesh or vietnam. fourthly, this politically sympathetic reduction in customs duties is technically difficult to manage, which is proof that after 20 years of mathematical formulae, swiss formulae or otherwise, the hong kong declaration is unable to find the solution. fifthly, the path to tariff reductions is an archaic dead end. the modern solution is the invention of deductible customs duties in the form of customs credits or drawings offered by the importing state to the exporting state, a credit equal to the amounts of customs duties levied on the exporter's products. mr mandelson, if you did that, you would be harry potter, you would have managed to marry both ricardo and frederic list, you would have solved the problem of global economic asymmetries, you would have both preserved the interests of the poor and the interests of the rich, free trade and the protection of our social model.

in writing. nothing in mr catania's report on european citizenship was worth supporting. but two proposals were particularly shocking. first, the demand for european union citizenship, including the right to vote and stand as a candidate in local, national and european elections, for all residents of a country, regardless of their nationality. secondly, the requirement for the harmonization of the rights of the nationality of the member states, on the pretext that their difference creates discrimination for non-europeans in access to european citizenship as defined today by the treaties. how far will the madness go? the only way to become a citizen of a country is to have that country's nationality. the conditions for acquiring the nationality of a state are a matter for the exclusive sovereignty of that state. giving foreigners the right to vote without their nationality gives them a double right, the right they can exercise in the host country in addition to the right they can continue to exercise in their home countries. so it is really an unfair measure. being someone's guest does not give you the right to meddle in their affairs. for all these reasons, he is glad that the report has been rejected.
in writing. the concept of 'citizenship of the union', which does not even have the qualification of european, is a machine for destroying our national rights to identity and sovereignty. the catania report provides the proof of this, which seeks to impose a vast set of rules in which the french, the poles, the spanish, the italians, the germans and the british will have disappeared, replaced by 'citizens of the union' enjoying the same political rights. article 17 of the report, which calls on the member states to grant the right to vote and stand as a candidate in national elections to any resident 'citizen of the union', 'without distinction as to nationality', would allow a czech resident in france to take part in the election of the president of the republic. this right to vote would even be extended to non-european immigrants, since article 18 proposes to 'extend to nationals of third countries residing in the european union the rights of citizens of the union'. the peoples of europe, threatened with being overwhelmed by a global immigration, need not european citizenship but the reaffirmation of their national rights. the french in particular are increasingly demanding a reform of the nationality code based on the principle that "being french is inherited or deserved".
in writing. while europe is going through a crisis of both representation, which has been manifested in particular by the french and dutch rejection of the european constitution, and of democratic participation, with a growing generalization of abstention from european elections, it has not ceased, year after year, and this since the maastricht treaty of 1992, to try to force us to swallow the pill of european citizenship. once again, this is a machine for crushing nations and national identities to replace them with a european identity. this new 'package', which has come straight from the bureaucratic upper echelons of the euro-federalists, is fully involved in the process of submersion and immigration-invasion desired by the commission. the right of every citizen to move and reside freely within the territory of the member states is conceived as the central right of european citizenship. the efforts of brussels to simplify and relax the conditions for entry and residence on european territory are therefore understandable, since they are a condition for the acquisition of this new citizenship. the dictatorship of the ready-to-think is under way by the systematic destruction of national values and identities. it is true that it takes courage today to display and defend a national conscience!
in writing. trafficking in women and the sexual exploitation of children are increasingly becoming a major parallel economy in europe. according to the un, nearly 4 million women and children are reported to have been abused or raped. the inevitable diversification of the forms of trafficking in human beings is also taking place. increased sex tourism and demands for children for economic exploitation (beggars, pickpockets, dealers, black-market labour, etc.), all forms of crime and exploitation which are, in most cases, the work of organised criminal groups. because of the dangerous schengen agreements which have removed all controls at the union's borders, they are used as drug smugglers or thieves. in addition, if the authorities arrest these minors, they will be exempt from prosecution. to claim to be acting to prevent all forms of trafficking in human beings is to attack these mafias, these illegal traffickers who are constantly expanding in a europe open to all the four winds. the addition of community programmes in this field and the pious wishes of the many ngos will do nothing. only if the people and our elites wake up to the ultra-liberal and pro-immigration policy of brussels can we hope to have a sense of security in europe.
in writing. worldwide, the number of women and children trafficked is estimated to be between 700 000 and 4 million per year. according to the un, 1.2 million of them are children. my colleague's report starts with a dramatic observation: despite the measures taken so far by the member states and even by europe, human trafficking is now considered to be the fastest growing criminal activity compared to other forms of organised crime. and unfortunately, the accumulation of community texts, resolutions or numerous reports by ngos on this global phenomenon will not put an end to it. the causes are identified: poverty, social exclusion, unemployment, lack of border controls, which allows the development of clandestine channels of organized crime of all kinds, violence against women, education, the explosion of pornography or the disappearance of moral standards, but the solutions proposed in this report are very vague, general and partial. the first step in the effective fight against all this organised trafficking in human beings is to re-establish controls at the internal borders of the member states. their abolition with the schengen agreements was one of the reasons for the development of this whole sex industry in europe.

the rapporteur. madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the european union is faced today with the need to reform its sugar sector. we all know that this reform is unavoidable. it responds to the concern to bring the common organization of the sugar market into line with the principles guiding the new common agricultural policy. it also responds to the need to adapt to changes in the rules of world trade. however, we must not lose sight of the consequences of the coming changes for the women and men who live off the sugar production in the fields and in the factories of the community and in the developing countries. in this context, it is important that the adjustment of the european sugar sector does not result in the dismantling of our sugar com, in the gradual abandonment of our production capacity, in the sacrifice of our producers and those of the poorest countries, caused by an uncontrolled opening up of world trade. the reform is certainly indispensable, but it can only achieve its objectives if the search for efficiency is carried out in compliance with the requirements of social justice. this double perspective, which is a source of balance, is the guiding principle behind the three reports on which the european parliament is called upon to give its opinion this week and which were voted on almost unanimously by the committee on agriculture and rural development on 29 november. these texts are the result of several months of discussions and hearings in the committee on agriculture, of exchanges of views with you, madam commissioner, and with your services, as well as with the various parties concerned at the professional level. they reflect a compromise, negotiated and approved by a large majority of the political groups in this parliament. this compromise is based on four main points. the first is the introduction of flexible sugar market regulation. flexibility, therefore, through the gradual introduction of a market logic in the sector: it is the reference price, the source of greater competitiveness in the sector. but also regulation, to avoid the disastrous consequences of a fully liberalised sugar market. internally, this means that the intervention system will be maintained temporarily in order to guarantee market stability during the next four years, which we all know will be economically difficult. on the external side of the reform, the concern for regulation is to maintain control of sugar imports from the least developed countries. it is essential today to take account of the damage caused by uncontrolled opening up of trade, as the recent example of the western balkans has shown us. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the health of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work is based on the principle of equal treatment for men and women. this mechanism would help to combat destructive triangular trade, while ensuring that the least developed countries have their local populations working in the sugar sector benefiting from the preferential trade regime with the european union. without any impact on the prospects for the development of sugar production in the least developed countries, the mechanism is fully in line with the objectives of the 'everything but arms' initiative. the second major aspect of the compromise which parliament is voting on is the implementation of european solidarity, particularly in relation to the most fragile regions. while the introduction of trade regulation is a means of stabilising markets and avoiding too abrupt price fluctuations in the future, it must be accompanied by measures to cushion the impact of the reform on the populations most affected by the cessation of activity, in particular the most vulnerable populations. i would mention farmers first of all, for the loss of income suffered by them must be substantially compensated and part of the aid provided for in the restructuring scheme must compensate those who lose their right to supply and are obliged to make new investments to convert to other crops. then there are the sugar factory workers. these are totally dependent on the forthcoming restructuring of the sector and must be taken into account in the event of industrial closure by strengthening the conditions which manufacturers will have to fulfil in order to have access to the aid provided for by the restructuring fund. finally, to avoid the most fragile regions being the main victims of the restructuring of community production, it is essential that the member states retain the last word as regards the cessation or maintenance of production on their territory. it is also essential to take due account of the specific situations and constraints of the outermost regions in an appropriate manner. the cultivation and exploitation of sugar cane occupies a fundamental and irreplaceable place in the economy, society and culture of the country. in this connection, madam commissioner, i would like to thank you for the quality of your listening and for the efforts you have made to ensure special treatment for these regions, particularly in terms of compensation and flow aid. i am convinced that the measures requested by the members of parliament will enable the sugar cane industry in these regions to look to the future with greater confidence. the third axis of the reform concerns the future of the sector through the development of alternative outlets. in a world context marked by rising oil prices and the need to combat greenhouse gases, the production of alcohol in the sugar sector represents an important asset in terms of the development of alternative energy sources. the committee on agriculture and rural development therefore proposes that these developments be anticipated by means of a voluntary public policy, focusing on both the agricultural and industrial sectors: agricultural by measures improving access to aid for energy crops, industrial by adapting the restructuring scheme to allow the creation of bioethanol distilleries. these tools are the components of a coherent legislative framework that would encourage the development of the bioethanol sector, a source of opportunities for farmers and industrialists in the sector. finally, the fourth and last major focus of our work, but not the least: prices. in contrast to the commission's initial proposals, which were drastic for the sector, for the rural fabric and for the developing countries, the committee on agriculture finally decided to reduce sugar prices by 30% in four years, but at a slower and more moderate pace. this level of price reduction would ensure the economic effectiveness of the reform, while helping to mitigate its impact on the industry. in doing so, it would ensure a better maintenance of activity in the production regions and the safeguarding of hundreds of thousands of direct and indirect jobs. this moderation also meets europe's commitments in terms of development, by allowing the acp countries and the least developed countries which export part of their production to the union to maintain profitable prices. at the end of november, in preparation for the world trade organisation conference in hong kong and without waiting for the final vote of parliament, the agriculture ministers of the 25 member states reached an informal and provisional compromise on the broad lines of the future reform. if this agreement was indeed intended to establish a common political line, the fact remains that the media exploitation of it by the various signatories in the sense of an early conclusion of the reform is unambiguous: it reflects, it seems to me, the will of the commission and the council to ignore the european parliament, whose prior opinion is obligatory before any decision is taken. in this sense, i find the procedure totally unacceptable and must be strongly condemned. in any event, this compromise is now on the table and, although it does not follow the amendments proposed by the committee on agriculture to the letter, it is clear that, as it stands, it confirms in a remarkable way the council's rejection of the measures originally proposed. the compromise on the four main lines i have just mentioned marks a significant shift towards the more moderate and balanced measures proposed by the committee on agriculture and rural development. in terms of regulation, it takes up the idea of maintaining the intervention system for four years before switching to a reference price, marking the introduction of market logic in the sugar cmo. secondly and most importantly, it confirms the correctness of the parliamentarians' analysis of the need to maintain a certain capacity to manage the supply of sugar on the community market. while the measures proposed are different, their philosophies converge in the direction of adapting the 'everything but arms' initiative. as regards the implementation of european solidarity, the council endorsed the increase in the aid for farmers, proposing a compensation of 64.2% for income losses, instead of the 60% originally proposed. it also adopted the idea of transferring part of the restructuring aid to farmers, up to 10% of the planned amounts. the proposal by the members for partial coupling and modulation of aid for lessfavoured regions was not accepted. as regards the third axis, alternative outlets, the agriculture ministers of the 25 member states confirmed the possibility of partial dismantling of plants to enable bioethanol distilleries to be developed. the financial incentives for the development of energy crops are also not being met. finally, in the field of prices, the 36% reduction in four years envisaged by the council is less rapid and less drastic than the initial proposals and is in line with the work of the european parliament's committee on agriculture. despite these undisputed and welcome progress, several proposals were not adopted, particularly as regards the tightening of the conditions to be met by manufacturers to qualify for restructuring aid. it is particularly regrettable that the council has so far neglected all the social criteria to be respected, as well as the power given to the member states in the end to validate or not any abandonment of production. moreover, even if this means going beyond the strict framework of this debate and my reports, i must express my indignation at the treatment of the acp countries. in the face of reform, and in particular a price cut with disastrous consequences for many of them, the sum of 40 million euros granted by the council for 2006 can only be seen as a ridiculous and offensive charity. the european union must urgently find the resources to remedy this situation, which is contrary to the repeated statements by heads of state and government in favour of the development of the poorest countries. it is clear, ladies and gentlemen, that the efforts of the agriculture ministers will have to be continued in the negotiations in february in order to reach a final agreement acceptable to all. in this context, i hope that parliament will vote with the largest possible majority in favour of the three reports before it, in order to send a strong signal to the members of the council that the remaining gaps in the november interim compromise must be filled in the direction of a reform of the sugar com that is both fair and effective.

for the greens/efa group mr president, commissioner, i thank charles tannock, who has taken over the task, for his availability and his attention to the very complex issues involved in defining the neighbourhood policy. the neighbourhood policy has been imposed on us with the arrival of new member states and has become, by integrating all the countries bordering the east around the mediterranean, one of the key elements and one of the strong points of the union's external policy. the union has taken on a great responsibility in this action and it will have the heavy task of not disappointing the hope aroused in our neighbours. a new dynamic has been created in these countries, which are now waiting for the union to support them in the process of democratization, stabilisation and sustainable development they have embarked upon. for some countries it is even a prerequisite for future membership. so we must avoid a number of pitfalls if we are to make this neighbourhood policy a success. it must incorporate a multilateral dimension and provide an institutional framework in which partner countries are fully involved in the definition of european policies. it must not be limited to a simple free trade area but must be based on a genuine sharing of common values, democracy and human rights. the neighbourhood policy must work towards consolidating civil society by creating a civil forum where ngos will follow action plans which will not be cooperation plans, commissioner, but concrete and effective plans, with a union determined to monitor them and implement them according to specific criteria. it is with great pride, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, that i will support the action plans for the countries of the south caucasus, because if armenia, azerbaijan and georgia are part of this neighbourhood policy, it is thanks to our european parliament and not to the commission and the council! mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i welcome this resolution on the neighbourhood policy. it provides a comprehensive review of all the priorities set by our institution for this policy: human rights, democracy, immigration, the environment and trade liberalisation. yet one vital area is totally missing. it is about development cooperation. let me remind you that of the 17 countries covered by the neighbourhood policy, 12 are developing countries, a third of which are low-income countries. with the reform of the external action instruments under way, these 12 developing countries will not be covered by the future instrument for cooperation and development. the result is that if no development policy is undertaken under the neighbourhood policy, these 12 countries will no longer receive development assistance from us. but i regret that in a political guideline text as general and extensive as this one there is no reference to cooperation. it is not reasonable to talk about increasing the prosperity of an area without, at the same time, committing to eradicating poverty. are the basic needs of the people of azerbaijan, moldova or palestine being met at the moment? how can these countries fight dictatorship and compete in market economies when a part of the population does not even have access to clean water, social services, health care or basic education? how can we ever hope to achieve the millennium development goals if we are not able to tackle this poverty at the doorstep of europe? i think that adopting a resolution on the neighbourhood policy which so completely ignores the objectives of eradicating poverty is a serious error of judgement which unfortunately places a responsibility on us for the future.

the agenda calls for the report by jacques toubon, on behalf of the committee on the internal market and consumer protection, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive laying down the rules on nominal quantities for prepackaged products, repealing council directives 75/106/eec and 80/232/eec, and amending council directive 76/211/eec (com (2004) 0708 c6 0160/2004 2004/0248 (cod)) (a6-0412/2005).
vice-president of the commission. mr president, the proposed directive on pre-packaging seems to be a very technical dossier. however, in reality, it is part of the major policy initiative strongly supported by our institutions on better regulation and simplification. there is community legislation on pre-packaging, but the current legal situation is neither satisfactory nor clear. in the european union, we have a stable legal framework for wine and spirits, where, throughout the community, products are sold in agreed quantities. for around 70 other products, current legislation has introduced voluntary harmonisation to which member states have adopted different approaches. member states such as belgium or the netherlands have deregulated package sizes altogether. in other countries, for instance sweden, community legislation on package sizes has been made optional for manufacturers. other member states have made regulation mandatory but only for home producers. some national rules are entirely based on the existing optional community directives, but in other countries, such as germany, national rules are different from community provisions. from a legal point of view, the situation is therefore quite confusing, to put it mildly. at the same time, products freely move from one country to another and consumers find a wealth of products on the market. until now, no consumer has ever complained that there was an excess of choice. the proposal of the commission intends to simplify the legal situation whilst leaving the benefit of free choice to consumers. the commission is proposing a single legal framework to be implemented throughout the union by all member states. in substance, the commission proposes to leave the free choice that consumers currently enjoy and to regulate package sizes only for a very limited number of sectors, in particular wines and spirits. the commission notes that the committee on the internal market and consumer protection endorses this approach in principle. however, we have different views on the number of sectors that should become subject to the community regulation fixing nominal quantities. as far as the commission is concerned, and based on a wide consultation of consumers in all member states and european trade federations, only the wine and spirits sectors should be regulated. however, on the basis of a prior commitment to parliament, the commission has also included in its proposal the regulation for soluble coffee and white sugar. whilst supporting the overall approach, the committee on the internal market and consumer protection suggests that additional sectors should become subject to regulation, including drinking milk, butter, roasted coffee, dried pasta, rice and brown sugar. the commission questions the justification for regulation in these sectors. european industry, with the exception of the coffee sector, is not in favour and consumers have not requested regulation that limits their choice. the proposed amendment would imply that a number of products that are placed on the market today would disappear. furthermore, it would also mean that member states that never had regulation or had abolished it would have to re-introduce regulation on package sizes. this is contrary to the political aims of better regulation and simplification and does not protect consumers. the commission appreciates that the parliament has carried out an impact assessment of these amendments. this initiative reflects the commission’s common concern for better regulation and simplification. to conclude, in the commission’s opinion, consumer protection today should not be based on limiting consumer choice, but should concentrate on providing correct information to consumers and on the prohibition of misleading practices, allowing consumers to make a well-informed and deliberate choice. it is fair to say that the commission, as well as the european court of justice, takes as the benchmark the average consumer, reasonably well-informed and reasonably observant and circumspect. vulnerable consumers do not become less vulnerable with rules on nominal quantities, but by better implemented existing community law on consumer protection, such as labelling and the prohibition of deceptive packaging. the commission is working with national authorities towards the better implementation of these community rules in order to effectively improve the protection of vulnerable consumers.
the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the report i am presenting on behalf of the committee on the internal market and consumer protection has made a major change to the commission's proposal. it was adopted by 28 votes to none. i propose to accept the liberalization of formats, which is the solution chosen by the commission to take account of the case law in the ruwet cider case. the commission also proposes to maintain mandatory ranges in certain specific sectors: wines, spirits, soluble coffee and white sugar. the commission is asking for this derogation to be limited to 20 years. the members of the committee on the internal market immediately questioned the relevance of the proposal and the quality of the impact study on which it is based. i have therefore proposed that other commodities should be subject to mandatory ranges. these are coffee, butter, rice, pasta and milk. the ranges i propose have quite wide ranges, not to mention that below the smallest size and above the largest, there is total freedom. i also propose that the system be reviewed in eight years, not in 20 years as the commission proposes. why this proposal from the committee on the internal market? firstly, to protect consumers who are far from having fully understood the unit price established in 1998, especially the most vulnerable among them, such as the elderly and the visually impaired. secondly, to take account of the independent impact study commissioned by our committee which confirmed that liberalization entailed risks for the consumer and would not lead to more competition between producers and distributors. finally, because better regulation does not mean no regulation at all. lacordaire said in the 1830s: between the weak and the strong, it is freedom that oppresses and it is the law that protects. you can see that this text, in its seemingly insignificant and technical aspect, allows us to ask important questions. in conclusion, i would like to emphasize three elements: an impact study commissioned by parliament itself and independent of the commission and lobby groups, a first; a concept of 'better lawmaking' inspired by the sole interest of our fellow citizens and not by an ideological attitude; the concern to stick to national cultures because our people are very attached to their food traditions and their consumption habits.

mr president, on 20 october 2005, the general conference of unesco adopted the convention on cultural diversity by 148 votes to 2, with 4 abstentions. this convention recognises the specific nature of cultural activities, goods and services which can under no circumstances be regarded as mere commodities. article 20 of the convention stresses that states take the convention into account when they enter into other international obligations, for example agreements concluded within the framework of the world trade organisation. the convention must be ratified by 30 states before it can enter into force. to date, canada is the only country to have done so. the european union, represented by its commission, played a major role in the adoption of the convention. should not our president and the president of our committee on culture and education send a letter to the council and to all the heads of state and government to ratify this agreement?

madam president, we are all in favour of protecting farm chickens from the barbarism of factory farming. here i have repeatedly denounced the shame of factory farms, where up to 80 million male chicks have been burned alive to heat the farm. i denounced the electric stunning of the chicken, which is not actually stunned so much that it is immersed alive in hot water: it is boiled to plume it! so we need rules, we all agree. but when european farmers read the directive, what do they see? the farmed chicken shall be subject to two medical examinations per day by a veterinarian who shall be within 3 metres of the chicken; the chickens shall be illuminated by a non-flashing light of 50 lux, 20 lux, 100 lux, not known, measured at eye level; the indoor temperature of the farm shall not exceed the outdoor temperature measured in the shade by 3 degrees; the litter of the chicken shall be 5 centimetres; a certificate as a chicken farmer, a certificate as a caster of chicks less than 10 days old is required; the footpads must be examined and the concentration of chickens limited to a density of 28, 30, 35 or 42 kilograms per square metre, without specifying whether this is a kilogram of live weight or metabolic weight. meanwhile, thousands of chickens are being slaughtered in nigeria, and avian influenza is going to wipe out 1.1 billion african chickens. all this because the 800 million euros that would have enabled each african chicken to be given the two necessary vaccines at a cost of 40 cents a dose have not been found. i could also do dark humor. in the face of this extravagance of precautions for the white chicken while black children die of leprosy, aids and tuberculosis, the little african will finally say: i, when i grow up, will not be a fireman, i will be a farm chicken in europe! in the meantime, our breton farms, for example, are being moved to brazil, the world's leading poultry producer, where not only the chicken is not protected, but the children are not protected either. these are treated like slaves to keep brazilian farms running, not to mention banana plantations, where eight-year-olds sleep exhausted on cardboard boxes and are exposed to pesticides that give them balance disorders, all for two dollars a day! so, each one has his own hierarchy. some people choose white chickens, i choose african children, asian children. this is what the unreasonable leads to when we try to make an angel, and with this directive we are making the beast!

on behalf of the pse group. mr president, i would like to thank our rapporteur, mr gunnar hökmark, and all our colleagues. it is a non-legislative report and i think the committee on economic and monetary affairs has done a good job of making a strong position of the european parliament known. we have come to a fairly clear view of things on the whole. i am one of those who think, with the pse group, that it is indeed necessary to review the state aid system. it is more than ever at the heart of the commission's powers, since europe remains essentially a europe of the internal market and competition until further notice. i am not sure that the 'no' vote in the french referendum will give us any other prospects for a long time to come. we are therefore truly at the heart of community competence and it is true that with the enlargement of europe, the european union and the commission are threatened with thrombosis if the system and the system of state aid are left in their present configuration. parliament first insisted that the internal market and competition should not be seen as representing the whole of european society. we are not just a market company; there must also be room for public action, whenever the market is failing, as the texts say, but also whenever we need to reduce social or territorial inequalities, manage externalities, promote innovation and possibly provide industrial impetus. we sometimes find ourselves in certain liberal slides asking ourselves: would we be able to make an airbus today or would we be able to make an ariane, given the prevailing ideology? for the greens/efa group mr president, the clause we are discussing today is the basis and the legitimacy of the european union's action with third countries in respect of human rights. the agnoletto report makes important proposals which, as you can see, have a very high degree of consensus in this parliament. this clause is flawed. first, there is a lack of uniformity. the wording of this clause may vary from one type of agreement to another. i would like to join the rapporteur in calling for an improved clause to strengthen its political and legal significance. for example, it must be clearly established that the parties to such agreements are obliged to comply with international standards and the obligations arising therefrom. secondly, in the majority of cases, as has already been pointed out, this clause suffers from a lack of specific terms and practical applications. the european union, in order to be coherent, must establish such arrangements. we cannot hope to remain credible to our partners if, on the one hand, we claim to want to make respect for human rights an essential element of our policy, but on the other hand we fail to take the necessary measures when these countries systematically violate these same rights. at present, the acp agreements are probably the most advanced model of this, so we must draw inspiration from them. the mechanisms for implementing the clause must also be graduated. we cannot only regard them as instruments for reprimanding human rights violations, but also as means of contributing to the strengthening of human rights in third countries. this is the importance of the positive approach to the human rights clause. as regards the role of parliament, in order to ensure the coherence, credibility and transparency of our policy, it is essential that parliament is involved in the various stages of implementation of the clause. when parliament in its resolutions refers to the clause, calls for appropriate measures to be taken, the council should act on this request and consider whether it is appropriate to do so. the second essential point is the link between the clause and the structures of political dialogue. the link between this clause and the creation of subcommittees on human rights must be made clear, and these subcommittees should also be strengthened. i regret the downward revision of the european union's requirements in this respect, particularly with regard to certain neighbouring countries. if we hope to implement this clause effectively, we must create the necessary spaces for a frank and constructive exchange on human rights. as regards the principle of reciprocity, this dialogue must also be reciprocal at the very moment when a number of member states are being accused of their policies in the fight against terrorism, for example, or of the inhumane conditions in prisons. we must be able to listen to the criticisms that our partners might make. finally, it is important that human rights should not be a concern of our foreign ministers alone but of all government bodies. for this reason, i support the rapporteur's call for a 'essential element' clause in all agreements and, in conclusion, for parliament to no longer give its assent to new agreements which do not contain a clause on human rights and democracy.

the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. mr president, as far back as 1957, the six founding countries of the european economic community had committed themselves to the creation of a single market in which people, goods, capital and services would move freely. almost 50 years later, the only thing that has not yet been implemented is the free movement of services. the proposal for a services directive, which is part of the process of economic reforms launched by the lisbon european council to make europe the most competitive and dynamic knowledge-based economy in the world by 2010, constitutes, as proposed today, a major political advance for the european union. for eighteen months the european parliament has been working to rewrite the commission's original proposal to a profoundly altered version. it is a balanced version of the treaty, which seeks to reconcile economic efficiency by opening up the services market with social justice by preserving the social acquis which protects the citizens of the union. this version also recognises the specific nature of certain services, in particular cultural and audiovisual services. these services have an identity and value and, in this sense, cannot be considered as consumer goods or market services like others. in addition, audiovisual services are already the subject of a sectoral approach at community level through the 'television without frontiers' directive. the latter fulfils the objectives of the services directive, namely to guarantee the freedom to provide services while allowing the pursuit of other objectives such as the promotion of european content, respect for cultural diversity and the promotion of programme pluralism. in view of these principles, the committee on culture and education, followed by the committee on the internal market and consumer protection, voted by a large majority in favour of inserting a cultural reserve clause and excluding audiovisual services from the scope of the directive. it is essential that the 'television without frontiers' directive, which is currently being revised, remains the only reference text in this field. but a directive on services is also needed to enable a genuine internal market for services to be achieved within the european union. in conclusion, i would like to congratulate evelyne gebhardt on the quality of her report, but also malcolm harbour, marianne thyssen, jacques toubon and othmar karas who have worked mr president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all, as a new member of parliament, i should like to say that during this debate, now eighteen months into it, i have discovered the richness and quality of the work that is being done here. i would like to pay tribute to our committee on the internal market and consumer protection, its late chairman, phillip whitehead, its rapporteur, evelyne gebhardt, and the rapporteur for the committee on employment and social affairs, anne van lancker. i would like to thank the leaders of our group, to whose work we owe the project we are discussing today: malcolm harbour, fictitious rapporteur and coordinator of our group; marianne thyssen, our vice-chair; and our tireless secretariat. i also welcome the work of marie-hélène descamps and roselyne bachelot, members of the french delegation. thanks to all of them, we have achieved a considerable result: the compromise is a new text. it first established the internal market in services. this project takes away from the court of justice the de facto monopoly it has had for 50 years on the implementation of the principles of the treaties. the internal market in services is based on mutual trust and involves cooperation and administrative simplification, the abolition of protectionist barriers, both for the establishment of service companies and for temporary provision. it applies to services of general economic interest for the sole purpose of freedom of establishment, while excluding many essential services such as audiovisual and cinema, games, health, legal professions. the compromise therefore proposes that parliament should vote on a framework law geared to economic growth, innovation and employment, which is what the people of europe want. but compromise also brings us respect for our model and our collective national preferences. will the directive lead to the dismantling of our social acquis? is it going to cause a leveling at the bottom? the commission's original proposal was undeniably risky. that's why we refused it! but the compromise proposed to you is a barrier to social dumping, is based on subsidiarity, implements the freedom to provide services in a pragmatic and limited way. the compromise explicitly excludes social and labour law. social competition is prohibited. in the area of freedom of establishment, many national regulations are respected. and freedom to provide services goes hand in hand with the guarantee for member states to be able to apply their national rules when the public interest so requires. it is a compromise, and it is being criticized on both sides, which shows that we are in the middle. i therefore hope, on behalf of my french colleagues, that you will support it by voting for it by a very large majority. it would be a victory for the european parliament, it would be a victory for the european union.
mr president, commissioner, mr president-in-office, completing the internal market is one thing, it is a goal we share. the dismantling of the european social model is another and we are fighting against it. we are fighting it because it is contrary to the interests of the citizens, the workers and the european consumers, but also because it jeopardises the citizens' commitment to the european project. the original bolkestein proposal for a directive was deeply rejected because it sought to base the completion of the internal market on the weakening of social rights, environmental standards and consumer protection which had reached a higher level in some of the member states than in others. by seeking to base the internal market no longer on competition between firms but on competition between the social systems of the various member states, the bolkestein proposal gave the impression of playing the interests of the member states against each other. it has created a state of distrust between old and new members, which is contrary to the european commission's mission of uniting all europeans around a common project. by including many social services and part of the economic services of general interest in the scope of the directive, the commission has sought to subject activities essential to social cohesion to the logic of competition and the market alone. with the country of origin principle, it has turned its back on the community method of sectoral harmonization; the commission has always tried to bring the provisions in force in the member states closer together, thus seeking to promote mutual recognition and economic integration without jeopardizing the european social model and - i repeat - the sometimes higher level of protection achieved in certain countries. it was about tuning up. with this draft, for the first time, the european commission has proposed legislation which, on the contrary, encourages the disparity of national rights and gives a premium to the least demanding states. the commission is not the originator of the original proposal. it has a responsibility, however: after having recognised that this text was badly designed, badly put together - member of the commission. mr president, the commission was asked last week by the european parliament to make a statement on innovative sources of financing for development cooperation. commissioner responsibilities towards its partner countries. quite the contrary: the european council of june 2005 forcefully restated its support for the millennium development goals with ambitious commitments on both the quality and the quantity of aid. in particular, the european council has committed itself to increasing official development assistance with the aim of achieving a target of 0.7% of gross national income in 2015. to that end, a collective target of 0.56% of gni has been fixed for 2010. however, more aid will not be enough. we need to ensure that current and promised increases in financing are provided in ways which actually help countries meet their commitments to achieve the millennium development goals. in the recently approved joint statement by the council, the european parliament and the commission on the european consensus for development, the european union commits itself to the more predictable and less volatile aid mechanisms. the commission believes that innovative mechanisms for financing development have a useful role to play. for this reason during 2005, at the request of the council, the commission produced a series of staff working papers providing technical analysis of innovative sources of financing for development. in addition, in april 2005, the commission adopted a communication to the council and the european parliament, ‘accelerating progress towards attaining the millennium development goals – financing for development and aid effectiveness’. amongst other things, this communication discussed innovative sources of financing and new delivery aid mechanisms and invited the council to ‘agree to accelerate work on the most promising options for innovative additional sources of finance’. the commission noted that any innovative sources of financing must be assessed in light of a number of criteria. for example: how much would each proposal raise? to what extent would the funds be additional to existing commitments? how stable and predictable would they be? what are the competitiveness and sectoral impacts? what would the launch and administration costs be? which proposals can go forward fastest? is universal support required or can proposals be implemented at regional – that is eu – level? the commission notes france’s readiness to start implementation of one of the proposals emerging from that debate, namely, the imposition of a solidarity contribution on all air tickets sold in france as of july 2006. this initiative may have a positive effect on other countries’ readiness to carry forward initiatives in the area of financing for development. the commission would also like to inform the european parliament that, to support the debate and preserve the momentum on these issues, a technical workshop between the commission and member state representatives was held on 9 february 2006. the workshop touched upon the existing initiatives, as well as possible alternatives with respect to innovative financing. the commission, however, also looked at ways in which existing aid arrangements could be modified and complemented so as to deliver resources in more predictable ways. finally, the commission would like to note that, during the workshop, the french representatives gave an update on the high-level conference to be held in paris on 28 february and 1 march. reaction will be based on this mission’s report. in terms of the european union’s response, you are well aware of the unequivocal message that the european union conveyed to belarus and reiterated in the general affairs and external relations council of 30 january: the european union has stressed the importance it attaches to a democratic election process and has also clearly voiced its resolve to issue targeted sanctions in the event that these elections prove to be fraudulent. to balance this message with a positive note, the european union has repeated its offer to have closer relations with belarus, provided that we see convincing progress towards democracy. let me now turn to the commission’s specific action and underline that the commission has made good on its pledge to raise its role in belarus. faced with growing repression and restrictions by the government of belarus on foreign assistance to non-governmental bodies, the commission has stepped up and speeded up such assistance to belarus. in 2005 alone, up to eur 8.9 million have been dedicated to democracy and civil society projects. creative tools have been developed to overcome the hurdles to assistance delivery. we have thus shifted part of our support to ngos located outside belarus. the eur 2.2 million we granted last december to the european humanitarian university in exile, as well as our support to independent media, are vibrant examples of this novel approach. in the field of independent media, i am delighted to say that the commission has been at the forefront of donors’ action. we have started with support to the radio broadcasting of daily news reports to belarus in both russian and belarusian. however, our main achievement is a eur 2 million media project which is now being launched. it includes radio and television broadcasting, internet activities, support to the belarusian independent press, and the training of belarusian journalists. the project will allow the broadcasting of specific tv and radio programmes as from february, well ahead of the elections. we believe this high-quality project, which is supported by a europe-wide team and sharply factors in belarusian sensitivities – that is, no propaganda, straight news and sheer entertainment – will rightly reach out to large segments of the population. in addition, the commission has decided to open a delegation in minsk but unfortunately the belarusian authorities have not yet given their agreement. pending progress on this front, we will post a chargé d’affaires to kiev who will travel frequently to minsk. finally, last monday the commission brought together all international donors to belarus in order to plan ahead. this meeting has set in motion a common reflection on assistance beyond the election date. this meeting was a signal that assistance and coordination will not dwindle after the election date. in conclusion, let me emphasise that the democratic process in belarus is likely to be a long process that will eventually succeed only with the support of the population. this is why we must continue our efforts to raise awareness among the belarusian population at large through support to civil society and facilitation of contacts between the people. as belarus stands at the crossroads, it is more crucial than ever that we all pool our efforts to implement a common strategy and be ready to react to developments in belarus as they take place. the commission remains committed to doing its part.

member of the commission. mr president, i have been greatly encouraged by the very engaged and highly interesting debate on this important issue, and i should like now to refer to some of the questions that have been raised during our discussion. on vertical integration in the commission, two main points must be noted. firstly, the commission has very recently set up a new unit in its directorate-general for agriculture and rural development with a much stronger focus on forestry. this unit is presently coordinating the preparatory work on the eu forest action plan and chairs the meetings of the interservice group on forestry. secondly, the interservice group on forestry, which was established in 2002 to facilitate cooperation and coordination of forestry-related work between relevant commission services, has proved to be an effective tool of coordination and is working very satisfactorily. its membership has increased and now comprises 11 commission services. it is very actively involved in the preparation of the action plan and will have a very important role in its implementation. regarding the legal basis, several legal studies have been carried out in the member states concerning the creation of a separate legal basis for forestry in the treaties. in our opinion, unless the position of the member states changes, the added value of further legal studies on this issue is questionable. regarding the concerns raised about the establishment of a european forest observatory, i believe that this should be discussed primarily among the member states, which have the main responsibility for our forestry policy. they can assess the added value of such an initiative in the light of the current structures and existing international institutions. i am aware of the importance of the problem of forest fires in the european union and the need to continue to prevent these situations from arising. i had the opportunity to see the horrible consequences of these forest fires last year during a visit to portugal. the current rural development regulation provides support to the member states for important forest fire prevention measures, such as fire breaks, water points and preventive sylviculture, as well as for the restoration of the forestry production potential in forests that have been damaged by fires. i should like to indicate that these actions will be continued during the period 2007–2013 under the new rural development regulation, and member states will, therefore, have the possibility to include forest fire prevention measures in their rural development programmes. the rural development measures will be complemented by the actions that will be undertaken under the life+ programme for the next financial period. in this respect, following an initiative of the european parliament, the commission will launch a study to examine the main causes of forest deterioration in europe, including forest fires, and the efficiency of the current measures, as well as possible future options to improve the situation. quite a few honourable members mentioned state-owned forests. it is clear that the main objective for rural development is to revitalise rural areas and not to finance public authorities’ activities. this is why the main target group of beneficiaries of the rural development measures related to forestry is the private sector, notably farmers, foresters and, under axis 3 in the rural development policy, the broader rural society. however, there are derogations concerning the exclusion of state-owned forests from support under the new rural development regulation in order to take into account the specific situations of certain regions and the characteristics of particular measures. finally, i shall make two comments on the content of the action plan. firstly, the action plan will be designed in accordance with the key principles of the european union forestry strategy. the main responsibility for forest policy lies with the member states, and actions at community level will continue to be based on the principle of subsidiarity. our intention is to concentrate community actions on those areas where there is a clear added value. the second point is that the action plan will also identify community instruments that can be used by the member states for the implementation of the proposed actions, for instance, the new rural development regulation, the life+ instrument or – as was also mentioned here – the seventh research framework programme. in this respect, the action plan will strengthen the overall visibility of forestry and increase the complementarity of different community actions in support of sustainable forest management. concerning the specific proposals in the report, the commission welcomes the recommendations contained in paragraphs 1, 4, 7, 11, 12, 14, 19, 20, 21, 24, 26 and 29. there are a number of recommendations, notably paragraphs 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 15, 16, 17, 18, 22, 23 and 30, which are addressed also to the member states, and the commission will discuss these specific proposals with the member states when we elaborate further on the action plan. the commission has also taken good note of recommendation 9, and we will look into it: coordination is certainly an issue to be addressed. finally, there are a number of recommendations, such as 2, 13, 15, 25, 27, 28, 30 and 32, which will go beyond the key principle of the european forest strategy or may not be completely in line with the regulations already adopted. once again, i thank you for an extremely interesting and very good report and also for this engaged discussion, which has been very supportive. in writing. i voted in favour, at first reading, of the proposal for a directive on services in the internal market as rewritten by the european parliament on the basis of the compromise negotiated between the european people's party (epp) and the european socialist party (pse). i welcome the considerable work done by malcolm harbour who has followed the file for the european people's party (epp) with my friend jacques toubon. it was urgent to legislate so as not to leave it to the judges of the european court of justice to "say the law" on the 4th fundamental freedom of the union relating to services. the compromise provides a framework to support the competitiveness and development of service activities, which account for 70% of gdp and have a high potential for growth and job creation, while combating the risks of social dumping. jacques chirac, president of the french republic, was right to oppose the first text presented in january 2004 by the prodi commission and the european parliament has done its duty as a co-legislator. it is a victory for responsible democracy and a major step towards building a social market economy.
in writing. after more than a year of debate in committee and in the european public, the european parliament has today delivered its opinion on the services directive. in keeping with my convictions and the commitment i have made to the many citizens who have asked me about this directive, i voted initially in favour of its rejection with the entire french socialist delegation. the proposal was rejected (153 votes to 486). the french socialists had three basic demands: the exclusion of sgeis from the scope of the directive, explicit reference to the rule of the principle of the country of destination, reference to a framework directive on public services, and the introduction of a system of national rules on the free movement of goods. i therefore supported all the amendments aimed at reducing the scope of the text and clearly excluding public services and sectors vital to our social model, such as education, culture, health, etc. these amendments were also rejected. the epp-pse compromise does not meet my requirements for the preservation of our european social model, so in the final vote i voted against the text. i would also point out that the support for the amendment rejecting the text as amended was wider (215 votes) than the result of the first vote on withdrawal of the text suggested.
in writing. the text put to the vote was intended to make it possible to achieve a genuine internal market in services, while correcting a draft directive whose philosophy, based on competition in the social and tax legislation of the member states, would have dramatic consequences, by levelling down the various social models. the first of these objectives was achieved, but not the second. it is true that parliament has contributed to a major change in the line of the original text, by removing the principle of country of origin, by excluding gis from the scope of the directive or by protecting labour law. yet many shadows persist. the economic component of public services (sgeis) and social services remain under the direct threat of unacceptable social dumping. the legal vacuum created by the abolition of the ppo also presages a new situation in which the judges of the european court of justice will have the power to define social legislation, without any guarantee of the outcome or democratic control. for these important reasons, and although i welcome the progress made on this matter, i cannot endorse the final text submitted to parliament.
in writing. the services directive as adopted today remains unacceptable, because it is only a poor make-up of the original directive. the vast majority of craft activities remain subject to competition, whereas in my country this sector is the largest employer and creator of jobs. even if the overly explicit references to the country of origin principle have disappeared, there are still areas where this scandalous principle will apply, in whole or in part. the remaining ambiguities, shadow areas and inconsistencies will give the luxembourg court of justice the power to interpret the directive. however, it has always ruled in favour of those who considered that certain standards, especially social standards, constituted an intolerable barrier to competition. the commission will have a pretext to push downwards harmonisation in areas which are not within its competence, such as social protection and labour law. amended or not, i say no to the bolkestein directive, no to the aberrant principles underlying it, no to social and legal dumping, to free competition that is unfair and generates unemployment, no to the announced relocations, no to this eurocracy that refuses to take into account the opinion of the people, to continue to impose policies on them that they do not want.

in writing. the services directive, the infamous bolkestein directive, is a machine for producing unemployment. the french referendum on the european constitution had given the french people a glimpse of the plight of its ultra-liberal and job-destroying philosophy. today, after some alterations to the facade, the interior remains unchanged. the abolition of the concept of country of origin does not mean that the concept of freedom to provide services has disappeared. the whole thing is a farce to force through what the liberals, the conservatives and the left, all equally pro-european, have been cleverly concocting with their respective national governments for almost two years. whether it is the bolkestein directive, the services directive or the gebhardt report, all these texts, which are the subject of polemics and compromises drawn in extremis by the political groups in the european parliament, are the same and must be rejected forcefully. we are firmly against this ultra-liberal and anti-national vision of the internal market in services, whose sole purpose, under the guise of 'free and undistorted competition', is to destroy our craft industry and our small french businesses.
in writing. i voted against this text which, despite some progress in relation to mr bolkestein's proposal, poses serious threats to our social model. the principle of the country of origin is only formally abandoned and not actually abandoned. the legal vacuum of the text makes it enter through the back door - (application in fact of the rome convention and the principle of proximity) - and leaves to the court of justice the arbitrations which the legislator should assume, with the principle of the host country. services of general economic interest remain within the scope of the directive, which threatens public services that are already badly undermined in europe. the votes confirmed an ultra-liberal orientation. the member states are deprived of the means to regulate certain professions and to control effectively the application of directives such as the one on the posting of workers, a fragile barrier to social dumping. the european union needs an alternative project that includes upward harmonization of social, environmental and consumer protection rules and excludes public services that require a framework directive protecting the environment.
in writing. for the last 50 years, the freedom to provide crossborder services has been one of the four fundamental freedoms of the common market. this was confirmed by the court of justice in recognising a ppo, a principle of the country of origin. for the blind, the general agreement on trade in services, signed in marrakesh in april 1994, established, at the global level, a "mode no. 4 of service provision, in the form of cross-border provision of services, that is, temporary immigration to the social dumping conditions of the country of origin. this is the old principle that european leaders are pretending to discover, while this ppo has been devastating european economies for decades. the french social model, with its pensions, health insurance, free schools, post offices, trains and hospitals, must not only be rejected if workers are to be paid the lowest possible wage in the most socially backward countries, but also the idea of a market without customs protection, which is the real cause of social dumping, of which the ppo rule is only a symptom. the starting point of the social cancer, the first mad cell, is the idea of the single market without the tariff locks. the country of origin rule is just a metastasis.
in writing. i voted in favour of the excellent report by my colleague mairead mcguiness on the proposal for a council decision on the strategic guidelines for rural development for the period 2007-2013. in the context of the reform of the common agricultural policy, rural development will become a key issue for 90% of the territory of the european union and 50% of its population. these guidelines are, for the most part, good and i am pleased that the european parliament is gradually recognising mountain areas as a privileged area for intervention. the commission will be very vigilant about the means, especially financial, that will be used. i regret that there is no greater emphasis on the need to ensure that rural areas have a level playing field in the current economic and social competition, in particular through a policy of major infrastructure works such as motorways, high-speed rail, air and port access, and the development of new information and communication technologies. the european union must guarantee equal opportunities for citizens and businesses wherever they are in europe.
in writing. can we have rural development without rural people? are there villages and landscapes in the wine-growing south, if our vineyards are torn down, if our cooperative and private cellars are closed, and if the mas of the vine growers are replaced by housing estates? the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. rural development in the second pillar is just a smokescreen. it is the elegant name for the disappearance of our agricultural products, for the benefit of producers in brazil, australia or the south pacific, with, as a consolation prize, a modest function of landscapers for the survivors of the peasant people of france and europe. rural development is the same hypocritical concept as "multifunctional agriculture". it is a painkiller, a palliative care applied to the women and men of the countryside who are being knowingly and ignobly sacrificed to the great "planetary deal". in the south pacific, agriculture, in europe, the illusion of the service market. europe has foolishly sold out its peasants and is inventing a farcical policy of 'rural development' in the human and economic desert that brussels has created in our countryside.
in writing. the eu has a unique responsibility and opportunity in this area. only this can meet the two conditions for the establishment of these new mechanisms: critical size and political will. the text before us does not live up to this expectation. the resolution does indeed provide support in principle for new sources of development finance by insisting that these funds should be in addition to traditional public aid and not replace it. but this parliament's position is very timid. support is lip service and the central concept in this debate, a "world tax" for development, is silenced. the various projects currently on the table (taxation of financial transactions, co2 emissions, arms sales, etc.) are not mentioned. no reference is made to the "global public goods", which these mechanisms should finance as a priority. because it is a first step in the right direction, i shall vote for this motion for a resolution. but i want to see it as an encouragement to move faster and further towards the practical implementation of these new tools at european level.
in writing. i voted in favour of the very interesting report on the implementation of a forestry strategy for the european union prepared by my colleague heinz kindermann. at present, the issue of forests and wood in the process of creating wealth and social progress, while respecting our environment, is not sufficiently taken into account in european public policies. it is time for the european union to give significant support to projects based on the forestry sector at the relevant site level. the link between a forestry strategy and rural development must be established and i regret that mountain areas have not been given special attention in this respect. similarly, in the context of the lisbon strategy, it is important that the union focuses more on supporting research programmes related to the recovery of wood, particularly in the construction and energy sectors. finally, a study should be carried out on the transport of wood, which is a heavy product, in order to bring together forest areas, consumption areas and road, rail and sea transport infrastructures.
