member of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i consider the report which parliament is debating today, drawn up by mr hamon and discussed by the members of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, to be very timely, given that the international monetary fund is in the midst of a debate on the strategic review based on the document presented by its executive director. the commission does not have a direct and formal presence, as you know, in the international monetary fund, nor does the european union; it is the member states. but we must be aware that the member states represented in the european union and in this house represent more than 30% of the shareholding of the international monetary fund. i therefore find this contribution to the debate on how to ensure greater economic and financial stability in the global economy, including in this concept of stability the development of the least developed countries and the eradication of poverty, extremely useful. and to achieve these objectives, we must certainly have the help of institutions with the capacity to act on a global scale, such as the international monetary fund. the first thing that strikes you when you look at the role of the imf in the global economy at the beginning of the 21st century is the relevance and relevance of the objectives that were assigned to it when it was created in 1944. while the objectives of promoting international monetary stability - facilitating the expansion of international trade, promoting exchange rate stability and reducing balance of payments imbalances - remain fully in place, the economic context in which the fund operates today is radically different from that of sixty years ago. this is of course recognised by the fund in its strategic review when it declares the centrality of the challenge of globalisation in order for the institution to be able to fulfil the tasks entrusted to it. the new approach of the fund is therefore to consider its essential tasks of monitoring and lending through the prism of globalisation. to do so, the fund takes into account both risks and opportunities. for example, in its strategy paper it recognises that the free movement of capital allows for a more efficient allocation of resources, but at the same time it also points out that it produces greater volatility and risk of extreme reactions of markets in the event of a crisis; it also notes the push of emerging economies, which are helping to a large extent the high growth rates in the world economy, but also that the power of these emerging economies is creating greater difficulties for the poorest countries to get on the train of global exchanges and global growth. the commission shares the fund's view of globalisation in its strategy paper; we convey our views to the international monetary fund in the fluid and frequent contacts we maintain with the institution's managers. in particular, as you know, we collaborate with the monetary fund in defining our policies and taking our decisions for the macrofinancial assistance which the european community gives to the countries of the western balkans or to some of the states which were part of the former soviet union. macro-financial assistance, based on resources from the community budget, is always subject to a number of conditions which are complementary to the assistance provided by the fund in those countries. in the field of development aid and poverty eradication, the imf, together with the world bank and the european union, are undoubtedly the main global actors and here too there is close and fruitful cooperation between the different institutions. all these aspects are in one way or another covered in the report we are debating today and the commission can perfectly well express its agreement with the positions taken by the rapporteur and supported by the committee on economic and monetary affairs. the report also stresses the need to adjust the distribution of quotas and votes in the governance structures of the fund, in order to reflect more evenly the relative weight of the different economies of the member countries, which will lead to giving a greater voice to the least developed countries and, in particular, to african countries, whose current share of representation and capital in the fund means that they are very poorly represented. as the imf notes in its documents, this reform of quota and voting distribution is the responsibility of the countries with shares and requires a strong political will to understand that increasing the quota of some at the expense of others can be beneficial to all in the medium and long term, because it will enable the fund to better fulfil its functions and the objectives it has been entrusted with. a final point i would like to make, mr president, is the external representation of the euro area and the european union in economic and monetary matters. i am grateful to the rapporteur and all the honourable members for including this point in the report we are debating today, although i do recognise - as i think i had occasion to say in this very house last year - that the commission would prefer a clearer and more direct formulation of the objective of a more adequate external representation of the euro area and the european union as a whole, such as that proposed in amendment no 5 tabled by mr purvis. the commission has started, together with the eurogroup presidency, a reflection on how to move towards this more effective external representation of the euro area and, in time, of the european union. progressively, with determination and realism, we will try to outline a consistent path that will allow us to make progress towards better coordination between the members of the euro area when they take their stand in the international financial institutions. in the short term, the aim is to identify points in the programmes of these institutions where a coordinated position of the member states can be achieved, for example in the area of budgetary surveillance. in the long term, the objective remains to achieve a single euro area constituency in the fund, enabling it to have an influence equivalent to the economic weight of monetary union. this will undoubtedly require strong political support from the member states. the commission believes that parliament can and must make a significant contribution to this endeavour by making its views as clear as possible. i would like to conclude, mr president, by expressing the commission's readiness to examine the way in which parliament can participate in shaping the positions which representatives of the euro area or the european union are called upon to express in the international financial institutions and bodies. the question certainly needs to be studied, and it is not easy to find a way of doing so, but i can assure all honourable members that the commission and i are fully prepared to look into this matter further when they consider it appropriate.
the rapporteur. mr president, i thank commissioner almunia and the committee on economic and monetary affairs for the positive reception they have given to my report. i would like to stress one fact which is important enough to be mentioned: the unanimous vote in favour of this report by the committee on economic and monetary affairs. i would also like to welcome the work of the committee on development and the committee on international trade, and in particular their rapporteurs, mr wijkman and mr bourlanges, who have contributed a great deal to enriching this report, which comes at a time when the international monetary fund is reflecting on its strategy and how to assess the evolution of its mission, the impact of its policies and the way it operates. i would like to return to the spirit in which the fictitious rapporteurs and the whole committee worked, namely to ensure that our parliament's report makes a useful contribution to the strategic review of the international monetary fund while taking into account the major challenges facing the fund: first the question of its governance, then the question of its economic doctrine and the impact of its choices on the millennium development goals and finally, more generally, the way in which, today, through its role of monitoring and crisis prevention, it remains the guarantor of global macroeconomic and financial stability. on the question of governance, let me remind you that the member states are now divided into nine constituencies, which means that today the european union, if one can speak of european union in this context, has no representation for the whole union. the european union therefore expresses itself through nine constituencies. the report also stresses the lack of coordination between the member states within the international monetary fund. that is why this report is in favour of better coordination of the european chairs and of a step-by-step approach to representation for the whole of the european union in the international monetary fund, with the single chair as a prospect, of course, and the single chair for the euro area in the meantime. today the report does not specifically mention the question of the single chair but sets as an objective the unity of the european union's vote and representation in the international monetary fund, which seems to me to be a very fundamental step. why is it essential? because that would give the european union the blocking minority it does not have today, namely 15% of the voting rights in the international monetary fund. the united states is currently the only country with this blocking minority, and we know the impact it can have on the major policy and strategic choices the international monetary fund has made. there is a key element here that is very important. i would add that the evolution of the representation of the european union may also help to unblock part of the question of the distribution of voting rights and therefore the weight of emerging and developing countries in the international monetary fund's board of directors. we believe that the representation of the emerging countries should be more proportionate to their economic weight. it is also necessary that the countries with the largest populations but the weakest economies, the developing countries, should have much greater voting rights than they do today, for the simple reason that they are the 'beneficiaries' of the policies of the international monetary fund. for this reason, this report is in favour of an increase in the allocation of basic voting rights: this is at least one of the options to be explored in the immediate future. the second point we wish to stress is the question of the legitimacy of the international monetary fund's interventions, especially as the scope of these interventions is becoming ever wider. we are in favour of improving the transparency of the international monetary fund and its operation. i am thinking in particular of the recruitment of experts and the need to diversify their profiles so that they can adapt their recommendations more easily to the diversity of situations encountered. the last point, which is not the least difficult, concerns the way in which structural adjustment policies and the recommendations of the international monetary fund for many years have been assessed. the fund is now being heavily criticised for the implementation of a number of its recommendations, for its macroeconomic doctrine and for its somewhat too rigid application of the washington consensus. this is why we asked the commission to be more flexible and to look at the best way of ensuring that local authorities and the countries concerned take ownership of poverty reduction strategies. we think this is a very important step. we have also pointed out that a number of fund interventions have not been infallible in terms of the results achieved, the social costs of structural adjustment plans, or the contagion of crises, or even their recurrence. these are the points we insist on in order to encourage the fund to change a number of its choices in the context of its strategic review. i would add, and i would like to stress this point, that we should not find ourselves in the future, in terms of global governance, faced with a form of implicit hierarchy of standards which would like the fund's recommendations to rise to the top on the pretext that they no longer only concern macroeconomic stability and growth policies, but also concern labour market policies, the financing of social programmes, education and health. the hierarchy of standards should not therefore place the fund's recommendations at the top of all international organizations, to the point of sometimes creating strong contradictions between the fund's recommendations and those of the major international conventions of the ilo or the world health organization. in conclusion, we would like the european parliament to feel more concerned, particularly in view of the prospect of a single representation of the european union, with the responsibility of the european union's directors in the international monetary fund. we want the fund to have regular relations with the european parliament, just as it has regular relations with the american congress, and to be accountable and responsible for its actions to the assembly of the peoples of europe.
the commission has already submitted a proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos. mr president, the committee on international trade has delivered an opinion which is very close to the excellent report by our colleague, mr hamon, and i think there are indeed very similar views, very similar concerns. we have three main concerns. firstly, like the rapporteur, we want to see better coordination of all development policies. we are pointing to a contradiction: the imf is part of a whole, it has a particular responsibility, but at the same time it is much more than part of a whole, because as a lender of last resort it enjoys, as mr hamon has just mentioned, a kind of de facto preeminence which is not without problems, which leads to the search for better coordination with other international organizations, in particular the wto, the ilo and the world health organization. we must think about these forms of coordination. secondly, we are concerned about the rebalancing of powers. we do not want to give in to a few excessive demographic dizzinesses that would cut us off from the world economic reality but we believe that at the present stage the emerging economies are not sufficiently represented and that a rebalancing of powers is needed in favour of these same economies. finally, we share the rapporteur's concern that europe should speak with one voice and act in concert. it is the height of desolation to see that europe, which has almost twice as many votes in its member states as the united states, has so little in the organization. can we now move on to the single chair? perhaps not, but we must move towards informal forms of action comparable to shareholder pacts, starting with the euro area and setting ourselves the objective in the second stage of making the whole of the european union speak with one voice. these are our concerns, and i do not think they contradict those of mr hamon.

vice-president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the questions put by president záborská and the other honourable members require a detailed answer: it is right and proper for me to give concrete answers. the various questions raised 16 different points, with very specific questions to which i shall try to give an answer. more generally, i think it is unthinkable that a sporting event, which should in principle be a celebration of positive values, could be used to tolerate or encourage forced prostitution. i've heard a very sad reference to this, that football and sex go together, as if forced prostitution is the inevitable consequence of a major sporting event. but that would be a denial of the healthiest values of the sport. it is therefore necessary to start with legislation, specifically with the relevant european legislation adopted in this regard, which provides for the criminalisation of those who contribute to the coercion of persons, women and children in particular, but it must be said, also men, into prostitution. as you know, there is a european framework decision, and currently, as far as germany is concerned, a national law has entered into force in 2005, which is a fully applicable law. we will also prepare a report to the council and parliament by the end of april on the application of the framework decision on trafficking in human beings and criminal penalties to ensure that all member states have adopted national laws transposing this framework decision before the world cup football championship. among the most important rules is one which requires member states to prosecute those responsible in the country of origin and not in the country where they committed the crime. the framework decision provides for this in order to ensure the effective conduct of a trial and the imposition of criminal sanctions. after the report has been submitted by the end of april, the council, and if parliament deems it appropriate, will be able to discuss in depth the subject of further measures which could be taken at european level, at european legislative level. in my opinion, in connection with these measures, we should think, even without giving a definitive answer today, about the punishability of those who, as customers, take advantage of the services of people, knowing that they have been victims of coercion and even in some cases of a real trafficking that has reduced them to slavery. of course, the question of the legality of prostitution is dealt with in very different ways in the member states, but in my view, if the client is aware that the person with whom he is dealing is a victim of trafficking, coercion or coercion, then further consideration must be given, including from the point of view of possible criminal sanctions. the role of europol and eurojust must obviously be strengthened in this context. one of the priority topics i raised when i met the president of eurojust and the director of europol was precisely that of strengthening the capacity of europol and eurojust to implement the action plan against trafficking in human beings which we presented, as this parliament recalls, at the end of last year. europol can play a very important role in coordinating action at european level against these heinous forms of crime. we have already done this successfully to tackle paedophilia, with europol's action dismantling a network of paedophiles in 13 european countries. this is another path to be pursued. then there's the specific issue of the world cup in germany: i had promised this parliament, when the subject was first discussed, that i would formally involve the german federal ministry of the interior. i have of course done so, and minister schäuble, to whom i prevention initiatives on the ground in all the cities in germany concerned by the holding of football matches. i can therefore say with confidence that the german federal government, through its minister of the interior, is not only assuring full cooperation but is also urging the council of ministers of the interior to consider the matter in april in order to develop an operational strategy, in this case not legislative but operational prevention on the ground, in order to prevent the sporting event from being used to transfer a huge number of victims of this odious trafficking. i should like to make two comments on the concrete measures which i, as the commission's representative, intend to put forward at the april summit of the council of ministers of the interior. first of all, as regards the issue of visas, i would like to confirm very clearly to mr groener in particular, but also to those who wrote to me after the seminar on 8 march, that i never intended, wanted or thought of introducing visas for women. visas are not issued for specific categories of persons, they are issued for specific countries and for specific nationalities. i had announced my intention to assess whether certain third countries, considered to be at risk, are still visa-free and therefore whether it would be appropriate to extend the visa period temporarily for a country of origin of a likely traffic; i'm sorry if i was misunderstood at the march 8th seminar. i've been digging into this, and i can even give you the answer. there are no third countries outside the european union from which, according to police data, visa-free flows of human trafficking originate. it will not therefore be necessary to introduce changes to the current visa regime simply because all the so-called third countries at risk - according to statistics - are already covered by visas. in any case, it would never have been a visa for women, it would only have provided for greater control over certain countries. the problem is not there, but it is clear that there is a need - and i will make a proposal to the council to that effect - for greater control by the consulates over the actual purposes of visitor groups' trips, since it is clear that sex traffickers give or cause to be given false reasons. so control is the responsibility of the borders and the consulates - this requires cooperation between all the member states of the european union - and there will have to be a reinforced control of the veracity of the stated objectives. as you know, it is often claimed as a pure and simple tourist purpose which is not true. a thorough check is necessary. it is also clear that, as some of you have suggested, concrete measures to support the victims are indispensable. i am personally in favour of the idea of promoting dedicated telephone lines, that is, telephone lines which can, through a simultaneous translation service, offer immediate help in as many foreign languages as possible. obviously this applies both to the period of the football world cup and the period afterwards: the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat the spread of the disease. these immediate and operational support measures can be considered in the european action plan itself, thanks to the projects and the funds that europe can allocate to concrete proposals of this kind. another measure which i think is necessary is a comparative study of all the laws of the member states relating to prostitution and the relationship between prostitution, where it is permitted, and human trafficking for sexual purposes. the link between the increase in demand and the incentive for traffickers to engage in this despicable activity is clear. there is a study that this parliament has sponsored, namely a study on transnational crime. i would like to propose that a comparative study be carried out to get a clearer picture of the link between the increase in demand and the increase in traffic. of course, within the framework of the daphne programmes, the european union will be able to co-finance initiatives in this field in order to raise public awareness of the need to reduce the demand for prostitution, since reducing the demand for prostitution limits or helps to limit the trafficking of people for sexual purposes. another proposal that can be made is for closer the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would first of all like to thank my colleagues for their confidence in me in the preparation of this report. one of the methods i used to prepare for this work was listening. i met all the social partners - employees, employers - and i met with the economic and social council and the committee of the regions, and i had a meeting with commissioner špidla and the commission's partners. we have also done a great deal of consultation with the fictitious rapporteurs and i would like to thank mrs bachelot, mrs mcdonald, mrs schroedter and mr beaupuy here for their sense of compromise and the quality of their work. when we hear about restructuring, we always feel that we are being taken by surprise and confronted with something new. yet, the phenomenon has been around for centuries and is inescapable. society is changing, moving forward, modernizing. it is only natural that its economic activity should follow the same trend. the technological advances made by man over the centuries have generated restructuring. i will take an example, which will not offend anyone in this house: from hunting to farming, our ancestors have undergone many important restructurings. it is true, however, that these restructuring phenomena have taken on a new face with the acceleration of progress and the now global dimension of the market. every new decision we take can be a generator of restructuring. i would therefore like to congratulate the commission here, if i may, for having recognized in its communication that the union, sometimes, as in the textile sector, being at the origin of restructuring movements, had to bear its share of responsibility by supporting them as best it could. as you have seen, i have insisted throughout my report on the need for restructuring, because i believe that it is the key to maintaining the economic competitiveness of our companies and, therefore, to safeguarding employment. but in studying this matter we cannot ignore restructuring based on false pretexts, behind which lies the simple pursuit of immediate profit. we are right to regard such behaviour as immoral, because it is unacceptable in europe today for an employed father of a family to find himself on monday morning outside the closed door of a factory which has been hastily emptied during the weekend. the role of our institutions, as well as that of the social partners, is to intervene as far as possible upstream, in order to better anticipate restructuring and mitigate its consequences in terms of social costs. indeed, whether justified or not, restructuring often leaves people stranded. restructuring is not a phenomenon affecting any one member state in particular. we must not give in to the siren song of trying to turn us against each other as soon as the subject of employment is raised in this house. there are no two blocs with the old member states on one side and the new member states on the other. no, there are 450 million europeans who, from tallinn to lisbon, could be faced with this situation overnight. in my report i try to define three fields of action. first, a field of action to support, say, citizen enterprises, with the strengthening of the tools for analysing the phenomenon, to prevent them upstream, increased aid to small and medium-sized enterprises, the encouragement of lifelong vocational training, which is a right for employees and an undeniable asset for companies, a reform of state aid to support growth and, above all, the establishment of a fund for adjustment to globalisation. secondly, a field of action to punish the 'gangster' companies - allow me to use the term - which are by far the fewest, but also the ones we hear the most about. this type of action requires better control of the use of european funds, to discourage subsidised tourism, to challenge certain restructuring measures whose motives are questionable, and to ensure that the community legal acquis is respected and properly applied. thirdly, a field of action to support those who are the first to be affected by the phenomenon of restructuring: employees. the aim is to set up permanent retraining units so that the time between job loss and new recruitment is as short as possible. it is a question of strengthening the role of the social partners, who are our real asset in dealing with these phenomena, and that is why i ask my colleagues once again to imagine the revision of the directive on european works councils. the aim is to encourage employees to participate in the capital of their enterprises and to set up a single point of contact to enable all citizens of the union to have equal access to health care. finally, i believe that we can help, together with the social partners and without political bias, to support the restructuring process in order to win the battle for employment. let us think about it when, in a few seconds, it is possible, on the other side of the planet, on the simple decision of a board of directors, to reduce to nothing, here, on our territories, the fruits of several decades of work. this series gives us the opportunity to make a difference in the lives of our citizens, because that is what all our technical terms are about: men and women who are only looking for happiness. in the spirit of the founding fathers who made europe a peaceful europe, it is our task today to contribute to the cause of social peace.

mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, after the hutchinson report, which we discussed last night, the cottigny report raises the question of restructuring and relocation of companies. i would like to thank both rapporteurs for raising these socioeconomic problems, which are among the most worrying and cause social insecurity for our citizens. it is a good thing that parliament is debating this. these questions pose the challenge to the european union of the economic competitiveness of our enterprises and the challenge of the employment security of our employees. in the minds of european employees, relocations and restructuring are linked and almost synonymous because they have the same consequences: the loss of their jobs after years of work in the same sector of activity, sometimes even in the same company, the same questioning of their professional value. this should not be the case, because restructuring is sometimes a sign of progress, of technical progress. restructuring does not cover the same economic causes as relocation and it is up to the legislator to provide a suitable solution to each problem. i would like to emphasize here the question of restructuring companies for reasons of technological change. this is the central question of the cottigny report. this question challenges the european union's ability to adapt to the ever-accelerating changes of our era of technological progress. it really challenges us to anticipate them. they say to govern, you must plan! in writing. in calling for the reimbursement of european aid paid to companies relocating their activities, mr hutchinson's report echoes one of the proposals made in the île-de-france regional elections by the front national concerning subsidies to the regional council. the european institutions are beginning to realise the economic and social consequences of their policy choices: many of our companies are being forced to relocate their activities because the destruction of frontiers puts them in competition with producers with extremely low labour costs. to protect our economies from this social dumping, to preserve our social model, we must implement a different policy: to re-establish our frontiers, to make our companies more competitive by financing our social security with a social vat that would replace contributions. this would require national governments to retain their sovereignty in taxation. these are some of the economic and social measures of common sense that could be taken, not by the current europe of brussels, which the french people disavowed last year, but by a europe of free and sovereign nations.
in writing. creating a single market between 25 states with very different wage, social and tax costs was to lead to the relocation of firms to countries with low production costs. that's what happened. the ten new states attract companies from "old europe" and even us companies based in mexico. it is all the more shocking that these states are offering themselves an attractive tax burden and then have their health, social, road and other facilities paid for by the western states, which, by increasing their taxation to finance the ten, are at the same time aggravating their production handicap. there is a substantive solution for relocations outside the union. the new technology tariff must be invented with three characteristics: it must be modulable according to the difference in production costs between two countries. be refundable. the customs duty borne by the exporter would become a 'tax credit' deductible by purchase on the economy of the importer. in other words, the customs duty would give the exporter a drag on the importer's economy, triggering a 'win-win' international trade multiplier. finally, they would be eligible for subsidies where the importer would wish to grant an advantage to the exporter. the customs credit would then become a 'matching credit' as international tax law already knows.
in writing. i voted in favour of this text. we must have a firm community strategy on mercury. but being firm also means being realistic. mercury-containing merthiolate is used as a preservative in some medicines, including vaccines. there are approximately 1 million doses of vaccine for which merthiolate is used in the manufacturing process for decontamination purposes. this represents 0.0000003% of the mercury used annually in europe. in view of the tremendous positive impact of vaccination on public health, including in developing countries, there would be no justification for an immediate ban on this product in vaccines. however, the search for alternative methods should be encouraged in order to reduce or eliminate the use of merthiolate in the future. i would also remind you that, in accordance with pharmaceutical regulations, manufacturers must prove that their products do not harm the environment.

mr president, commissioner, you have given us the figures: today, european shoe production has fallen by about 30%, import prices have fallen by more than 20% and, above all, the sector has lost almost 40 000 jobs. six months after the textile crisis - as we had foreseen at the time - the community market is again confronted with unfair trading practices. we have, as you have pointed out, evidence of state intervention and disguised subsidies for producers in china and vietnam. however, when faced with the finding of such a violation of trade practices, the european union has a duty to react and to correct the injury caused to the community industry, in accordance with wto rules. that is why, as you have shown, commissioner, it is necessary to introduce anti-dumping measures on these imports. the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter, but it is not yet known whether the commission will take a decision on the matter. the aim is rather to guarantee the conditions for balanced trade, which safeguards the interests of consumers and producers. therefore, intervention to limit the negative effects of dumping should not be seen as protectionism. the european union is committed to harmonious and open trade relations with its asian partners, to lift these populations out of poverty, but it is also committed to fair and equitable trade rules for all.
mr president, commissioner, since the abolition of the quota system last year, imports from china have, as has been mentioned, increased dramatically by some 500%. this has serious consequences for the competitiveness of the european footwear sector, which, faced with this surge of imports at very low prices, is experiencing a number of dramatic bankruptcies, not to mention the accompanying job losses. in addition, our traditional suppliers, the candidate countries and the countries of the euromed zone, have been excluded from the community market. the commission is silent on this and does not seem to want to assess the impact of the damage caused by this liberalization. following complaints from the players in this sector, you opened an anti-dumping investigation. its alarming results reveal undeniable evidence of state intervention and social dumping, with material damage to our industries. to combat this distortion of the basic rules of international trade, you are proposing measures today. i am concerned, however, about the gradual entry into force of these anti-dumping duties over a period of five months, a precedent which seems to me to be ill-timed, legally questionable and not without adverse effects. these duties should eliminate either dumping or injury. the proposed progressive rates do not meet either of these two alternative conditions. finally, the exclusion of children's shoes seems to me unjustified and incomprehensible. your proposals could very soon prove inadequate in the face of the extent of the damage suffered by our companies. other initiatives to counter these unfair trade practices could be taken, for example the possibility of opening an investigation under the transitional safeguard mechanism for chinese imports, which has the advantage of being simple and effective. if the member states were to ask you to do so, would the commission consider doing so? mr president, in romans, in the drôme, the unemployment rate is 18% - double the french average - because the shoe industry is in disarray and ancestral know-how is disappearing. this bankruptcy stems from the anachronistic application of the ricardian model which underlies your policy. the new international division of labour has pushed low-wage countries to specialise in labour-intensive industries, while high-saving countries focus on highly capitalist industries. today, capital, thirsty for growth, is also going to these countries. the countries of the union, which had high productivity and high wages, are being overtaken by countries with equal productivity and low wages. the european union must be able to take action to protect its citizens, and to protect the union's citizens. without this, all our labour industries will follow in the footwear industry's footsteps.
the rapporteur. mr president, madam president-in-office of the council, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i welcome the opportunity we have today to discuss the european judicial area, on the basis of the report i have drawn up on the evaluation, which is still very recent and therefore necessarily fragmentary, of a year's experience of the european arrest warrant. we have already had occasion to discuss this matter. before i turn to the european arrest warrant, i would like to make a brief reminder that behind this concept of an area of justice, which was born very gradually after the geneva appeal in 1996, there was the ambition to give the citizen a common sense of justice in an environment where the authorities are doing everything possible to prevent this freedom from being abused or their rights violated. in october 1999, the tampere summit marked an important milestone with the introduction of the principle of mutual recognition. this was a radical change. it implies mutual trust, the exercise of shared sovereignty and the recognition of the european space as a common territory. as we have seen since then, difficulties persist and there is a need for greater awareness. the spirit and ambition of the heads of state in tampere, it must be said, did not animate the discussions on the texts presented since then with the same enthusiasm. mutual recognition has inspired many projects, but the most emblematic measure is the creation of the european arrest warrant. it is a sure step forward, but it is faced with persistent difficulties. what was the purpose of this measure, which officially entered into force on 1 january 2004? the european arrest warrant applies to a wider range of offences than those covered by extradition. thanks to this mandate, the handover, and this is an advantage, has become a completely judicial process and no longer political. finally, eu law is becoming readable to practitioners, whereas the current law on extradition is based on a thousand bilateral and national conventions. moreover, it is recalled on several occasions, in particular in article 1 of the framework decision, that, in issuing and executing the arrest warrant, member states and judicial authorities must ensure that the principles recognised in the charter of fundamental rights are strictly respected. the principle of this instrument is laid down, but what about the practical application? we have today an evaluation carried out by the european commission over a short period of time, as i said, and we must therefore remain cautious about the results of this evaluation, which will have to be completed. some of the objectives have been perfectly achieved. for example, recently the arrest warrant was instrumental in the prosecution of an ethiopian man by british authorities who was suspected of involvement in the london bombings. his extradition by the italian authorities was obtained in record time. another success was the arrest of a corrupt magistrate, wanted by her country, greece. the european arrest warrant is a clear success, with 3 000 warrants issued in 2004, 1 000 arrested and 650 surrendered. the figures for 2005 will certainly show an increase but will not be officially available until june/july. the extradition process is very short. with the replacement of the former extradition procedure by the european arrest warrant, the average length of proceedings has been reduced from nine months to 43 days, which is a considerable gain for both judges and the persons subject to them. and, last but not least, the procedure is no longer politicised at all, since it no longer goes through governments but only through the judiciary. however, it is clear that there are several obstacles to its application. for example, last autumn the spanish courts declared the european arrest warrant issued by germany void in response to berlin's refusal to extradite the german-syrian national mamoun darkazanli, a suspected al-qaeda figure. several member states are also trying to recover elements of the traditional system, i.e. double criminality control. in addition to the optional grounds for non-enforcement provided for in the framework decision, some states added other grounds for refusal. more importantly, the issue of fundamental rights has given rise to significant transposition problems in poland and germany. this difficulty must be interpreted as a misunderstanding of the principle of mutual recognition. this principle is precisely the basis for the whole construction of the european judicial area. in conclusion, i would say that the european arrest warrant is a great step forward in the fight against crime, first and foremost in the service of citizens, and in the establishment of the european judicial area. however, the challenges are still many and should not be underestimated. the first difficulty is that our judicial systems are too disparate. the second difficulty is that most states are still too keen to control international mutual legal assistance. even if the judicial system is a product of history, the questions that arise will have to be resolved. conclusion: is more or less harmonization needed? i think we need more. should we go further in mutual recognition of systems? i think so too.
on behalf of the pse group. mr president, i would like to thank our rapporteur for his very comprehensive work. this report gives us an opportunity to assess the european arrest warrant, the first concrete instrument of the european judicial area, but also to redefine our priorities for the implementation of a genuine european judicial area. the european arrest warrant, as we have said, has been a great success: 2,600 warrants have been issued throughout the european union since its inception, and judicial proceedings have been considerably speeded up. so borders are no longer an obstacle to justice. this success shows that the member states are willing to work together. we are thus strengthening the principle of mutual trust, which is the cornerstone of the european judicial area. the european arrest warrant has nevertheless encountered obstacles in its application imposed by certain governments, and i regret the delay in its transposition in italy. this delay led to a late assessment of the country by the commission. in addition, member states have different interpretations of the term 'mandate' in their national laws. this also illustrates the lack of political will on the part of the states and the limitations imposed by the way decisions are taken in this area. however, the success of the european arrest warrant shows that it is impossible to limit ourselves to civil law. we must be more ambitious and extend judicial cooperation to criminal law. that is why we believe it is essential to use article 42 and the bridge clause to achieve a minimum of harmonisation of european criminal law. we will thus be able to put an end to the unanimity rule which is a hindrance to the establishment of a genuine area of freedom, security and justice. we must also close the democratic deficit, and only if the european parliament is fully involved in the creation of a european judicial area can fundamental rights be protected. secondly, how can we move forward effectively if we limit ourselves to the safe zone? we have made progress in policing, but we must also be demanding in respect of fundamental rights. the proposal on procedural guarantees must therefore be dealt with in parallel. finally, i would like to ask the commission and the council a specific question: when will we finally be able to move forward with other concrete instruments, such as the exchange of evidence and the exchange of data between criminal records?

member of the commission. mr president, i should like to begin by imparting to you some breaking news: the decisions of late 2005 have created a solid political framework for our enlargement policy for 2006 to 2010, and in some cases even further. for instance, the accession negotiations with turkey are likely to take 10 to 15 years. i do not expect anyone seriously to question our existing commitments in south-east europe because it is really a matter of our own security and stability that we can enhance peace, democracy and increase prosperity in that very sensitive area. we now have a consolidated and sufficiently demanding enlargement agenda. the enlargement train is no bullet train, no tgv, no eurostar; it is a normal train or, in some cases, even a local train, but, most importantly, this train is moving, it is in the process and is thereby transforming the countries that are in the immediate neighbourhood of the european union. concerning the borders of europe, the commission works on the basis of article 49 of the treaty on european union, which states that any european country that respects and applies the european values of democracy, human rights, the rule of law and fundamental freedoms may apply for membership of the union. that does not mean that every european country must apply or that the eu must accept every country, but at the same time it means that it is not sensible to close the door forever by drawing a line across the map to define europe once and for all, which would seriously damage our possibilities of having a beneficial influence and strategic leverage in our immediate neighbourhood. meanwhile, although no final borders of the union have yet been determined, the eu is developing other forms of partnership and cooperation with our neighbouring countries, for instance in the form of the european neighbourhood policy, which can be further developed and upgraded. a few comments and points have been made concerning absorption capacity. i would like to give a very brief historical overview. that concept was first explicitly mentioned in copenhagen in 1993 when the european council stated that the union’s capacity to absorb new members, while maintaining the momentum of european integration, is also an important consideration in the general interests of both the union and the candidate countries. that concept and its consequences have been examined regularly by the commission. in its agenda 2000 – and i am happy to refer to that because i was a member of the steering group for agenda 2000, which was adopted in 1997 – the commission examined the impact of the accession of central and eastern european countries from two angles: its impact on eu policies such as agriculture or regional policy, and its budgetary consequences. as a result, this work led to the setting of critical parameters in the negotiations that followed, in the decisions of march 1999 at the berlin summit and in 2003, when the countries of eastern and central europe were allowed to join the european union. this facilitated the accession of eu-10 and, by those means, we successfully combined our historic mission of reunifying the european continent and taking care of the practical considerations, which are also of concern to our citizens today. later on, we examined that concept during the accession negotiations, in some chapters in particular, such as that on the free movement of persons and the financial chapters, and more recently the commission also examined that concept in our 2004 issues paper on questions arising from the turkish accession perspective. i would recommend this paper of october 2004 to all members of the european parliament. it is still worth reading and outlines very well the broad consequences of possible turkish accession to the union if, one day, turkey meets all the conditions for accession. thus, the upsurge in capacity is an important concept, and it has also been referred to in the negotiating frameworks for turkey and croatia. i can assure you that we bear this in mind throughout the negotiations, and it is also a leading concept in our strategy document of last november. we base our work on that concept and it is a very important consideration. finally, referring to what mr eurlings said about deepening and widening, i belong to the camp that thinks that the deepening of political integration is indispensable in order to make the european union more effective and democratic. we must make the union function better, and that was and is the purpose of the constitutional treaty. therefore, we need a constitutional debate and, in time – sooner rather than later – we need to decide on how we reform our structures so that they are more effective and democratic and so that the european union can have more clout in external relations, in common foreign and security policy and in preserving the security of its own citizens against international crime and terrorism. that must be done in the near future, not in the distant future – not in 10 to 15 years, for instance, when turkey might be able to join – for the sake of europe, and we need it already for the european union of 25 or 27 member states. therefore, rather than talk about absorption capacity, i would prefer to talk about the functioning capacity of the current european union to ensure that we serve our citizens better in terms of both policies and institutions.

its objectives, but for this we need a real partnership between the european institutions. the 2005 report shows that the caricature of a paralysed europe was far from the truth. we have made considerable progress. the commission has focused on its objectives and has achieved a rate of implementation of close to 90% for its priority actions. the stability and growth pact, the revised social agenda and the sustainable development strategy have been given a new direction. but above all, i think we will see this week that the revision of the lisbon strategy for jobs and growth has marked a real turning point, finally giving it the tools to turn aspirations into reality. the hampton court summit helped to achieve a new consensus on the key elements of union action in a globalising world. it opened the door to the measures that are emerging today. i am thinking, for example, of a european energy policy and the european globalisation adjustment fund. the union has demonstrated its ability to respond quickly to needs after the tsunami or after the london bombings. it has also shown that it is able to work in unison: the european consensus on development, to which the european parliament also subscribes, is the expression of a genuine common approach. of course, our work is not finished. however, as regards the financial perspective, i believe we are closer than ever to an agreement. if we can find a solution very soon, we will still have enough time for most programmes to be in operation by the beginning of next year, which is particularly important for the less wealthy countries and regions of our continent. as for the future of the european debate, we can still take advantage of events and use this period to reach a real consensus on the direction to take. i believe we are on the right track: the annual progress report on the lisbon strategy, the green paper on energy policy, biofuels, the european institute of technology, the roadmap on gender equality are all major initiatives already on the agenda. so what about 2007? i believe that 2007 will be a key year for the achievement of the strategic objectives set by our commission for its mandate. our five-year strategic objectives - prosperity, solidarity, security - and of course their external impact, remain valid. they form a coherent policy framework to guide the action of the european union. they reflect the challenges facing europe and the main concerns of european citizens, which they seek to address. they will remain the cornerstone of the commission's action. i think they are a good basis for a new look at the direction our union should take. with the fiftieth anniversary of the treaty of rome in 2007, attention will rightly be focused on the european union's main values and overall objectives. the main target must continue to be sustainable growth to provide more and better jobs in europe. with a more positive macroeconomic outlook, we must seize every opportunity to accelerate reforms and put them into practice. i know that this parliament is committed to playing its role in a real partnership for growth and jobs. in 2007, several member states should be speeding up their preparations for adopting the euro. provided they meet the necessary conditions, in 2007 we shall see the accession of bulgaria and romania, and i look forward to their contribution to the european union. energy will continue to attract our attention. we will pay particular attention to the promotion of sustainable management and the protection of natural resources. we will make proposals for a european union maritime policy. we will follow up on the green paper on labour law. the year 2007 will also be the european year of equal opportunities for all. in the field of security and freedom, the main target will be the extension of the schengen area, migration and border controls and the fight against crime. health issues will remain central, with greater preventive efforts against pandemics. beyond our borders, we will ensure a proper follow-up to the doha round, progress in the stabilisation of the western balkans in particular in kosovo and completion of partnership agreements with the acp countries. as you can see, we will be very busy in 2007. the year 2007 will also see new directions for the second half of the commission's mandate. we shall be preparing for the future, with intensive work on the comprehensive review of the union's budget leading to a white paper in 2008-09. this review needs to be based on a profound reflection and must take the full range of views into account. this will naturally include the european parliament and i welcome your intention of close association with this process. let me also say a few words on our ability to deliver on these priorities. we need to translate them into practical actions and implement them through the most appropriate instruments. the commission has made progress in this direction. firstly, we have a strategic planning and programming cycle ensuring an effective and timely delivery of our priorities and concentrating our resources on these tasks. the commission states its intentions, consults on them, adopts its work programme and reports regularly on its implementation. however, we need to further strengthen the political relevance and substance of our discussion on our strategic planning and programming. secondly, we have implemented a range of instruments to promote better regulation and good governance, which i believe is having a real impact on the rigour of our work and the quality of our output. we have made significant efforts to carry out impact assessments on our major proposals. we have completed more than one hundred so far, and we will continue to improve their quality and ensure that they make a real difference in our decision-making process. the commission will also carry through its simplification agenda, covering various fields from environment to industry, the modernisation of labour law, the promotion of consumer rights or key internal market sectors. however, let us not forget that governance and better regulation are the shared responsibilities of all the european institutions and the member states. as i have said before, better regulation is crucially important for liberalising our economic potential, in particular for small and medium-sized enterprises. what our business needs in europe is a red carpet, not red tape. efforts must be pursued at all levels to show that european initiatives are well founded and add real value. in many areas be it at european or national level we do not need so many regulations. as montesquieu said in the best possible way and i shall say it in french: "unecessary laws weaken necessary laws". roughly translated, that means "useless laws weaken indispensable ones". this is the very principle of the good european tradition. so what are the next steps? the annual policy strategy decision forms the basis for our dialogue in view of preparing the commission's work programme for 2007. every commissioner now stands ready to discuss with initiative last year to draw together the threads in its report. that had a real impact on this year's work program. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission is putting this strategy forward in a spirit of partnership. i look forward to your views on where europe should devote its energies in 2007. in writing. we partly agree with the conclusions of this resolution: concern about our countries' energy dependence and its possible economic and social consequences; the need to promote indigenous renewable energy sources that are more environmentally friendly; investing in energy efficiency or looking for new energy savings. it also lacks consideration of the predicted exhaustion of world hydrocarbon resources. on the other hand, we do not agree with the commission's self-appointed role in the energy sector, a role which is not in the treaties, a role which even your european constitution reduced to a statement of the existing situation, but which this parliament wants to develop. the liberalization of the electricity and gas markets only produces higher energy prices for consumers, supply disruptions and a widespread movement of companies towards concentration. even my country, which has a tradition of producing electricity in excess, with almost 90% of its electricity coming from nuclear or renewable sources, is now facing this type of problem. thanks to brussels ! the logic of the market alone is not compatible with the pursuit of national strategic objectives or the safeguarding of vital interests of a country. states must remain the sole masters of their energy policy.
in writing. european political parties are only associations with a highly lucrative purpose. the report essentially calls for more money and more ease of use for them, as well as favourable status and a special tax regime. but for what? just exist and come together, for now. the aim is to give these parties a monopoly on the spread of the good word on europe. their creation depends on an inadmissible european "well-thought-out" certificate issued by this institution, on the basis of the programmes they are obliged to submit to its bodies. and we know that you would like at least part of the seats in this parliament to be reserved for members of lists drawn up at european level, lists which could only be put forward by european parties. the ultimate goal for you would be to allow them to participate as such in national and local elections, thus allowing unacceptable political interference at all levels of state decision-making. democracy is about allowing people to govern themselves or to elect representatives who represent their interests in decision-making bodies, parliaments or governments. the imposition of artificial entities representing only themselves and subject to brussels ideology is anything but democracy.
in writing. from china to europe, russia, not to mention africa, a gigantic demographic problem is taking shape. the world is getting old. worse still, in some european countries, such as germany and russia, the population is declining or will decline. the demographic consequences are well known: increased expenditure on health and pensions, the need for millions of jobs in the field of personal assistance, a shortage of personnel leading to a desire to emigrate, a psychological shift of societies towards caution and immobility and malthusian policies of no future, the expression of which since maastricht has been the 'budgetary austerity pact'. in other words, who is going to pay the taxes to finance this situation? the gods of the stadium or the old men in the last stadium ? certainly family policies will try to create contributors and contributions. but, while waiting for the arrival of additional births and, therefore, new assets, in the vacuum of the next twenty years that opens before us, the belgian, dutch or swiss legislation on euthanasia, masquerading as the right to choose one's death, shows the journey at the end of the night that politicians, especially in europe, have begun.

procedures. the amendments also provide for a better definition of the role of the european coordinator, who may be appointed when a project is experiencing significant delays or implementation introducing the declaration of european interest and the possibility of appointing a coordinator are essential tools for the realisation of a genuine internal market in gas and electricity, to ensure security of supply. but this european network can only be completed by improving and increasing the number of interconnections. i would ask you, ladies and gentlemen, to support the common position as amended by this compromise package. our vote will provide the union with one of the tools needed to achieve the objectives it has set itself.

member of the commission. mr president, first of all i would like to thank you for this debate. trans-european networks are an extremely important part, but they are just one part, of european energy policy as i see it. one very important precondition is cooperation between member states. i think the great news i have had over recent months is the cooperation in the energy sector between baltic countries. governments are looking for a common energy policy even if their markets are isolated; but that still clearly indicates that governments should look towards that policy. the european council gave a lot of assurances, because the heads of state and government again came back to the interconnection issues – the 10% decision from barcelona that was neglected – and called for a priority interconnection plan. in this respect trans-european energy networks actually provide the basis of an answer. there have been critical remarks to the effect that networks could give rise to some types of speculation. that is why i am saying that regulation is as important as interconnection. regulation is absolutely necessary for the market, and the commission has been always rigorous in asking member states to implement eu legislation. but there are two stages. first of all we must get each member state to transpose the legislation. we have achieved that in 23 cases and 2 cases are before the european court of justice. so that is one stage. then there is conformity. the new package addresses the conformity issue. perhaps there will have to be new cases because the conformity issue does not arise only from commission studies but is also raised by market participants when they find the directive has not been implemented correctly. so that is not the end of the story. it is clear, however, that networks and the good development of networks are absolutely necessary. networks do not only mean interconnection, they also mean storage: it takes a long time to build gas storage, for example. i know that the challenge is huge. there was some talk about avoiding duplication and i know that there are a couple of projects in the same area. here i think governments should help by seeking a common approach and not building competing networks; instead they should look to the development of the best projects, which serve the interests of most of the member states and the european union. finally, in answer to the question as to what european energy policy means, it does not mean the sum of eu member states’ policies. it is based on member states’ policies, but it creates a new area of action for the european union in a situation where globalisation in energy markets has given rise to new challenges, where the action of one member state does not fully or adequately respond to the expectations of the citizens of that state, and where it is our duty to act at the scale of and within the scope of the european union as a whole. trans-european networks are definitely one of the instruments we can use. i would like again to thank the rapporteur, mrs laperrouze, and all the shadow rapporteurs who have had the patience to negotiate with the council and, at the appropriate moment, reached this overall compromise that i can accept.
the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we are now dealing with a report which for the first time has a political dimension. indeed, in the debates of the 2005 referendums on the ratification of the constitutional treaty, the notions of a free and open area of competition - as it is currently called - or undistorted - as it would have been called if the treaty on the european constitution had been adopted - were at the centre of the debate. our problem today is to prove that competition policy can be of service to the people, that it must be of service to the people, that it is already of service to the people. there is a broad consensus in our committee on this point, but as soon as i, as rapporteur, had to point out clear cases which called for a review or reorientation of competition policy, or which, on the contrary, called for strong encouragement of competition policy, disagreements arose. the report, in its present form after amendment, is typical of the european parliament's reports, which practically no one can or wants to read because they say nothing at all. i hope that on at least three points strong ideas will be reaffirmed to show the people that the european institutions are at their service. competition policy is divided into three main areas: the fight against the formation of monopolies, the fight against cartels and the fight against illegal or harmful state aid to healthy and undistorted competition. i shall take these three examples and offer you, ladies and gentlemen, some strong ideas on these policies. firstly, the fight against monopolies: the policy of the european union has been admirable in its battle against the abuse of microsoft's dominant position. my committee, the committee on economic and monetary affairs, has chosen not to support the directorate-general for competition in this fight. i ask you, ladies and gentlemen, to reaffirm the european parliament's support for the competition directorate and the commission in their battle against microsoft. secondly, i shall deal with the formation of these monopolies and the fight against cartels. overall, the directorate-general for competition has been admirable. i am thinking in particular of the vivendi/hachette case. i believe that mistakes were made in 1999 in a hurry, inadvertently, in the merger between rhône-poulenc and hoechst. we have to try to understand where these mistakes come from. we have no right to revoke the measures taken by the commission and i am not asking for it, but i am asking for a committee of inquiry into what happened to understand how tens of thousands of employees, tens of thousands of small shareholders could be ruined for lack of control which the commission had promised to exercise. the third point on which i would ask you to speak and to give strong ideas concerns the area of state aid. the competition directorate and the 2004 report approve such aid when it is consistent with the gothenburg and lisbon policies. we must support her on this point. on the contrary, when the competition directorate approves the city of charleroi, which heavily subsidises ryanair, i think it should be criticised because it distorts competition between cities, between companies and between modes of transport, to the detriment of lisbon and gothenburg policy.
mr president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, this annual meeting is important because it is the only time when the european parliament can fully discuss and assess the competition policy as it is being conducted by the commission. it is therefore important that this parliament should ensure that free and undistorted competition remains genuinely free and undistorted and that, where there are cases which deserve a little more attention, we can do so, including in this house, whether it is microsoft, rhodia-rhône-poulenc or ryanair-charleroi. since you are going to be reopening the debate on the important concept of concentration, which plays a key role in competition policy, i would like to draw your attention to one point, and i hope that this parliament will follow us on this. it seems to us that the threshold criteria currently in force in the commission prevent it from declaring itself competent whenever it should. for example, in the case of the merger between the london stock exchange and deutsche börse, you were ultimately not competent, on the grounds that the turnover in question was below the thresholds. there is a real question here. my second thought concerns the mittal-arcelor case. does free and undistorted competition mean that the conditions of ownership of the undertakings concerned must be completely disregarded? i think that there is also something to think about. finally, i will not surprise you by saying that for the socialists competition policy only makes sense if it contributes to the lisbon strategy. it must integrate social objectives, environmental objectives, long-term objectives. i hope that in this way we will be able to bring the concept of free and undistorted competition back into balance so that the union is indeed the most competitive area in the world, while respecting full employment and sustainable development.
