in writing. the reports from our european parliament on employment and social affairs policies are the repetition of a tiresome europeanist preaching which, in addition to excessive paper production, gives a result that deserves zero points. apart from the daily failure of the lisbon process, it is not a few ill-conceived revisions of the guidelines of a council decision that was decidedly badly 'decided' that will save french employment and the economy. the soup is meant to please everyone. the commission's liberalism is maintained, but it is also felt that the european institutions should be allowed more control over self-disciplined nations. to make it beautiful, the whole thing is spiced with good intentions when it comes to protecting, within this monstrous model, the weaker ones who are willingly mixed with immigration, so as not to have to endure any controversy on this issue. the solution to our problems lies precisely in these points. to revive our economy and employment like the phoenix, we must stop settlement immigration, promote natalist policies, apply community preference and protection in europe and national preference and protection in france.
in writing. the explanatory memorandum to mr lipietz's report is much more informative than the text of the report itself, which merely praises the commission's 'remarkable' work in its search for the slightest obstacle to free competition. the explanatory memorandum deplores the absence of studies on the actual consequences of the commission's decisions or on the dogmatic application of the provisions on state aid. it is mentioned that the market, which is also endowed with all the virtues, may not be sufficient on its own to achieve certain political and even economic objectives. it suggests that the liberalisation of certain markets has led to the replacement of good old public monopolies by private oligopolies, removing benefits without creating 'more' for consumers. finally, it stresses the commission's complete lack of self-criticism when its unwelcome decisions lead to economic disasters, as in the rhodia case for example. but the general impression is that brussels' competition policy is the expression of an ultra-liberal doctrine, that of the commission in the fight against 'economic patriotism', paradoxically applied by a fussy bureaucracy constantly intervening in the strategies of companies or the policies of states. in the context of fierce global competition, this can only lead to unemployment.
in writing. i voted in favour of the report by my colleague david hammerstein mintz on the transparency of european council meetings when acting as legislator. at a time when it is becoming necessary to move towards a political europe, it has become increasingly incomprehensible that the european council should continue to meet behind closed doors when acting as a legislator. this position is not only contrary to article 1 (2) of the treaty on european union (maastricht treaty of 7 february 1992), which provides for the principle of openness in european decisions, but also does not correspond to the transparency which our fellow citizens expect from the functioning of the european institutions. we shall never succeed in reducing the rift that has arisen between the european construction and the peoples with such behaviour. while awaiting the ratification of a treaty establishing a constitution for europe, the european council, while maintaining private spaces for exchanges between heads of state, must urgently reform its own rules of procedure to anticipate this development towards greater transparency in its deliberations when acting as legislator.
in writing. i voted in favour of the excellent report by my colleague and friend georgios papastamkos on the assessment of the doha round following the world trade organisation ministerial conference in hong kong in december 2005 because i believe that economies, especially western economies, must support the doha development agenda which provides for open and fair trade to reduce poverty in the world and be a factor of progress for both developing and developed countries. if we do not, we will pay dearly politically, especially by the rise of extremes. i am glad that multilateralism is being recognised in this negotiation and that international trade is a source of wealth and therefore of social progress. everyone will be able to see the great usefulness of a united and strong european political union in this global struggle where national egoisms are advancing in the face of weakened international institutions.
in writing. the wto is now trying to find solutions to problems that would never have existed without it and its attempt to force global free trade at all costs to the people: dumping of all kinds, problems of counterfeiting, restricted market access in most countries except those of the european union, transparent subsidies - in europe - or disguised - elsewhere, especially in the united states - that distort competition ... the world market is a jungle in which the weakest, the poorest, are the designated victims, and the only region that plays by the rules, europe, is a collateral victim. the least developed countries must not be integrated into the wto system, but must be protected from it, if they are to achieve development. like some nobel prize winners in economics, we believe that free trade can only exist in a way that benefits all countries at the same level of development, while trade must be regulated with others, which, by the way, does not prevent trade provisions that are favourable to developing countries. nor does it make it necessary in each of the 'zones' thus constituted to have a centralized common commercial policy in the hands of a supranational bureaucracy. in short, free trade is not an end in itself.
in writing. i voted in favour of the excellent report by my colleague josé manuel garcia-margallo y marfil on the state of the european economy in the context of the preparatory report for the broad economic policy guidelines for 2006, which highlights the conditions for sustainable economic growth. this report is essential to understand why europe is one of the world's slowest growing regions, especially in the developed world. the over-regulation that makes our economy less flexible, the fact that we do not have enough global leaders, that our small and medium-sized enterprises are growing at a slower rate than in the united states of america, too low an employment rate and average working hours and, finally, too little investment in vocational training, research and development, explain much of the current situation. in the global economic and social competition facing europe, it is becoming urgent that the member states, through their national reform plans, create, together with the european union, the conditions for the success of the lisbon objectives, which aim to make europe the best performing economy in the world.
in writing. as every year, the european parliament's report on the broad economic policy guidelines is, in its observations, a catalogue of truisms and, in its proposals, a list of recommendations which the members of this parliament, from the right and the left, adopt with enthusiasm, but which the parties to which they belong take care not to apply when they are in power in their country. in addition to this hypocrisy, i would like to highlight three points which i found surprising: the total absence of reference to the unjustified interest rate increases by the european central bank, which contribute to the stagnation of the euro area; the report considers the european union to be a perfectly homogeneous area, composed of countries facing very similar problems, whereas situations have become extremely heterogeneous since the last enlargement. the demand for european legislation that is 'compatible with that of our competitors' may be an unacceptable call to action, at least in social and environmental terms. if we did not already consider that the whole of brussels' policy is largely responsible for our economic difficulties, these three points would have been sufficient to justify our negative vote.
in writing. i did not approve of the broad guidelines of economic policies which have only endorsed the liberal guidelines of the eu for several years and are the cause of weak growth, unemployment, the precariousness of employees, the decline of our social protections. the report does not support any of the guidelines for an alternative policy: support for purchasing power, raising wages to boost popular consumption and growth; support for ambitious public investment for modernisation and employment; harmonisation of taxation and upward social standards to combat dumping; the european council in brussels in december last year called for the creation of a genuine economic government capable of competing with the ecb.
for the gue/ngl group mr president, commissioners, in any battle, it is in the interest of each individual to evaluate each stage correctly. we should not underestimate the successes, which can lead to a feeling of failure, nor should we overestimate what we think we have achieved, which can lead to disappointment. in the case of the so-called 'bolkestein' directive, where are we in this respect? the points made by the opponents of the original text at parliament's first reading are undeniable. the abolition of the country of origin principle and the adjustment of the actual application of the directive are the most emblematic setbacks imposed on the hardliners of liberal europe. the exclusion of a number of fields of activity from the scope of the directive and the granting to the host state of a power of control, even if limited, conditional and difficult to exercise, are also not negligible elements. finally, the exclusion of labour law brings us back to the law in force today. we shall be looking at the commission's new text with a magnifying glass. if it appeared that the company was trying to recover part of the land it had to give up, in particular by granting itself a right of control a priori, this would be an unacceptable claim in our view. if, on the other hand, it turns out that the commission has incorporated parliament's demands into its new version of the draft directive, this would be both a further sign of the growing weight of our parliament in the european institutional triangle and also, and perhaps above all, confirmation of the structuring effect of the citizens' entry into the european debate, particularly since a certain 29 may 2005. that is to say, our group has no inclination to tolerate these developments. that said, and in any event, does the result achieved so far have the effect of stopping this spiraling of competition between workers against which our fellow citizens are rising up more and more massively? that's the real question, and our answer is no. the amendments to the directive, which go beyond the exceptions set out above, consolidate the rules establishing a system of integration based not on the harmonization of legislation but on the free market. the current state and major trends of the community acquis would merit renewed attention in this respect, particularly at a time of enlargement of the union to countries with social standards attractive to economic and political leaders obsessed with lowering costs and removing 'barriers to competitiveness' in the famous open market economy where competition is free and undistorted. how far are we prepared to go from this repressive logic? at a time when the great debate on the future of the european union is taking place, this is a central issue on which i propose to open the debate, particularly on the left.
mr president, the council and the commission have taken note of the vote on the gebhardt report on the services directive and we can only welcome it. for once we are in the majority, we do not hide our pleasure. we have done a great deal to eliminate the most objectionable elements of the services directive, starting with the famous country of origin principle. however, a number of areas remain in the shadow, particularly with regard to economic services of general interest, and it will be for the council to resolve them, in agreement with parliament. for now, the danger is elsewhere. the commission is considering a more liberal revision of the directive on the posting of workers, which could partially cancel out the legislative work of the european parliament. finally, we condemn in the strongest possible terms the commission's decision to prosecute france for adopting anti-opa decrees in 11 sensitive and strategic sectors, particularly in the field of defence. the commission prefers to play against its own side rather than defend europe's well-understood interests in the wto or on world markets. it is therefore up to the states to correct this institutional and political anomaly.
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, we believe that the final text we have to reach must respect the balance that the members of this parliament have reached. if a directive on the free movement of services has to be adopted, it is because it is a real necessity, not at any price. the commission's original draft was a clumsy, misunderstood, reckless text. parliament has today completely revised this text, making it possible to complete the internal market while preserving our social model. we are grateful to you, commissioner, for giving up the temptation and we suggest that you join parliament in working out a compromise. the ball is now in the council's court, and we expect it to act as a responsible co-legislator. the services directive is now a building whose balance rests on pillars of equal importance to us. to question either of them would be to risk bringing down the whole structure. the council cannot ignore the political message we have sent it. commissioner, the vote in parliament on services has paved the way. our fellow citizens would not understand that we were going backwards.
the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the following areas: madam president, mr president-in-office of the council, commissioners, this debate is essential. finally, it deals with the commission's monopoly of legislative initiative. indeed, whether it is better regulation or lawmaking, what matters is how the initiative for legislation is taken. and if the treaties have granted the commission a monopoly of initiative, it is because it must represent the general interest. it must embody this capacity not merely to be the sounding board for the various industries concerned but to represent all those who cannot necessarily organise themselves. in this sense, i think we are all convinced that better regulation is important for business, but that it must also sometimes translate into more legislation. and this is what parliament said very clearly to you, mr barroso, when your commission proposed to withdraw 68 proposals for legislation and when, very clearly, for example, we said that legislation was needed on mutual funds. i have tabled an opinion on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs on mr gargani's report on the simplification of legislation and i would like to make three comments on this. first, we must be aware that in this area, of course, any technical question obscures the political question of content: what is being simplified? what community acquis is being developed behind simplification? secondly, some people sometimes think that better regulation is synonymous with self-regulation. in the committee on economic and monetary affairs we have, with the example of accounting standards, the absolute example of a situation where, in the absence of very precise democratic control, dangerous deviations sometimes arise. finally, the search for simplification must also lead to the introduction of better-designed legislation, where parliament defines the principles, the rest being referred to committee procedure. as you know, we fully support such an approach as long as it is based on an agreement on comitology which fully recognises the rights of the co-legislator in this area, namely the european parliament.
the committee on constitutional affairs has tabled a number of amendments to the report. madam president, i would like to thank mr gargani for the clarity and commitment of his report. i welcome the fact that a very large part of my opinion has been incorporated and that his report takes up the two objectives which were mine, namely, firstly, the emphasis on the fact that simplification is necessary but must not be achieved in any way, and secondly, the affirmation of parliament's willingness to take part fully in the simplification strategy. we can only welcome any initiative to make the regulatory environment more readable and more coherent. it is impossible to continue to function properly with a body of work of more than 80 000 pages. how can we, in these circumstances, speak to citizens in a credible way about accessibility and transparency? the simplification strategy must therefore be supported in principle. it should eventually lead to community and national standards which are easier to apply and less costly. however, this simplification also has a number of limitations and even dangers, and therefore caution is warranted. the report states in particular that simplification should not result in lowering standards, that there are problems with the application of the interinstitutional agreement governing the recasting procedure and that it is therefore necessary to clarify the applicable rules in order to avoid conflicts of jurisdiction and procedural deadlocks. the report also clearly states the desire of parliament to take part fully in the simplification strategy and it stresses both the need to protect parliament's prerogatives and the question of adapting its rules of procedure. simplification cannot take place outside any democratic control and, in particular, outside the control of parliament. parliament must also consider improving its internal legislative procedures and techniques in the context of simplification. this will be the subject of a specific report which i am responsible for drawing up. finally, as regards alternative forms of regulation, i am pleased that this report calls for strict control of the use of co-regulation and self-regulation, since it is essential to provide safeguards in this area.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, under the guise of a technical debate, there is a debate of great political importance. it is better to legislate, but without deregulating and without dismissing the legislator himself. in this respect, i would like to express my strongest reservations about certain mechanisms such as alternative regulatory mechanisms such as regulation and self-regulation. they have their function, but in the interests of citizens and consumers, in my view, these remedies should in no way replace the law, which confers rights but also duties and is therefore the most legitimate democratic tool. as regards the consultation prior to the legislative process, i invite the three institutions to organise, alongside economic operators, the effective participation of the social partners and civil society in its diversity. it is the responsibility of public authorities to support the organisation of these actors throughout europe, associations of consumers, users of public services, associations fighting against exclusion or popular education. finally, let me comment on the simplification slide programme which is supposed to facilitate the lisbon strategy. i am surprised that it includes as a priority the reworking of the organic regulation when producers in this sector are not asking for much and that at the same time proposals as important as those on the status of the mutual and the european association have been withdrawn from the legislative programme.
madam president, you are a leading expert on ancient japan in the tokugawa period, when the people were deliberately kept in the dark about laws classified as state secrets and whose knowledge was reserved for a small number of high-ranking lords, because it was thought that in this way the people were kept in a much higher standard of which they were completely unaware. well, i sometimes wonder if we are not actually taking inspiration from this ancient japanese legislation. in fact, ladies and gentlemen, i believe that the complexity of european law is the perverse effect of a group dynamic in which we are fully involved. what's this about? firstly, the initiative belongs to the commission, but behind each commissioner there is of course the directorate-general and the officials who make up that directorate-general. then it goes to the council. the council is theoretically composed of ministers. they agree on a text, provided that each of their respective bureaucracies includes all the standards that must appear in the joint draft, and then the text is sent to parliament, which appoints a rapporteur. and naturally the rapporteur - and rightly so - wants to leave his name in history. it will leave a much better mark if it adds standards rather than if it removes them, not to mention the colleagues who table amendments, the important role of lobbies, etc. this is how we arrive, ladies and gentlemen, at a veritable normative monster. i have been in this parliament for 17 years and in the first year that i sat here a debate on the simplification of community law was already taking place. i feel that we are exactly where we were 17 years ago, except that the situation has gotten worse. so what do you need? we need to agree on the meaning of the terms. we need a real dictionary of community law, a code such as the civil code, the commercial code or the criminal code, which is rationally organized, divided into parts, subparts, chapters, sections and articles, so that when we are working on a text we know in advance that we are going to amend this or that article. in short, a great effort is required to simplify. i fear that despite the good intentions of the rapporteurs, we are not quite there. thank you.
vice-president of the commission. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your kind words. let me try to explain again what this is and what it is not about. it's not about less legislation. it is not about worse legislation, it is not about deregulation, it is not about neoliberal market radicalism. it is simply a matter of designing the european legal system in a way that citizens can understand it, and designing it in a way that the european economy can use it to grow, invest and create jobs. it is really the simplest thing in the world, and i am always amazed at what motives can be conjectured behind such a clear and unambiguous concept. whether or not we think we have too many european laws and that they may not always be good enough, it does not matter at all. it is not a matter of belief that we are talking about here, but we are talking about the fact that a shockingly high proportion of european citizens are convinced that this is the case. we are talking about the fact that the european businessmen and the european trade unions are unanimous in saying that this is the case. too much bureaucracy, too many laws, too complicated laws, too many unnecessary restrictions. it doesn't matter if it's true, it matters that those for whom we make the laws are convinced that it is true. so something had to be done. the better regulation project proposed by the commission works with all the instruments mentioned here - different ways of simplifying and modernising the law without changing its content. i must say it again: it is not about changing the substance of regulations, but about making them user-friendly and transparent. i would like to ask the european parliament to support me once again. it is really two big, different projects. the first project is the retrospective review of the entire legal framework. let's not kid ourselves. when european integration was still in its infancy, laws were made from different points of view than today, and if we go back a little further, we find some very surprising things in the annals of our law books. no one disputes that it needs to be modernized. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the question to be asked is: how do we want to make arrangements in the future? how do we want to make laws in the future? in this context, the issue of impact assessment plays a very central role. i support all those in this room who say, it is imperative in a democracy that the legislator knows what the consequences of his actions are for those affected. that does not mean that the legislator refrains from doing something if he knows that. it will always be a matter of balance. when the commission tells you that legislation is costing the economy x billion euros, but tells you on the other hand that it is necessary to introduce this legislation to meet the needs of citizens to protect their health, the balancing act is not difficult. the commission will then say: the protection of the health of citizens is paramount, even at a cost. i want to make it clear that impact assessment does not automatically mean that when it turns out that we are doing something that also has a cost, we simply say: we are not doing it. it's about knowing exactly what we're doing. important thoughts have been expressed here on how best to organise such an impact assessment, and i will tell you frankly: we are in the middle of a process of discussion in the commission on this issue, and both president barroso and i really believe that we have to change the current system. i fully share the view of those who have said here that the final decision on the validity of an impact assessment cannot be taken by those who have made it, and it cannot be the sole responsibility of those who make the relevant legislation to deal with an impact assessment. president barroso and i agree. we're discussing the best possible solution. the president said in his opening statement that he was considering setting up an independent body under his own responsibility to review the impact assessment. we are therefore happy to continue to talk to parliament. the same applies to the comitology procedure, where we largely support parliament's concerns, and to all the other suggestions that have been made here. i would like to remind you once again that this is a project which we must not treat in a technical, bureaucratic or formal way. it's a highly political project, highly political! it is intended to help to strengthen citizens' confidence in the overall system of european integration and to help to provide our economy with a stable and reliable framework for solving the great social question of our time, the question of the future of our jobs.
european legislation is too complex and sometimes superfluous: an intelligent renovation must make it possible to combat this unhealthy and damaging opacity! on the one hand, improvements are needed by reducing and simplifying existing legislation. in this simplification work, as in all new measures adopted, the principles of proportionality and subsidiarity must be respected: the european union where necessary, when it is more efficient than the states acting alone, as much as necessary, but not more than necessary. the application of these apparently technical principles implies judging their social, cultural or other appropriateness, even though no effective control mechanism for their application exists! this gap was filled by the draft constitution. in the meantime, we must ask ourselves how they are being applied. on the other hand, the control of the transposition of community law must be improved, because legal uncertainty is undermining the competitiveness of our enterprises. the establishment of national correspondents is a positive measure if the controls include a quantitative and qualitative analysis and an analysis of the impact on the social, economic and ecological environment. these impact analyses must be comparable and therefore must be standardised. to achieve this, the european parliament must strengthen its power in this area.
author. mr commissioner, i believe that when the commission has been notified of the first employment contract, it will be important for it to be able to draw up a precise analysis of the conditions under which this law authorizes, in respect of young people under the age of 26, treatment which allows the employment contract to be terminated during the first two years. as you said, directive 2078 allows for differential treatment, including age-related treatment, but only in the context of positive measures, measures which are proportionate to the objective pursued. recently, a judgment was handed down by the court of justice - mangold judgment of 22 november 2005 - which concerned another piece of legislation, the german hartz 4 law on provisions for older workers. the court held that the method of renewing fixedterm contracts solely for these older workers was not proportionate to the objective pursued. i believe that in the case of the first employment contract, no one can consider that the measure in question is favourable to young people under the age of 26. it is therefore discrimination against them, depriving them of the benefit of a number of elements of labour law. i hope that the commission will rely on the case law of the court of justice to condemn this epc.

the agenda calls for the commission's declaration on world health day.
member of the commission. mr president, the global shortage of doctors, nurses and other health professionals has reached a crisis point in many parts of the world. ageing populations in europe, the united states and most wealthy countries, combined with increasingly sophisticated medical treatments that require specialised staff, mean that demand for health workers in the developed world is outstripping supply. indeed, the demand for health workers is not only outstripping our internal capacity to produce doctors and nurses: it is placing a huge strain on the international market for health workers. however, the shortage of health workers in rich nations does not even begin to approach the severe shortages being experienced in many parts of africa, where the lack of health workers can often mean the difference between life and death. with less than one health worker per 1000 people in africa, compared to over 10 health workers per 1000 people in europe, it is hardly surprising that the shocking and unacceptable death toll of children and their mothers continues. more than one in five children die before their fifth birthday and more than one in a hundred mothers die as a result of complications of pregnancy in many african countries. progress towards the millennium development goals in africa is unacceptably slow, with progress reversal in some countries as a consequence of hiv/aids. the burden of caring for the sick falls on families and communities who have few resources to cope with this significant burden. the world health report for 2006 focuses international attention on the health worker shortage, and is very much welcomed. it puts a spotlight on a crisis that has been evolving over many years, but that now represents probably the most significant barrier to progressing towards the health-related millennium development goals – reducing maternal and child mortality and controlling communicable diseases such as hiv/aids, tb and malaria. without doctors, nurses, pharmacists and other health workers, it will be impossible to improve healthcare, or to meet our commitments to increase access to essential services. the causes of this crisis are complex. there has been chronic under-investment in health services in developing countries for many years, including under-investment in training of health workers. many countries in africa are still trying to run their health services on a budget of less than eur 10 per capita – that is much less than the minimum of eur 30 recognised as necessary for providing essential services. but the problem is not just lack of investment in africa. many countries in europe and elsewhere have underinvested and inadequately planned for health worker training to meet the needs of ageing populations. the rich world can attract health workers from other countries; the consequences for poor countries is that they train health workers who leave the country, effectively providing a perverse subsidy to health services in developed countries, by shouldering the burden of training costs. training more health workers worldwide is only part of the solution. many health workers who are trained do not want to work in the poorest and most remote areas where needs are greatest. there is a pattern of internal migration from rural to urban areas, and from the public to the private sector, and from poor countries to richer neighbouring countries and then to the richer, developed world. however, it is difficult to blame the individual, once you have seen the conditions under which they have to work. we need to better understand the motivations of health workers, and to create incentive systems that encourage them to work where there is the greatest need. the ‘push’ factors of poor working conditions, low salaries – which are paid irregularly, lack of drugs and equipment and lack of career prospects all contribute to the migration of health workers. indeed, it is surprising that, given these poor conditions, you still get a hard core of dedicated health workers in many african countries who continue to do a remarkable job in very difficult circumstances. it is important not to lose sight of the achievement and the increasable contribution of many health workers who continue to serve their people, despite the challenges of their jobs and working environment. the ‘pull’ factors for migration – better salaries in rich countries, better working conditions and greater security, which are sometimes coupled with aggressive recruitment practices by private recruitment agencies – also play a significant role in increasing health worker mobility. these issues have all been described in the communication from the commission to parliament on the eu strategy of action to address the crisis in human resources for health in developing countries. if we are to overcome the crisis, developing solutions must begin in the countries most affected and must support strengthening of their planning and financing of health worker training, support and finance, and improved terms of conditions of services. it is essential that country action be supported by regional and global action, sharing knowledge and best practice, sharing training resources and changing international recruitment policies to make them more ethical. it is important that we look closely at our own health worker training programmes and increase our own production capacity, to make us more self-sufficient. the commission has been leading and coordinating the development of a coherent european response. the communication on human resources for health has been debated and strong conclusions are due to be adopted by the council. eu member states have agreed a statement of commitment, which is being announced for world health day. that should demonstrate to the rest of the world that europe takes this issue seriously and will support a significant response to the crisis.

nearly 11 billion euros to date, which naturally raises questions about the procedure and the ambition of the projects discussed, because it is intolerable that 11 billion euros may not yet have been union will allocate an additional 50 billion euros a year to this budget, even though it had politically committed to only spending half of this amount on africa, namely 25 billion euros. it is clear wonder about the share of aid to developing countries (dacs) that will be managed by the european union, which will be around 20%. in this case, although the word may be a little strong, the edf will be relegated to the status of a marginal aid instrument. the problem of budgetizing it, which is absolutely necessary and must be done as soon as possible, and of its 'fungibility', that is, the possibility of giving very ambitious regional projects, such as railway infrastructure, a place in the general framework of action of the european union, is therefore even more acute. this would ensure coordination between the member states and the european union. the edf can become this lever of coordination and the joint parliamentary assembly can become a specific element of control, since all the least developed countries in the world are members of the joint parliamentary assembly. finally, there is the problem of the readability of the european union's action. what i have just described as community expenditure on development aid is paid for by our taxpayers. as such, the action must be legible because the populists should not take the figures i have announced to you and exclaim: "what the hell are you doing with all this money?" we therefore need a political vision and clarity of this issue.

for the greens/efa group mr president, i would also like to thank margrietus van den berg for her excellent report. he'll be covered with laurels, that's what he is. it is clear that the fight against corruption is absolutely essential, not only for the effectiveness of european aid but also for its credibility. how can we convince our fellow citizens or the member states to give more if corruption is still rampant? it is also a condition for the viability of a rule of law and an economy. it is therefore a vital battle that we must constantly fight, a battle that has become somewhat more complex with economic globalisation, because of the easy movement of capital, and also because of the new process of budgetary support at the level of the european union. the rapporteur stresses all the issues raised by this new system of budget support in the fight against corruption, as well as the increased difficulty in the present context, due to the increasing pressure on raw materials and, in particular, on oil energy, which is becoming scarce. there is also reason to fear a resurgence of corruption in the quest for access to the last remaining fossil-fuel reserves, as well as an increase in conflicts over arms trade and smuggling. the arms and oil industries are the two major sectors, on a macro-economic scale, in which considerable corruption is taking place. the rapporteur rightly stresses two issues: transparency and accountability. transparency is essential if we are to have a clear and precise picture of the budgets that are being used. in this area, we must indeed support much more vigorously a number of initiatives such as the publish what you pay initiative or the extractive industries initiative, which have the disadvantage of being based on voluntary work only. we need to make progress in the area of law rather than simply relying on the goodwill of economic or political actors to publish, if they wish, the accounts or the income they pay to the governments concerned. budgeting oil and mining revenues is also an essential aspect of budgetary transparency, but the european union must make this a condition for not being able to give budgetary aid to a government which does not clearly disclose the profits it derives from the oil, mining or forestry industries. public opinion cannot understand that the european union continues to help countries which, normally, should have a large budget to finance the proper functioning of a state. finally, the report states that a government's military expenditure must also be disclosed. the role of national parliaments and civil society must be strengthened, including financially, with increased support to enable both parliaments and civil society to play their role in this area. the last point is transparency with regard to the various donors. the governments of these countries are also helped by cities, regions or states at all levels, and we lack a database that would indicate what is really paid by this country, this state, this region or this city. but we don't have that data today, and that also fuels corruption. i therefore think, in conclusion, that we must sweep up our own house, as has been said, and that corruption is also a matter of concern in the european union. the question of the exercise of power, of the financing of political life, arises in the north as well as in the south.
member of the commission. mr president, i welcome the debate that we have had here today. i think it is important to underline that the problem of fraud can never be considered as solved. constant vigilance at all levels and in all circumstances is needed in the high-risk field of external actions. these actions are carried out in poorly governed states, where countervailing powers and mainstreaming good governance practices in all eu-funded programmes and projects on the one hand, and in the implementation of specific programme interventions on the other hand. country strategy papers and national indicative programmes between the european union and beneficiary countries generally include specific interventions in the fields of rule of law, democratisation, public administration reform, public finance management and reinforcement of civil society. i shall now make a few comments on some of the questions that have been raised today. on the discussion on companies, we must make sure that companies do not benefit from corruption. we must do the best we can. we can exclude companies from participation in our tenders if they have been found guilty of fraud or corruption. we can also suspend a project that has been financed if we discover fraud or corruption at some stage. we once used that option on a project in zimbabwe. on support for national parliaments, the commission sees the strengthening of the national parliaments’ supervisory role as an important means of trying to improve the overall effectiveness and impact of our development effort in these countries. for instance, through the edf and the budget line for south africa, the capacities of national parliaments of some 11 acp countries have been strengthened to a total amount of eur 35 million since 2000. on the subject of watchdogs, it is true that we work with private sector organisations. we would be worse off if we did not have these watchdogs. several members raised public spending is at the heart of our budget support programmes. finally, through its permanent dialogue with the partner governments and the various regions, the commission encourages the broadest possible participation of institutions at various levels, particularly at parliamentary level. i have noted the view on the positive influence of the participation of women.

in writing. i voted in favour of the report by my colleague monica frassoni on the recent reports of the european commission on the monitoring of the application of community law. this report was highly anticipated as a follow-up to the december 2003 institutional agreement entitled 'better lawmaking' aimed at reducing the volume of community legislation while simplifying it and with a view to ensuring that legislation is normally applied everywhere, which is a necessary condition for the creation of an area of law. unfortunately, it is clear that the member states are not transposing community legislation correctly and, worse, are not applying it correctly, with impunity, which the european commission is complicit in. it should be remembered that it is the member states which are responsible for monitoring the application of community law. everyone can see how the current system is not working and is a factor of division between the european construction and the citizens who measure every day the injustice of this situation. the undersigned wonders whether the time has not come to consider the creation of a european body of independent inspectors whose task would be to monitor the application of community legislation in the member states.
in writing. the reports put to the vote today show that the application of community law is becoming increasingly difficult and that more cases are being brought before the court of justice. at 31 december 2003, the 21st commission report shows that 3 927 infringement cases were under examination, compared with 2 270 in 1999 and only 124 in 1978. the reasons are the abundance of community law, but also the importance of the european commission's repressive arsenal against member states that would be reluctant to apply community legislation. the question of the application of community law is first and foremost a political question, not a legal or technocratic one as some think and claim. the main aim is to hide the problem of the conflicts between national sovereignty and european power. in this respect, the recent judgment of 13 september 2005 of the court of justice of the european communities, which for the first time operates a kind of communitization of criminal law, and this, without any legal basis, is symptomatic of the evolution of this institution. it is therefore understandable that member states are reluctant to apply community law which they have not chosen.

in writing. i voted in favour of the report by my colleague arlene mccarthy on a european parliament motion for a resolution on the implementation, consequences and impact of the legislation in force on the internal market. the application of european legislation is a permanent source of division between the european construction and the peoples. it is therefore urgent to introduce the necessary coherence between community legislation, its transposition by the member states and its practical application. unnecessary legislation must be stopped and necessary legislation properly implemented. the undersigned supports the idea that the european parliament should be closely associated with the monitoring of the application of european legislation by the member states. in addition, given the problems encountered in applying community law, the committee wondered whether the time had not come to consider the creation of a european body of independent inspectors directly linked to the european union, whose task would be to monitor the application of community legislation in the member states for the normal functioning of the internal market.
in writing. one of the reasons for the non-application of european directives and texts by the member states of the union, which is curiously not mentioned in any of the reports, is in particular the way in which they are adopted. this is the perverse effect of extending qualified majority voting in the council: states which are in the minority and have refused to adopt a text for reasons of their own will naturally have difficulty applying it in their territory. all this obviously creates a real legal uncertainty for all the institutions, countries and peoples. the priorities must therefore be to rapidly codify existing community legislation, but also to provide a framework and limit the powers of the various union bodies, including the court of justice, which are so prolific in creating the law, so that the member states no longer have to bear the consequences of too many and too restrictive legal or case-law rules.
in writing. it is a good thing that legislation which is unnecessary, harmful, in contradiction with other community provisions or, above all, incompatible with the stated principles of subsidiarity and proportionality can be withdrawn from the legislative process. but the satisfaction is soon eclipsed by the description of the commission's exorbitant legislative powers. this institution - which, i would remind you, has absolutely no democratic or electoral legitimacy - can, at any time and at its own discretion, withdraw or amend a legislative proposal, inform parliament of the reasons for its decision or not, take parliament's opinion into account or not, in short, do whatever it wants. the worst part is that this parliament is content to take note of it. it is true that he is making a vague threat of censure against the commission in case it really goes too far. but we know that even at the height of the scandals that had engulfed the santer commission, he never had the political courage to disavow the 'symbolic institution' of the european superstate. the fact that a technocracy is exercised with the tacit consent of an assembly does not change its nature.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, to vote on these financial perspectives would be to dismiss ourselves and not to give europe the means to achieve its ambitions. in june 2005, parliament voted almost unanimously for €974 billion. this is the key to success in enlargement, a policy of active growth, support for research and preparation for the future. today, these same people are preparing to vote on the amputation of the financial perspective of 110 billion euros. sorry about that. and understand who can. to vote for this would be to consider that there is a two-speed enlargement: yesterday's enlargement to the south, which allowed greece, portugal and spain to develop fully; today's enlargement to the east, which inspires a discourse of greater pomp and circumstance, all the more so because it conceals insufficient funding. i would wager on all the benches in this house that we will have to suffer the long litany of regrets about an insufficient budget, month after month, year after year, report after report, but it will be too late. today the european parliament must confirm that it is the driving force of european life. to quote the words of the bolivian president, evo morales ayma, who came to visit us here the day before yesterday: 'let us not lie to each other, let us not be weak, let us be strong, let us not accept financial prospects which are financial prospects at a discount'.
the financial perspective, which amounts to eur 864 316 billion in commitment appropriations, is the disappointing result of a compromise between the commission, the council and parliament which has weakened the european spirit and threatened to paralyse the union. the eu27 will have a relatively smaller budget for 2007-13 than the eu15. even if the cap funding is preserved and the budget for smes appears to be strengthened, the galileo project, the transeuropean transport networks, research, regional policy, education and training, culture will be sacrificed. the rigorous rules on national budgets did not allow for an increase in national contributions, which explains the approval of this compromise by meps. the budget is unfair, complex and no longer able to finance future policies, and it must be reformed. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a common position on the proposal for a directive on the approximation of the laws of the member states relating to the labelling of foodstuffs. these resources would be equitable, legible, controlled by democratic procedures and consistent. the revision of the community budget, planned for 2008, must allow us to make this reform possible without amending the basic treaties, by agreement between the european parliament, the commission and the council acting unanimously.
in writing. one of the causes of counterfeiting is the fraudulent copying of designs. it is the theft of business intelligence that distorts international trade rules and causes the loss of about 100,000 jobs in the eu every year. it is also a danger to consumers when copied products can harm their health or safety. finally, it is a source of tax and social fraud which weighs heavily on the accounts of the states. all the means to combat this scourge must therefore be constantly strengthened. the protection of designs - the hallmark of creativity and innovation in business - is an essential part of the anti-counterfeiting arsenal. but international registration is often a complicated and costly process, especially for smes. all measures to simplify these procedures and to save money will therefore encourage companies to comply with them and will have a positive impact on research and innovation. the report by michel rocard on accession to the geneva act on the international registration of industrial designs is in line with this and i have therefore supported it.
in writing. europe is going through a dual crisis, institutional and political. a strong bond of trust must be re-established between european citizens and their institutions. the first sign that political leaders must address their citizens to restore this trust is to have a budget that is commensurate with the ambitions they are displaying. at a time when the eu is opening up to new countries, when we need more than ever a europe that is strong in the world, a social and competitive europe, the budget proposed to us today is not acceptable. implementation of the lisbon strategy, development of r & d, education and training, external development aid and cooperation, transnational infrastructure projects, structural funds and cohesion funds sufficient to demonstrate the necessary solidarity with the new countries: all this will be achieved only a minima. moreover, any new policy is impossible, any recovery is inconceivable, it is the budget of sclerosis and renunciation. that is why i cannot vote for financial perspectives which forget the european interest in favour of national egoism and disappoint our peoples as to the future of europe.
in writing. i voted on the financial perspective of the european union for the years 2007 to 2013 on the basis of the böge report, and in the light of the long, painful and distressing negotiations which have taken place since the first half of 2005. i did so not because i thought it was the best or the least bad budget, but because it was the only one possible and because i did not want to be part of the group of those who would not hesitate to aggravate the crisis facing the european union with a budgetary crisis that would not have been understood either by our citizens or by the new member states that joined in 2004. it should be remembered that it is not the european union that is in financial crisis but the member states, some of which are on the verge of financial bankruptcy due to a disastrous management of national public finances. we must get rid of the british rebate which has been poisoning european relations for too long. finally, i am pleased that this agreement, together with the 2008/2009 review clause, is the beginning of the indispensable reform of the eu's finances, which is becoming an indispensable and urgent step in the process of european integration.
in writing. i voted in favour of the böge report because the absence of an agreement on the financial perspective for 2007-2013 could destabilise the european union in its work from next year onwards. i pay tribute to the parliament's negotiators led by mr böge, who obtained an additional 4 billion euros for important initiatives in the fields of competitiveness, education, research and youth exchanges. i deeply regret that the council has not agreed to allocate more resources to european farmers, particularly in the field of rural development, where an amount of eur 20 billion less will be available compared to the commission's proposal. i take this opportunity to remind the council of its obligations to ensure that the principles of the 2003 cap reform are respected. i am completely opposed to the council's proposal on voluntary modulation which transfers 20% of direct aid to rural development without any obligation to co-finance. such a system is unacceptable as it could destabilise the market and could be a first step towards the renationalisation of the cap. (parliament adopted the legislative resolution)
in writing. like the french socialists, i voted against the böge report which endorses the interinstitutional agreement on the financial perspective for 2007-13. our parliament rejected a budget last january which it considered to be mediocre at the time, considering that it did not provide the necessary financial levers for employment, growth, research and the large transeuropean networks. on 6 march the committee on budgets unanimously adopted a resolution condemning the financial perspective and calling for negotiations between the commission, the council and parliament to result in a budget more in line with parliament's wishes. the balance is still not there today and the budgetary arbitrages needed to meet the justified and ever-increasing demands to finance all eu policies will be very difficult in the coming years. we will have to explain to the european citizens that the responsibility for this budget of austerity lies with the intransigence of the heads of state and government who have refused to give the union the means to achieve its ambitions.
in writing. i voted against the european budget for 2007-2013 because i believe it represents a dramatic lack of european ambition and a return to intergovernmental logic which i disapprove of and which will paralyse all european public action, at the expense of european citizens. at €864 billion, or 1.05% of the gross international product of the 25 member states, the financial perspective does not match the historic enlargement of europe to ten new member states and the challenges ahead. i believe that we are far from the requirements set out at the start of the negotiations (in june 2005 the european parliament voted for a budget of €974 billion, or 1.18% of gdp); the budget is unfortunately accompanied by a reduction in the structural and cohesion funds, a reduction in competitiveness, growth and employment, and will make any modernisation impossible. as a european elected representative it was therefore my responsibility to reject such an agreement which goes against my idea of a great europe.
in writing. i voted against the sousa pinto and böge reports, which reflect europe's retreat into its national egoism, which undermine any major political project and seriously threaten existing public policies, notably the cap and the structural funds, which are instruments of solidarity for the most fragile regions. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament and the council adopt a common position on the proposal for a directive on the approximation of the laws of the member states relating to the labelling of foodstuffs for human consumption. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment in the event of a natural disaster is a very good one. the union's cohesion policy is undergoing the same drastic cuts, with a 10% drop in the structural funds/cohesion funds, even as many european regions are suffering from development delays that called, on the contrary, for a substantial effort in the field of community solidarity. the outermost regions, which are directly affected by this budget surrender, will also not be able to count on the development of new regional synergies, with the european neighbourhood and partnership instrument losing an additional 6 billion.
in writing. i will not go into a battle of numbers to explain my negative vote on the reports by mr reimer böge and mrs sousa pinto, both on the financial perspective. i hope that the supporters of this compromise, which they themselves call 'tolerable', will not resent me for having a different ambition for europe and its citizens than their own. i do not want a europe reduced to a simple free trade area modelled on the anglo-saxon model, but rather a europe based on the values of solidarity and sharing between peoples, which have always been the vehicle of european progress. these financial perspectives are dramatically lacking in ambition for the future of the european project and serve only intergovernmentalism. with a 37% reduction in growth and competitiveness and a 10% reduction in the cohesion funds, they destroy any idea of european recovery and forbid any new policy for seven years.
in writing. i voted in favour of the excellent report by my colleague zita plestinska on the proposal for a decision of the european parliament and of the council on the financing of european standardisation. the text proposed by the european commission, which was voted on at first reading, provides a legal basis for the financing of european standardisation. standardization is one of the tools needed to implement community policies, particularly those relating to the internal market and to enhance the competitiveness of enterprises. i am pleased that access to this funding has been extended beyond the traditional beneficiaries usually referred to as european standardisation bodies and to more activities. this is a considerable challenge, especially for those european standards which are in competition with other standards worldwide.
in writing. i voted in favour of the excellent report by my colleague dariusz rosati on public finances in economic and monetary union. it was essential to state that the situation of public finances is very worrying, not to mention that some member states are in a situation of financial bankruptcy. moreover, it is clear that the community procedures, whether the stability and growth pact (sgp) or the excessive deficit procedure (edp), are only imperfectly capable of resolving this dramatic situation or are ineffective in a context where weak economic growth and social requirements are undermining the european union's capacity to reform. the lack of political will to bring reason back into the necessary budgetary adjustments is reflected in a dramatic increase in debt. how long will this irresponsibility ... ? it has become incomprehensible that the heads of the executive bodies of the member states concerned do not understand, through common sense and the examination of success stories around the world (canada, denmark, for example), that sound public finances are essential to achieve more growth and employment.
for the greens/efa group mr president, this year the subcommittee decided to change the structure of the annual report on human rights. it is no longer an assessment of the situation in the countries, but a report on the implementation by the commission, the council and parliament of the european union's instruments for the promotion of human rights and democracy. we did it, even though it was difficult. we can congratulate the rapporteur and the political groups. the role of the parliament is to guide, monitor and evaluate the policy of the council and the commission. that is why it is essential that parliament continues to draw up its own report. if we were to write a three-handed report, for example, we could not criticise the action of a member state - which we can do with the present report - because it would be enough for that member state to veto it. the amendment we have tabled to article 8 goes in that direction. mr howitt's report puts forward a number of interesting and innovative proposals for mechanisms to promote human rights. the report advocates, in particular, qualified majority voting in the council and possible restrictive measures against a third country. it is logically part of the continuation of the report adopted by parliament: the agnoletto report. it also proposes to ensure that the newly created un human rights council is not chaired by of goods. the report also stresses the need to develop human rights policies in parliament which are transversal. it is in this spirit that the subcommittee proposed that delegations be allowed to submit nominations for the sakharov prize. the report refers to violations of the rights of tolerance in some member states, the use of torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or the return of implementing one of the first such programmes in belarus, a country which is responsible for numerous human rights violations, has no diplomatic relations with the union and offers no guarantees on the protection of migrants. i don't think these programs are appropriate.

for the greens/efa group mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, we have long subsidized development in the fields of agriculture, industry and transport, which has degraded the environment and led to the alarming situation we are experiencing today, and we are paying the price: natural disasters are the forerunners of these errors. today we are dealing with the damage of these disasters and we all agree to support the victims, to help them rebuild and rebuild their lives after the disaster and to support the disaster fund in order to show solidarity with all these victims and to show that the european parliament is interested and cares for its fellow citizens. however, we also ask, on behalf of the greens, for investment in prevention and restoration, rather than just curing the ills. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment and the environment from the adverse effects of certain substances and preparations is a very good one. what shocks me is that the committee on agriculture is asking that the aid not be charged to the cap. we have just seen a year of a huge battle to secure funding for the conservation of natura 2000 biodiversity, and we have failed. yesterday we all saw that failure. as a reporter for life+, i cannot accept that this program, which is already a real pain in the ass, is being used as insurance against disasters that are becoming less and less natural. the commission has already made a number of proposals in this area. the danube floods are an example. the dams had to be removed because the delta of the danube, which is flooded, was practically dry. today we must ask the crucial question: what kind of agriculture and transport do we want to have tomorrow if we consider the kyoto protocol to be the centrepiece of climate change and the fight against it? we must look for the causes of these changes, and we in the european parliament know them: they are changes in transport modes. yes to a solidarity fund, yes to aid for victims, but let us really look for the causes, otherwise we will be fixing a bottomless pit.
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to congratulate all the rapporteurs, and in particular mr galeote and mr berend, on the accuracy of their reports and the quality of their reporting. i am pleased to note the agreement reached between our parliament and the commission that the scope of the next solidarity fund will now cover not only natural disasters but also industrial accidents, terrorist attacks and major public health crises. i thank the members of the committee on regional development for supporting my amendment to specify that special attention will be paid to remote or isolated regions such as the island and outermost regions. this clarification guarantees the possibility, as from 2007, of making the fund available to the doms, even if they do not fully meet the general eligibility criteria, so that they can benefit from emergency aid in the event of a major crisis. the own-initiative report of the committee on regional development underlines the disastrous impact of these disasters on the economy, employment, natural and cultural heritage, the environment and tourism, and rightly emphasizes the need for effective measures in terms of alert, civil protection and assistance to the regions and populations affected. i thank the rapporteur for including my amendments on the outermost regions in the european strategy which he calls for, aware that, because of their geographical location, these regions are exposed to natural hazards of a specific nature and intensity. in the face of the multiplicity of threats that regularly afflict these regions, from tsunamis and volcanic eruptions, to earthquakes and cyclones, and now the reactivation of the virological risks conveyed by mosquitoes, such as chikungunya in réunion or mad cow disease in guyana, the overseas populations are awaiting an appropriate response from europe in terms of security, prevention and solidarity. our parliament today proves that it has heard them perfectly well.
in writing. as a representative of a french region particularly affected by unemployment and relocations, le nord-pas de calais, i naturally support the ambition expressed in the report to support growth and employment. but european regional policy cannot achieve these objectives. the french cantons of hainaut have already lost structural fund objective 1 funding in 2000. between 2007 and 2013, european regional expenditure will increase by 31%, but as a consequence of unprepared enlargement, the share allocated to french regions will decrease further. above all, european regional aid does not call into question the policy of a europe without frontiers in brussels, which, while confining our companies and farmers to increasingly restrictive directives, leaves them to the savage competition of countries like china, which practice genuine social dumping. almost a year ago the french and dutch peoples said 'no' to this europe of economic stagnation and social regression. only a different europe, based on the sovereignty of its nations and on free cooperation, will enable our countries to enjoy genuine economic and social growth.
in writing. i voted in favour of the excellent report by my colleague, mr rolf berend, on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council establishing the european social fund at first reading. the fund, which was set up in 2002 and is only responsible for natural disasters, needed to be reformed urgently in order to broaden its scope, simplify its use in the face of emergencies and, finally, avoid abuse. major changes in climate, industry and technology, but also terrorism, health risks, etc., made it essential for the european union to provide its citizens and member states with a tool capable of coping with a disaster that a member state alone would be helpless to face. the reform of the fund is an essential element of security in today's risky society.
in writing. although the basic idea of the energy community treaty (ect) seems to be good, since it is intended to help the countries of south-east europe which are experiencing considerable difficulties in this field, we believe that this treaty suffers from two major shortcomings. firstly, the treaties do not confer any competence, let alone such important competence, on the european union in the field of energy, the commission having used the provisions on competition policy to confer it. secondly, the ultimate objective of the ect is to create an internal energy market between the european union and nine other countries, even though within the eu this policy has shown its limits: gradual replacement of public monopolies by monopolies or quasi-monopolies with the undermining of public services, increase in electricity prices even in countries whose electricity production is very little dependent on the price of oil, risk of shortages in the short term due to a policy favouring deregulation over security of supply... there were other ways of helping our european neighbours to meet their energy needs than by creating a controversial institutional and political system within the european union itself. but as usual, the europeanist ideology won.
in writing. i voted in favour of the report by my colleague richard howitt on human rights in the world in 2005 and the european union's policy on the matter. at a time when attacks on the great achievements of human rights are permanent and insidious, the role of the european union, a humanist civilization in the making, is essential. the european parliament, as the representative of the citizens of the union, has a heavy and immense responsibility in this respect. first, within the union itself, by ensuring that the member states ratify and implement the major international human rights treaties. secondly, the union, as an area of peace and democracy, must remain the guarantor of human rights in the world by ensuring that our declarations based on our values are followed up in all european policies.
in writing. this report will not improve the human rights situation in the world any more than previous reports on the same subject. but his real goal is elsewhere. it aims to increase the powers of the europe of brussels in foreign policy. in referring to the 'considerable impact that the european union can have on human rights when it speaks with one voice', particularly at the un, and in making proposals to increase this 'impact', mr howit's report is in line with the logic of gradually dispossessing the member states of their sovereignty in foreign policy matters, to the benefit of the european institutions. this is the ambition of the common foreign and security policy, the cfsp, which consists, among other things, in depriving france of its seat as a permanent member of the united nations security council. on the other hand, article 97, which requires european governments to be even more lax than they are with regard to non-european immigration, is endangering the human rights situation in our own countries. the increase in the number of lawless areas in our agglomerations is one of the consequences of the uncontrolled immigration that our peoples have been suffering for the last 30 years.
in writing. the absolute search for prevention and, to this end, the conduct of technological research and development, public awareness, emergency coordination and the deployment of a civilian force in the event of a natural disaster are essential elements that we must plan and implement as soon as possible. i am, however, opposed to any establishment of an observatory. this structure may cost a lot of money for a meagre result. and above all, the funding for the operation of this observatory would cut all the more the necessary support for field activities. it is always very easy to create observatories, but almost impossible to remove them!

for the gue/ngl group mr president, a preliminary remark, if i may, since we are inaugurating a new type of debate today. i think it is not possible to give a serious answer in three or four minutes to a speech ex cathedra of three quarters of an hour, which is more profound. i think we'll have to revise the procedure. i have a lot to say about some of the ideas put forward by mr verhofstadt. for example, the idea of reducing the reasons for the union's crisis to a question of method, which in his view is not federal enough, bypassing the content of economic and social choices. that is an analysis which i find short and which my group does not share. or the idea of establishing, in the name of socioeconomic governance, social maxima alongside the already existing minima. i do not quite understand his reasoning, which seems to me to be going in the wrong direction. i would also like to say a lot about mr verhofstadt's plea for a military europe and its further integration into nato, a plea in which we do not agree. i shall not be able to go into these various points now, because i would like to dwell on another point which i think mr verhofstadt has gone too far too quickly. i think that is the main problem we have today: the reasons for the growing gap between europeans and the union. the results of the commission's consultation do, however, give us valuable information on the origin of this dissatisfaction, and i would like to mention three of them. first, 47% of those interviewed in this consultation see globalisation as a threat to employment. in october 2003, 56% saw this as a good opportunity; they're 20% less in this case today. in october 2003, europe was no more federal than it is today. another result: what is the opinion of the respondents about the role played by the european union in some 15 areas ranging from environmental protection to the fight against terrorism and social policy, with the protection of social rights appearing at the bottom of the list? satisfaction rate: 4.7 out of 10. this has nothing to do with the more or less federal nature of the union. the satisfaction index for europe's ability to combat unemployment, which is at the bottom of the list, is 3.8 out of 10. this is an average of the 25 member states. what would you think of the academic performance of a student who scored 3.8 out of 10 in a core subject? this is the perception of europe's current ability to respond to the problems of globalisation. i think that's the first problem. we can't treat it with a twirl. finally, what do the majority of europeans surveyed consider to be the 'key element for the future of europe'? the answer most often given is to achieve comparable living standards throughout the union. this is the view of 51% of the 25 member states and 74% of the new member states. our new citizens clearly do not want their countries to be a kind of low-cost europe, a discount europe, as businessmen dream of. in short, globalisation is seen as a threat to the social model, and the single market is not seen as a solution to this fundamental problem. the unhampered transatlantic market project on the agenda of the forthcoming eu-us summit will not ease the worries. i think that leaving this part of the debate aside once again will not help us to break the deadlock. only by accepting real changes, not only institutional but also in economic, social and political orientations, will we have a chance of reviving the european dream.
