the rapporteur. madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank all my colleagues for their support of this text and for the efforts made by each of them to find a solution. i also thank the council and the austrian presidency for listening to parliament and making the regulation on paediatric medicines a priority. finally, commissioner, i would like to thank your staff for their technical contribution and the proposals they have made to us. i really enjoyed working with them. thanks to the work of all of us, we will be able to adopt a regulation of great importance for health in europe, and we will be able to do so as soon as the second reading. we all agreed on the objective and our discussions have brought us back to the same point on the implementation of this regulation. it seems inconceivable that in 2006 our children cannot have access to a therapy tailored to their needs. it is a reality. today, many of the medicines given to children are not designed for them. often the products used for the young are the same as those prescribed for adults, only with lower doses and sometimes with catastrophic consequences. a child's metabolism is different from an adult's. children therefore need a specific form of the drug, not only to make it better tolerated but also to make it more effective and safer. with this european regulation we are meeting all the conditions for the creation of paediatric medicines, in particular by supporting innovation and research and by creating incentives for pharmaceutical laboratories, while obliging them to develop a paediatric form for any new medicinal product and to make these products available in all member states. the council had already followed the recommendations of the european parliament at first reading on many points. i am thinking in particular of the incentive system which extends the term of protection certificate for any new paediatric indication by six months. the council also adopted, at first reading, the european parliament's request to avoid additional clinical trials being carried out on children when they are not necessary. by the time we got to the second reading, we had little to disagree with. the commission had to agree on technical details. we have therefore reached an agreement between the three institutions, in particular by applying the principle of better regulation. i am thinking in particular of the question of the independence of the members of the paediatric committee and of pharmacovigilance. we have already adopted strong measures on these points in previous legislation. it is therefore more relevant to refer to it rather than to pile up the rules. this agreement also follows from the european commission's acceptance of our request concerning the use of potentially dangerous substances in the packaging of the medicinal product. we welcome the official declaration which has been presented to us and we naturally expect concrete results. there is also another point to which i would like to draw the attention of the european commission. this is the time between the granting of the marketing authorization and the medicinal product being made available to the patient. there is a directive on transparency, which sets deadlines for fixing the price and refunding the products. the differences between member states in terms of time limits are too great. this situation has negative consequences for patients. i have discussed this with my colleagues from all the groups in this parliament and we would like to ask you what can be done to reduce these disparities. finally, the commission's initial proposal stipulates that any application for extension of the supplementary protection certificate due to a new paediatric indication must be submitted at the latest two years before the expiry of the said certificate. i share this approach, but we must be pragmatic first and foremost. if we adopt such a measure suddenly, we risk being deprived of medicines which, at the time of the implementation of this text, would be in that two-year period. in view of this article, it would then be impossible to carry out investigations to develop a paediatric indication. the transitional clause which we are proposing, with the agreement of a majority of my colleagues, is intended to correct this perverse effect. we therefore ask that for five years any application for extension of the supplementary protection certificate on the basis of a new paediatric indication may be submitted at the latest six months before the expiry of the certificate. after this deadline, the original proposal of the european commission will apply. we appreciate your following us on this point. in conclusion, this text gives us the opportunity to turn words into action in support of our european research: that is what we are going to do tomorrow. there are major debates under way on how best to promote europe to our citizens. europeans need no more fancy phrases, they want action. the regulation on paediatric medicines is a concrete response to this expectation. this text clearly shows the added value of europe in everyday life: a member state acting alone would not have the means to promote such a policy in favour of all children.

in writing. a free trade area is an area without barriers, including customs barriers. it is a common market, like almost all of europe. the transatlantic free trade area is thus a common market from warsaw to san francisco, from helsinki to patagonia and from malta to the canadian far north. while european public opinion imagines that the political debate is about the future of the european constitution, the reality is simply that, from 2010 to 2015, that is to say in 5 years, the construction of a political-economic ensemble of more than 45 nations out of the 193 that the earth counts. the mann report discreetly announces the transition from the european construction to the political construction of the fourth quarter of the world. with a parliament of 45 nations, a common commercial court and the beginnings of common legislation. 90 years later, paul valéry's prediction that "europe aspires to be led by an american commission" is coming true. good-bye europe, hello the world! erika mann has written a double message: the death of the european idea and the birth of the world organization.
in writing. the european union is moving forward with the new member states joining the single currency. the langen report attempts to strike a balance between dogmatic adherence to the maastricht criteria and the stability pact, praise for the euro and common sense considerations about the state of readiness of the countries or even the capacity of the euro area to withstand an enlargement which will increase its heterogeneity and therefore its difficulties. the single currency has a significant role to play in the low growth of the countries that have adopted it (inadequate interest rates, punitive exchange rates, etc.). there is no need to bring new victims into this situation. and i wonder whether the citizens of these countries, who only yesterday shook off the communist yoke, are aware of the irreparable loss of sovereignty that the adoption of the euro represents? are they aware, above all, that the loss of their national currency was scheduled in their accession treaty? it is not a question of informing them about the actual changeover to the euro in their country, but of consulting them again, by referendum, about the disappearance of their currency.

member of the commission. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the environmental policy of the european bank for reconstruction and development (ebrd), which was adopted in april 2003, aims to ensure that projects financed by the bank respect the environment and the applicable regulatory requirements. in this respect, the ebrd reserves the right to reject any project submitted to the governing council where it considers that it does not comply with this policy. it is a publicly acknowledged fact - as the honourable members know - that the policy of the ebrd in relation to environmental standards and the precautionary principle is extremely rigorous. since 2002, the ebrd has been paying particular attention to sajalin 2, working closely with the company, sajalin energy, to assess all aspects of the project, in particular its environmental and social impacts, and to develop appropriate monitoring and mitigation measures in line with the bank's environmental policy. however, the commission acknowledges that there have been and continue to be significant concerns with respect to the sajalin 2 project, in particular with regard to the protection of the western grey whale population living in the area. the bank has responded to this concern by helping to set up a group of renowned scientists, with the participation of representatives of non-governmental organisations, to monitor the situation of whales and propose measures to reduce the potential negative impacts of the project. the company has implemented these measures and the latest comments from the group have been largely positive. in another difficult issue, river crossing, the bank has also been firm, calling for improvements in the company's performance and, in particular, the development of a river crossing strategy that imposes restrictions and ensures that there will be no net loss of salmon spawning areas. in short, the ebrd has put considerable pressure on sajalin energy to improve the environmental quality of the project. we will soon have new information from ongoing evaluations and public consultations which will enable the community manager to the ebrd, the european commission representative to the ebrd, to take a position on the degree to which the project is in line with the bank's environmental policy.

mr president, commissioner, on 13 september 2005 the court of justice of the european communities recognised the possibility for the community legislator to take criminal measures to ensure the effectiveness of the standards it sets. everyone understood - at any rate, in vienna, we understood - that the court had turned the principle of subsidiarity upside down to decide that, as far as community law is concerned, it was not worthwhile for the states to ensure its observance since the brussels commission could do it alone. the commission has obviously not failed to address this gap: while, strictly speaking, this new criminal jurisdiction concerns only the environment, a commission communication of november 2005 extends this jurisdiction to other matters, including the four freedoms, including the cap, including fisheries. mr cavada, our rapporteur, even extends this competence to discriminatory behaviour, which can cover all human activities and even the protection of the financial interests of the union. and that is where we see the danger of yet another coup d'état by the judges in luxembourg. on 6 april 2006, just two months ago, the european court of first instance ordered mr frattini - the commission - to pay damages to an official for a serious and manifest breach of the requirement of impartiality. rape by who? the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat fraud, including the creation of a european anti-fraud office (olaf). to give criminal jurisdiction to this commission, on which the court of auditors, in its special report no 1 of 2005, observed that respect for the fundamental rights of persons under investigation was not ensured, is to risk creating a small, liberty-threatening hotbed, a kind of normative micro-guantanamo, in berlaymont. the rapporteur for the committee on civil liberties, mr cavada, is aware of the problem, since he asks that the judgment be applied with caution and he could have added: with jurisprudence, the caution of the law, and in particular of the law of the treaties, which does not allow the transfer of competence from the third to the first pillar. but since 1962 and its costa v. enel judgment, the court has been practicing the imprudence of the permanent federal coup d'état. the great british jurist dicey warned that judges must be lions, but lions under the throne, careful not to fail in any point of sovereignty. putting someone in jail is criminal law. it's not nothing.
mr president, i thank the commission for its communication on the consequences of the court's judgment on criminal sanctions and i share its conclusions. i believe that the interpretation of this judgment should not apply to the environment alone, in order to strengthen the democratic control of parliament and thus to enable citizens to be better protected. the court's judgment clarified the jurisdiction in criminal law between the first and third pillars. it provides that the purpose and content of the act itself must be taken into account in determining whether criminal sanctions are necessary. this leads us to conclude that the protection of fundamental rights is an area to which the consequences of this judgment can be extended. fundamental rights and the protection of the interests of the union should be given special attention in the use of criminal sanctions. i do not think, however, that we should limit this use to these two areas alone and amendment no 16, which i tabled with my colleague maria berger, goes in that direction. that's why i'm asking you to support him. finally, this judgment is a further signal that we should make provision, through article 42 and as you have said, for the community to be involved in all police and judicial cooperation in criminal matters. i say this tonight, it would allow for greater legal certainty and, above all, greater consistency in criminal measures.

the rapporteur. mr president, the european union is known throughout the world for the high level of protection of fundamental rights, and in particular the protection of personal data, which it guarantees its citizens. this principle is enshrined in article 8 of the charter of fundamental rights. in the community, two directives regulate the fair processing of such data in the context of the internal market, and when a citizen makes, for example, a purchase on the internet, the company from which he makes this purchase is obliged to ask him for permission to use his data to send him commercial offers. the citizen is thus informed of the use made of data concerning him and, in principle, he can request the rectification of these data. however, this european data protection area currently contains a serious gap. there is no coordination of the 25 member states on the protection of personal data used in police or judicial work. as we work towards the establishment of a european area of freedom, security and justice, this coordination has become absolutely essential. the police forces of the member states need to work closely together and exchange data in order to combat organised crime effectively. we can strengthen this cooperation, but we must ensure that data concerning citizens is protected in the same way throughout europe. i would remind you that the european parliament has for many years called for an instrument for data protection in the context of judicial and police cooperation. we therefore welcome this commission proposal and the purpose of my report is to strengthen this proposal in order to ensure consistency with the existing data protection instruments under the first pillar. we also want this framework decision not to be limited to data exchanged between member states, but to ensure a minimum level of data protection within the member states themselves. if that were not the case, we could have two different data protection systems in the same investigation. this would not only threaten the protection of citizens but also complicate the work of the police or the judiciary. we have strengthened safeguards for the use of personal data by, and the transfer of personal data to, private parties when they process personal data in the public service. we also want guarantees regarding the use of personal data by, and the transfer of personal data to, third countries. i would remind you that the court annulled the council decision on the agreement between the european community and the united states on the processing and transfer of personal data and the commission's adequacy decision on the adequate level of protection of such data, on the grounds that the legal bases were inadequate, as you know. commissioner frattini told us that he wanted to table a new proposal for an agreement on the basis of the third pillar. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives in this area, including the establishment of a european data protection supervisor. when adopting the data retention directive in december 2005, the council gave a moral commitment to the european parliament - i would remind it - to proceed with the swift adoption of the data protection text, in full respect of the principle of sincere cooperation between the european institutions. however, this adoption has been very late and its implementation during the year is now threatened. we therefore want the council to make clear commitments today, particularly on the crucial points for the european parliament, and we expect in writing. since its establishment in 1993, the main tasks of the drugs and drug addiction observatory have been the collection, analysis and dissemination of transnational data on drug problems. thirteen years later, the record is not glorious. while there has been some improvement in the knowledge of the drug phenomenon in its various aspects throughout the european union, there has been no positive impact on consumption. on the contrary ! one thing is certain. today, drug use is no longer limited to traditional products, but we are seeing with concern the emergence of new markets for synthetic products, which are easier and cheaper to produce. they generate more profits for traffickers and are even more harmful to the health of consumers. the monitoring centre for drugs and drug addiction is in fact a mere database with no operational value. in fact, all the figures provided are just a cover for the failure of the various national drug control policies. it is high time that states took responsibility and stopped sheltering behind organizations which have neither the vocation nor the mission to act for them.
in writing. the judgment of the court of justice of the european communities of 13 september 2005 constitutes a real legal coup d'état in what is commonly called the community legal order. this is the first time that the court has ruled on questions of criminal jurisdiction and has decided that the european union, in order to protect the environment, may require member states to provide for criminal sanctions in the event of serious infringements. in principle, criminal legislation, like the rules of criminal procedure, falls within the strict competence of the states. with this court decision, part of the criminal law of the member states has just been communityised, and this without the formal agreement of the peoples. the european parliament has also called for the harmonization of criminal law, which was implicitly rejected by the french and dutch "no" votes in the referendum on the constitution. but worse is coming. there is a risk that this case law will be extended to all community areas, in particular to those concerning alleged fundamental rights, such as the fight against 'discrimination' and 'racism', data protection, the right to asylum and migration policies. this development is not in the direction of freedom. she's a worry.

mr president, the idea of sustainable development is a good one. it smells like mrs. brundtland's norway, which she invented 40 years ago. it's a concept from the good old days, the club of rome, zero growth. it's a new version of the old idea of reverend malthus. at the banquet of humanity, there's not enough room for all the generations. so we have to limit ourselves, especially as the ice melts, the water rises, the greenhouse effect will suffocate us, the sun will go out and the raw materials will run out because the chinese consume everything. in fact, the only thing that is sustainable is underdevelopment. look at africa! the only thing that is sustainable is poverty, which is a socially transmitted disease from generation to generation. but all development is only temporary. even the stone age ended, not because of the lack of stones, but because of the invention of bronze. and the age of oil will end, not because of the lack of oil, but because of the transition to the age of fusion or hydrogen. in short, the scourge of sustainable development is the idea that the rich explain to the poor that to save humanity, they must deprive themselves of the present.

member of the commission. mr president, i would like to thank the honourable members for the valuable remarks they have made, and i have taken note of the various points raised. i shall try to reply briefly to some of them. first of all, i agree that women should be given and should take every opportunity to establish gender parity. the commission will do its utmost to bring this about by all available means with regard to fisheries, particularly coastal fisheries, where women are more prominent than in the other fisheries sectors. on three specific points that have been made, the granting or otherwise of tie-up aid is a national matter and the reporting and control are aimed more at larger vessels than at smaller ones. smaller vessels are in many instances either exempt, or have less stringent requirements to comply with. with regard to the specificities of inshore fisheries, i need to underline again that up to a distance of 12 nautical miles these are largely subject to member state jurisdiction. the eu is not really involved in the control of fisheries within the 12-nautical-mile limit, other than in exceptional cases. i also agree that the specificity of different coastal areas has to be taken into account. we are actually doing that in the mediterranean proposal, and i hope that later this year i will go back to council to try and have the mediterranean proposal adopted. as i said in my opening remarks, there is quite extensive provision for the promotion of small coastal fisheries in the european fisheries fund. i would also like to say that, after a long and difficult balancing act, we have finally hammered out a compromise deal allowing coreper to agree on the european fisheries fund, and it will now feature as an ‘a item’ at this monday’s agricultural and fisheries council. to outline how the european fisheries fund seeks to attain this assistance to small coastal fisheries, first of all there is a reduction of the private contribution to modernisation of vessels for owners of smaller ships to 20%. the european fisheries fund gives them more favourable treatment and conditions for engine replacement for vessels of up to 12 metres, in which case engines can be changed without reduction of capacity on a one-to-one basis. member states are urged to give safety tonnage, preferably to smaller vessels. the european fisheries fund also allows for young fishers to be offered favourable conditions for training and the purchase of a first second-hand vessel. the fund can also be used for projects aimed at bringing about gender equality. it provides for the promotion of processing and marketing, which could be beneficial to coastal communities and fishers. the commission will carefully examine the results of the study it commissioned earlier this year when they are available, and will decide, on the basis of the findings, what measures can be proposed next year and whether there is scope for a community initiative on coastal fisheries. mr ó neachtain’s report will also be taken into account. however, my view is that we should not over-regulate in such a sector; we should help mainly by providing assistance for coastal fishers to overcome the handicaps that they face in exercising their profession.

in writing. the union's growth and competitiveness depend to a large extent on its capacity to develop research and innovation. in lisbon in 2000, heads of state and government committed themselves to promoting the europe of knowledge and to dedicating 3% of gni to it by 2010. the report by jerzy buzek, which i voted for on thursday, focuses on the objectives and challenges of the 7th cfp. i would like to mention two chapters in particular, which concern regional development: the regions of knowledge and support for smes. it is necessary to strengthen the research potential of the regions of the union by encouraging regional research clusters involving universities, research centres, enterprises and regional authorities. it also advocated strengthening the innovation capacity of smes, encouraging them to network and facilitating their access to the framework programme. it thus makes research a real tool for regional development, even though it is regrettable that the resources allocated to this great european ambition are being reduced by the reduction in the financial prospects.
in writing. for obvious ethical reasons, human cloning must be banned altogether. there can be no doubt about that. unfortunately, this is what the seventh framework programme and some of the amendments tabled today do, by excluding from community funding only cloning for reproductive purposes and not cloning for therapeutic purposes. this semi-legitimization is dangerous. it is based on the idea that human beings, whatever their future, can be regarded as mere material, and this is unacceptable. the programme also provides for the possibility of financing research on embryonic stem cells. i know, and i do not approve, that some countries in the european union allow it. it is not for us, in a vote on research funding, to take a position on their legislation. on the other hand, countries which prohibit such practices should not be required to fund them through community funds, and this type of research should therefore not benefit from fp7 resources. that is why we voted against these provisions, reserving our approval for the other research programmes mentioned in this report.
in writing. i voted in favour of this new pcrd because we substantially improve on the commission's proposal and are more ambitious than the council. with a budget that matches our ambitions, more than €50 billion, three times as much as before, we are enabling our researchers to stay in europe and to attract those from third countries. the 7th fp7 with its four specific sub-programmes will structure the european research area around ten main themes. i also supported the creation of a specific security component, which remains a priority for our citizens. i am also pleased that my amendments on the health side have been widely accepted and adopted. the programme also includes several new features, including joint technology initiatives, which will make it possible to associate companies, especially the smallest ones, with research centres in a specific sector. our ambition is therefore also to boost innovation in europe and thus support our businesses and jobs.

for the greens/efa group mr president, ladies and gentlemen, spain in 1936 is above all a lesson, or rather four lessons, for us europeans. the first lesson is the courage, the self-sacrifice, the extraordinary imagination of a people, the spanish people, on the march towards freedom and democracy. who has forgotten the extraordinary social creations of free catalonia? who has forgotten all that the spanish people have tried to do during this extraordinary period? the second lesson is the barbarity of fascism. as has just been said, guernica is a symbol of this: a symbol of murder, assassination, imprisonment; it is also a symbol of an international project of fascism, for it is obvious that spanish fascism could never have won this struggle without the help of national socialism. by 1936 the european project of domination by fascism was already visible. the third lesson is more difficult to understand because it is the lesson of cowardice: the cowardice of the europeans, the cowardice of the french - even if it was difficult for léon blum - the cowardice of the english..., the cowardice of all those who thought that if the spanish people paid, they would not pay! this attitude, as in munich in 1938, proved to be one of the great mistakes and one of the great lessons we must learn from that period. the belief that we can just sit back and wait for the storm to pass is often misguided, as history has shown. this is a great lesson that for many europeans was very difficult to accept for a very long time. pacifism can be a nightmare. sometimes it's a symbol of courage! knowing which one to choose is always very difficult. but if we are to speak of cowardice, we must also emphasize courage: that of pierre cot, for example, who was leon blum's minister and who, as a minister, smuggled arms into spain. it should be remembered that pierre cot, who acted like a hero in this difficult period, is the father of one of our colleagues, jean-pierre cot. i thank the latter for reminding me of these facts. the fourth lesson is the terrible intolerance of communist totalitarianism. because we must not forget that there are two great images in this spanish war. the first image is of the international brigades who wanted to save the spanish people. but at the same time there was the image of the intolerance of the communist brigades who murdered trotskyite members of the poum, who murdered anarchists, because they did not respond to their orientations. that too is a lesson from the spanish war! this lesson that liberation is not about being right against everyone, it's also about accepting diversity and democracy. these four lessons, ladies and gentlemen, must be fully understood by the european union. these lessons must be learned when the barbarism in bosnia is unleashed. these lessons must be learned when a duty of solidarity is to be exercised towards oppressed peoples. if these lessons are learned well, then, i believe, the future can be a little brighter.

in writing. human trafficking affects more than 800 000 people a year. this "trafficking", which is linked to organized crime, is as lucrative as the international arms and drug trade. trafficking in human beings is a modern form of slavery, which is aimed at sexual and economic exploitation and violates basic human rights. the fight against this scourge is difficult and costly because the networks are often international and traffickers take advantage of the disparity of national laws and the shortcomings of the coordination system. i voted in favour of the council's proposal for the conclusion of two additional protocols to the united nations convention against transnational organized crime because they strengthen coordination and harmonization of procedures. however, while progress has been made in preventing and prosecuting traffickers, there is still a need to strengthen the protection of victims. victim status and related rights must be better recognised and enforced; legal, material and psychological assistance must be offered systematically, as must the granting of a temporary residence permit or repatriation assistance. special protection must be given to victims who have had the courage to denounce their traffickers, because too often they live in perpetual fear of reprisals.

in writing. shipping accounts for about 45% of the european union's external trade in value and about 75% in volume. the application of the general rules of competition law to the international tramp and cabotage sectors does not in fact pose any problems as these activities are already deregulated and operate on the basis of fair competition. only the abolition of the exemption from the competition rules granted in 1986 to maritime conferences was the subject of intense discussions between all the players in the sector. the solutions proposed in my report and in that of mrs wortmann-kool seem to me to be perfectly balanced and respectful of the interests involved. indeed, there is no evidence today that the maritime conference industry needs to be protected from competition in order to provide its services. in addition, in order to preserve legal certainty in the maritime sector, it has become necessary to establish guidelines which should enable operators to adapt to the new regulatory framework and contribute to a smooth transition to a competitive regime. if all the precautions taken by parliament in this matter are respected, there is no doubt that shipping will benefit.

in writing. beyond the political agreement on the financial perspective for 2007-13, the negotiations which marked the council meetings of 15 and 16 december 2005 confirmed the need for change in the own resources system. at a time when the construction of europe seems to be at a standstill, due in particular to a tendency to fall back on national egoism and a disconnect between the people and the community institutions, the opacity of these negotiations and the desire of each member state to conceive the budgetary question only from the point of view of its own particular interest have highlighted the urgency of having a clear and legible system of own resources, which will remove the union as far as possible from the current national budgetary contingencies. it is essential that the european parliament, as the representative of the peoples, should be involved in this process. the lamassoure report, which is now before us, is part of this process and its conclusions, which reflect many of the concerns expressed above, are in the right direction, that of a europe which is in control of its financial resources and closer to its citizens. so, although i would have liked to have already mentioned the possibility of a european corporate tax as a new own resource of the union, i voted in favour of this text.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, there are 175 million migrants in the world and this number has almost tripled in the last 40 years. the phenomenon is not new, but it has taken on a particular dimension in the context of globalisation and, above all, it now evokes human tragedies for us. every day, dozens and dozens of africans are driven by poverty and despair to the northern shores of the mediterranean or to the canary islands, and the only response from the european states is to increase checks and patrols, which push those who are about to leave to take ever greater risks. but this eu migration policy is based on an illusion! the illusion that we can make our borders watertight, which is based on a vision that is primarily defensive and security-oriented and which leads to the shifting of all responsibility to the southern states. even the euro-african conference in rabat on 10 july will certainly be discussing the issue from the point of view of repression and border controls and we will still not hear the voice of africa. this one-sided and selfish view is echoed today in the discourse and policies of "choice immigration" that are all the rage in europe. immigration 'chosen' for the north, but immigration increasingly 'subjected' to the south, and so it is now that a different logic must prevail in europe. that is the spirit of my report. it is in this dynamic that i want to be part of, to propose a new approach, new tools and to make migration a lever for development. first, we must make better use of the tools that already exist, but, above all, we must meet our commitments in terms of development aid, and we know that development leads, in the first phase, to an increase in migration rather than a slowdown. of course, increased aid is not in itself a solution, it is a necessary but not a sufficient condition. secondly, i would like to see a real look at the aeneas programme, to refocus it on the development aspect alone, as in the programme which will succeed it in 2007, but we are far from that! today, this programme is used mainly for actions to protect the northern borders. in 2005, for example, only seven of the 39 projects funded were in the global south. in addition, if we were to set up a single new financial instrument, i believe that a guarantee fund should be created to ensure the sustainability of micro-projects in poor countries. the european union must also act where migrants are, where migration begins. it is easy to target the main areas of immigration - often the poorest regions - and to finance, with targeted budget support, the installation of infrastructure: drinking water, electricity, roads, health centres and schools, in order to keep the poor people there. it is also easy to identify migration centres, we know them: they are states or large cities with modern means of transport and communication, which are both reception areas and departure areas for the main migratory routes, which start from the sahel to the north, for example. this identification means that actions can be developed more than is currently the case to support the population - especially the most vulnerable, such as women and children - and help them to become self-sufficient, to achieve themselves in other ways than through mobility. a programme of information on these areas for migrants could also be set up. i believe that europe must also take advantage of the potential of migrant communities in rich countries to help develop their countries of origin. i believe that this is a promising path which, in the name of solidarity and mutual aid, is intended to transform migrants into agents of development. it's called co-development. in this context, it is necessary to encourage the transfer of funds to the countries of origin, to make them more transparent and less costly, and to study a new financial product which could take the form of a 'development savings plan'. the union, and especially its member states, must put in place innovative policies such as the payment of the wage differential for certain migrants wishing to return to their country of origin, or systems of double chairs for researchers or doctors, in the framework of institutional partnerships between research institutes, universities or hospitals. we must also encourage circular migration, which allows migrants to go back and forth, of course in consultation with the countries of origin and by making the transfer of social benefits more widespread. i believe that such measures would make it possible to replace the current brain drain with a brain circulation. we know very well that for many countries in the south, migration means the departure of the best educated and most enterprising citizens. this is a tragedy for poor countries, since this phenomenon often affects such vital sectors as health and education. in this respect, i welcome the commission's proposals to take account of these issues. but what i want more generally is that the situation be reversed, that a new logic for europe be imposed and defended. the opportunity is there because the un will be addressing the issue of migration and development for the first time in september. i would like to thank the colleagues who supported me on this report.

in writing. we need to establish a genuine common policy on asylum and immigration. it is essential for the union to establish mechanisms for the exchange of information between member states. if member states are better acquainted with their respective legislation and regularly exchange best practice, they will be better able to identify areas where european legislation is needed and thus reach an agreement acceptable to all. it would be simplistic and wrong to say that this instrument could allow member states to prohibit regularization. regularization is necessary in some national contexts. an exchange of information on these measures will therefore help to understand them better. in addition, a tightening of the fight against legal immigration may have the effect of diverting flows to another member state. such hardening should therefore also be reported.
mr president, mr gargani is right to ask that parliament be consulted on the revision of the immunities protocol. it is also right to ask in its report for a right of appeal by the european parliament to the court of justice in the event of member states failing to respect the immunities of members of parliament, which have been established to defend the rights of parliament and, in particular, to protect members of parliament from prosecution by a hostile executive power through the prosecutor. especially after the real forfeiture - the word is not too strong - committed by the french court of cassation in the case of our former colleague mr marchiani. but, mr president, the legal affairs committee should also respect fundamental law itself, and not examine an application for parliamentary immunity on a manifestly inadequate basis - in this case article 9 - when article 10 applies. it should adopt the same case law in defence of freedom of expression when the fumus persecutionis is manifest, as was the case in my case. finally, and i would have finished with that, parliament's legal services should not, when proceedings are brought before the court of justice, attempt to diminish the scope of the european parliament's resolutions, or even of articles which it has inserted in its own rules of procedure.
in writing. if we needed proof of the delicacy of the pseudo-europeanist political elites, of the mental confusion in which they are operating, of the loss of benchmarks and the inversion of values from which they suffer, we would have it with mr lambridinis' report. what he is proposing is nothing more or less than a generalized, institutionalized extra-european preference, a discrimination against europeans on their own soil, accompanied, financially, by a kind of marshall plan for what he calls 'the 26th state of the union', and politically, by the unilateral granting of rights which can only be those of nationals of one state. i'm not going to sleep. 40 million officially admitted non-european immigrants, that's a beginning of overwhelm. the member states are already spending hundreds of billions of euros each year on so-called integration policies which are obvious failures, costs for their societies and handicaps for their economies. remember the ethnic clashes in the uk. remember the reasons why theo van gogh died. remember the riots in france, those young people shouting their hatred of our institutions, our values, of everything we are. the multicultural societies you want to create are explosive. unemployment, social and housing problems are the lot of millions of europeans. they are the ones we must think of first.
in writing. there are now some 50 million immigrants in europe, mostly from africa or asia, and the number is growing by one to two million each year. the explosion of ethnic violence, the islamization of many of our cities, the questioning of our social security systems which cannot bear to take care of these newcomers are the most serious consequences of this immigration, which is all the more difficult to assimilate because it comes from cultures alien to our civilization. the integration proposed by the rapporteur, far from solving the problems, is making them worse. in france, three weeks of rioting in november 2005 reduced to ashes dozens of buildings built under this policy: party halls, gymnasiums, schools, etc. the other proposals, such as 'encouraging the political participation of immigrants', i.e. giving them the right to vote, as mr sarkozy wants in france, will further dismantle our societies. instead of wasting billions on pseudo-integration, our governments should, on the one hand, implement a genuine policy of cooperation with the countries of emigration based on reciprocity and, on the other hand, launch a great family policy to ensure the sustainability of our nations.
in writing. european immigration policy cannot be limited to fighting illegal immigration. there is an urgent need for a european policy on the integration of third-country nationals. the commission's communication on a common programme for integration is therefore an important step forward. and the creation of a european fund for the integration of third-country nationals is a good example of this. migrants must benefit directly from this fund. it must therefore allow for greater participation of migrants at all levels of educational, cultural and political life. we must encourage the exchange of best practice on the integration policies of the member states in order to pave the way for a genuine european integration policy. i also support the rapporteur's proposal to establish rapid and humane procedures for granting longterm resident status, to promote family reunification and to encourage longterm residents to become naturalised.
in writing. the main fault of mrs carlotti, which is found in all the european parliament's reports on the subject, is to consider that immigration, renamed for the circumstance of "mobility of human beings" is a human right. no, each of us does not have the absolute right to settle indefinitely in any country of our choice, according to our own will. states must be able to decide who may enter their territory, who may remain there and for how long. the philosophical, almost religious, bias of the rapporteur leads him to wrong solutions. there is obviously a link between development and migration. hundreds of thousands of people are being forced to emigrate because of poverty and it is obvious, as the national front has been proposing for years, that development policies must be implemented to enable these people to settle in their own country, because they would find the means to live there in dignity. one of these ways is to organise the return of immigrant populations to their countries of origin, so that they can benefit from the experiences and skills acquired during their stay in the european union. this is the only option which mrs carlotti's report does not consider at all. that is why we shall vote against his report.
in writing. on the eve of the rabat conference, it is urgent to recall that the european union's cooperation with the countries of origin of migrants cannot be limited to helping them to strengthen their borders. we need to engage in dialogue to address the root causes that drive people to risk their lives crossing oceans in search of a better life in europe. we must enable co-development to be targeted as closely as possible to the people in order to reduce poverty and inequality, which are the main causes of migration. the establishment of a european fund for co-development will perpetuate this principle. finally, we must remember that migration must be an opportunity for the countries of origin. we can promote the investment of migrants in their countries in order to maximize their impact on the development of their countries.
in writing. in mr schmidt's report, the european parliament wanted to express its opinion on the need to give fair trade a genuine european policy framework. this was necessary. the pressure currently exerted by the increasing opening of global markets is a serious threat to the economic, ecological and social viability of the various global agricultural models: by forcing them to produce at ever lower prices, it puts farmers at risk by undermining their incomes, and contributes to the deterioration of the working conditions of agricultural workers and the environment. fair trade can and must help provide an alternative to this situation which, by promoting the lesser, undermines the millennium development goals. in this context, the commission must now send a strong political signal in favour of a trading system which provides producers with a remunerative income and helps to remove any temptation to social and environmental dumping. the growing success of fair trade products among european consumers can only encourage such an initiative. so, although i regret that parliament has not wanted to advocate special tariff measures (differentiated approach, gsp+) for fair trade products, i will vote for the schmidt report.

member of the commission. mr president, thank you for what has been a very constructive and helpful debate. i would like to thank those who have supported the commission in its negotiating stance and its negotiating approach. it is never easy finally to judge precisely the best thing to do at the best time, but we do our best and i think it is true to say that amongst the key negotiating partners the eu has considerable support for the approach that we are taking. this is not as important as the support we have from our own side, from our own member states and from the members of this house. i shall make one observation immediately. we have a number of interests in these negotiations – agricultural, non-agricultural, relating to services liberalisation and rules. our job as negotiators is to get an outcome that is balanced across the range of those negotiating subjects. we will give in some places more than we will give in other places. there will be swings, there will be roundabouts, we will gain, and we will lose. nobody can make a final judgement about what europe will be able to gain from these talks until the very end – not simply when the key modalities are put in place, as i hope they will be this summer, but when all the other negotiations have taken place on the individual country schedules and when all the negotiations about rules have also been put in place. it is very important that those who are particularly concerned about agriculture in europe understand and accept that we will not pay over the limits in agriculture for what we want elsewhere in the talks. we will do what is fair. we will do what is reasonable. we will do what is in our mandate as far as agriculture is concerned. that is clear to me. it should also be clear to our member states. having said that, it is important to keep a sensible perspective in these negotiations. we must be careful not to devote such energy to protecting our defensive interests in agriculture in these negotiations that we fail to prioritise our offensive interests in non-agricultural market access and in services. there really must be a sense of proportion and balance as regards how we weigh the various economic and social interests that are at stake here. as far as the united states is concerned, let me just say this in response to one speech: i do not feel that, should the talks fail, we as european negotiators are in a race with the united states to see who can shift the blame most effectively to the other. i look to the united states as a genuine partner, as a country and an economy that shares some of our interests but at the same time places a different emphasis from us in various areas of these negotiations. we will not reach a successful conclusion unless the eu and the us work together as a team – not at the expense of other negotiating partners, not instead of sensible negotiations and links and agreements that we will have with our negotiating partners in various areas of the negotiations. however, if at the end of the day the eu and the us are at loggerheads and simply cannot agree the ground on which they will stand together to bring these talks to a successful conclusion, then there will be no successful conclusion to these talks. we will lose from that, the united states will lose from that, the global economy will lose from that and in particular developing countries will lose from that. i should like to thank members who have spoken, including those who have asked what my plan b is if these talks fail. i am afraid i am not preparing for failure: i am going to continue to negotiate for success only, whether it be in relation to hormone beef, which is not part of these negotiations – we do not welcome us hormone-treated beef in the european union for health reasons, not trade reasons – or in relation to gmos, which again are not the subject of these talks and where our policy firstly has to be in line with the regulatory framework we adopted in the eu a few years ago and in line with wto rules. it is this that governs our approach, rather than something i am negotiating in these talks. i am glad that we – the commission and members of this parliament – are able to cooperate in geneva and elsewhere. i do not cooperate with this parliament as an act of generosity on my part. there is nothing altruistic about this. the reason i cooperate is because i want the members of the european parliament there on these occasions. you give me valuable insights, you collect information and intelligence, you are able to tap different sources of opinion, which i do not always have easy access to, and you are also, on a good day, able to help us deliver a message to our negotiating partners. that is why i welcome members of this parliament being present and why i shall remain very firmly in cooperation with you.
the debate is closed.
the agenda calls for debate the oral question to the commission by mr enrique barón crespo, on behalf of the committee on international trade, on the indication of the country of origin of certain products imported from third countries ('marking of origin') (o-0065-2006 b6-0316/2006).
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, my first words are to congratulate mr barón, who constantly points out the council's failings when it does not sufficiently involve members in decisions on international trade. we are looking at the way forward to make governments understand the need to involve citizens, and therefore their legitimate representatives, the parliamentarians, in major decisions on international trade. i also commend my friend strudy for the wisdom of joining in this compromise. i shall vote in favour of the joint resolution, although i regret that it merely takes note of the draft regulation on origin labelling. more political support will be needed in the future, in the face of a very divided european council. the text of the draft regulation unfortunately has some imperfections in terms of wording and needs to be clarified in terms of its operation. for example, article 3 (2) of the draft regulation refers to the member state 'where the goods are to be marked'. it is clear that we must speak of the member state of destination, because the marking is made in the country of origin of manufacture and not in the state of consumption. as regards operational details, it is essential, for example, to clarify the concept of 'last substantial processing' which determines the origin of goods when several countries are involved in industrial production, pursuant to article 24 of the community customs code. finally, we must ensure consistency with customs regulations, particularly in the context of the control procedures envisaged in the future reform of the community customs code, which the committee on international trade would like to see referred to, mr president. ladies and gentlemen, the traceability of products and, more generally, of intangible elements are elements of product valorization, a necessity for the fight against fraud and counterfeiting and, finally, an indispensable tool in the economic and social struggle that awaits us. this economic and social struggle, but also the environmental struggle, as you know, is about respect for our values. if we want to enforce our convictions, both in terms of social and environmental clauses in international trade agreements, we must impose the traceability of imported products and our internal market is an important weapon in this fight.
member of the commission. mr president, i am glad that almost every member who has contributed to this debate has supported the original proposal made by the commission. very properly, some important questions have been raised about our ability to meet new customs codes, etc. these are important technical issues that we shall continue to address and to discuss with members of this house. however, overwhelmingly, there is support for the essence – the principle – of our proposal. if we can overcome our disagreement about the method or manner or channel of depositing this proposal with parliament, we would benefit from concentrating subsequently on the substance of this proposal. very simply, it seeks to re-establish a level playing field with our trading partners, many of whom have already instituted forms of origin marking. it creates transparency about the origin of goods and establishes a single standard by which origin is determined. it permits informed consumer decisions. it reduces the incidence potentially of fraudulent or misleading origin marking and it contributes to improved competitiveness. for the consumer to be king – or queen – the consumer needs full information, or as much information as possible. i do not think it is unreasonable that amongst the information that consumers receive is the place of origin of the production or supply of particular goods. let me just stress that it is not a ‘buy europe’ campaign. products will not be stamped ‘this is foreign – do not buy it’! that is not part of my or the commission’s motivation. indeed, the more people know about the origin of goods and come to associate that origin with particular features or the quality of those goods, it may encourage them to buy those goods from those sources and places of origin. why not? however, that is not the point. the point is not whether we want to encourage people to buy goods from particular places of origin or discourage them from doing so, but to give them the information to enable them to make an objective judgement about where they purchase goods. i hope that members of this house will see the ‘origin marking’ proposal as an alternative to protectionist instincts and measures and not as paving the way for them. i do not believe that we run the risk of putting up new non-tariff barriers to trade. i would certainly be very resistant to that. people in europe are entitled to express or to demonstrate whatever preferences they have. those preferences will include the origin or source of production of those goods. this is no more than a simple way of enabling them to do so.
i have received, in accordance with rule 108 (5), seven motions for resolutions. i would point out that the committee on international trade has withdrawn its motion for a resolution b6-0381/2006. the debate is closed. the vote will take place at the end of the debate this afternoon.

member of the commission. mr president, this parliament and the commission are certainly joined in seeking a peaceful and democratic existence for the people of somalia. that has been brought out in the debate this afternoon, following mr smith’s original introduction of this subject. i hope i shall be able to respond to paragraphs 6 and 8 in particular, concerning governance and institution-building in somalia and protection of humanitarian relief and humanitarian relief workers, as he asked me to do. the discussion today on somalia is timely, as the situation of the country and the region as a whole remains very fragile. the commission is very much concerned about the risk of somalia returning to war and to chaos. ever since the establishment of the transitional institutions in 2004, the commission has been spearheading the international community’s efforts to support the somali transitional federal institutions. my colleague, mr michel, follows the situation very closely and is in regular contact with president yusuf and prime minister ghedi of somalia, as well as with leaders of the region. i should like to focus my speech on three main aspects: firstly, the current state of play in the dialogue between the transitional federal institutions and the council of islamic courts; secondly, the regional dimension of the crisis in somalia; and, thirdly, the extent of the commission’s support for the peace process as the most valuable way to promote respect for democratic principles, human rights and the rule of law. concerning the first – the current state of play in the dialogue between the institutions and the islamic courts – on 22 june the transitional federal government and representatives of the union of islamic courts met in khartoum and reached an agreement of principle to engage in dialogue, to mutually recognise each other and to convene for further substantive talks on 15 july, again in khartoum. this agreement was welcomed by high representative solana and by the commission. the commission takes the view that there is a window of opportunity for an inter-somali political dialogue and it is crucial to engage the islamic courts with a view to reaching a political solution within the framework of the transitional federal institutions. confronting the islamic courts is not the solution: it would not only radicalise the positions of all involved but also offer an opening to the extremists to further their agenda to create an islamic state, to introduce sharia law and provide a safe haven for al-qaida cells. secondly, the regional dimension of the crisis in somalia is crucial. it is essential that all regional partners show unity of purpose and engage constructively in the somali peace process. destabilising interventions in somali affairs by other countries in the region must be rejected and condemned. we are committed to work closely and support the initiatives of igad, the african union and the league of arab states in finding a political solution to the crisis, as mr coveney was asking us to do. the commission intends to anchor somalia in a broader regional strategy for peace, security and development for the horn of africa. the outline of that strategy was presented by commissioner michel to the igad heads of state last february. finally, the commission is the main donor for somalia, with an ongoing overall aid programme of eur 300 million. we have supported the somali national reconciliation conference and the establishment of the transitional federal institutions and are now committed to further enhancing the functioning of the transitional institutions. on 28 may 2006, president barroso and commissioner michel signed a memorandum of understanding with the transitional federal government. i can confirm that the commission intends to make eur 22 million available immediately to support the short-term governance and capacity-building priorities set out by the transitional federal government. we remain unequivocally committed to supporting the peace process. the commission’s humanitarian arm, echo, is also providing direct relief assistance to the civilian population affected by the fighting, as well as by the consequences of drought. everyone has a responsibility for ensuring the safe delivery of that humanitarian assistance and providing the safe custody and security of the humanitarian workers, all of whom are involved in this very valuable work.

the next item is the debate on six motions for resolutions on mauritania.
president. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, mauritania is a member of the acp and yet it is one of the forgotten countries of the world. for too long european countries have turned a blind eye to the dictatorship of president ould taya, who imprisoned, tortured and forced opponents of the regime to flee. parliament and the european institutions were silent when we asked for a mission to observe the 2003 presidential elections, even though some candidates were in prison. the union was cold-blooded after the events of 3 august 2005, when the dictator was overthrown without a drop of blood being spilled, even though we knew that the country was on the verge of explosion. i am pleased to have organised in 2004 in the european parliament the first discussion platform bringing together, on neutral ground, mauritanian civil society, political parties and official representatives to prepare the way to democracy. today we welcome the union's support for the democratic process in which mauritania has committed itself, based on a popular consensus behind the military council for justice and democracy. the transitional authority has already given its backing, with the creation of an independent national electoral commission, the abolition of media censorship and the holding of a referendum on 25 june, which was welcomed by international observers. and i welcome the commitment of the union to send a long-term observation mission to the elections in november this year, thus ensuring that every mauritanian citizen can exercise his or her voting rights. finally, the dividends from the black gold must be used for the education, health and development of the mauritanian population. the exploitation of oil, which will not last forever, must not be done at the expense of marine and coastal biodiversity but must, for example, preserve the argouin bank from pollution and ensure sustainable management of the fishery resources that mauritanians so badly need. i welcome the fact that the authorities have engaged with the union in a more open discussion on fisheries agreements in order to reach a fair agreement. the ban on factory ships such as the atlantic dawn, for example, is a precondition for this. finally, and i conclude, the cooperation project on the fight against immigration must promote the development of employment in mauritania and provide migrants with a welcome worthy of european values.
author. mr president, on 3 august 2005, the regime of former president ould taya was overthrown, and a military council declared its intention to put an end to totalitarian practices and establish democracy. it is therefore conceivable that these are merely statements intended to justify what the international community has called a coup d'état. but then you realise that not a drop of blood was shed, that the transitional authorities have started a dialogue with all the political parties and civil society, have set an electoral calendar and, exceptionally, decide to run in the next elections themselves. we are thinking that something is happening in mauritania and that this may be an opportunity to get the country out of dictatorship. our role now is to support the democratic process under way in accordance with the timetable which the mauritanian people have set themselves. in this respect, i welcome the holding of the last constitutional elections, supporting the ceni, which must however ensure that all mauritanians can obtain their identity papers to be able to vote in the next elections, and that mauritanians abroad can participate in future elections, also supporting the political parties so that they have the means to express themselves and campaign around electoral platforms with proposals to improve the situation of the mauritanian people.
member of the commission. mr president, following last year’s coup d’état the eu decided to open consultations with the islamic republic of mauritania under article 96 of the revised cotonou agreement. the opening meeting was cordial and constructive. it was attended by representatives from mauritanian political parties and civil society, who were given the opportunity to air their points of view, and by a group of ambassadors from acp countries. mauritania gave 23 undertakings in the areas of respect for democratic principles, fundamental freedoms and rights, the rule of law and good governance. a further undertaking was also given regarding monitoring and reporting. at the opening meeting, the commission encouraged the mauritanian authorities to ensure the widest possible registration of voters in the country and abroad, as well as participation in the constitutional referendum and in the several elections due to take place during the transition period. the commission also encouraged the creation of an electoral level playing field through the adoption of equitable mechanisms of party financing and the guarantee of impartial behaviour by the military, the transition government, the administration and the judges. the commission invited the transition authorities to take account of past problems, the most important of which are the sequels of slavery and the consequences of the inter-ethnic violence of 1989-1990 that led to loss of life and property and to the departure to neighbouring countries of tens of thousands of mauritanian citizens. while recognising that the duration of the transition period will not allow the new authorities to solve all problems, the commission encouraged them to take decisive action in all those areas. the undertakings given by mauritania have, in the commission’s opinion, addressed all the main problems that the country is facing. their formulation by the authorities was largely based upon the conclusions of the october 2005 national consultation workshops, which benefited from the participation of all stakeholders and reflected a broad national consensus. progress in the implementation of mauritania’s undertakings allowed the eu to recognise that steady progress had been made and to conclude the consultations at the end of may 2006. however, given the measures still to be put in hand, the eu will conduct an enhanced political dialogue with the government over an 18-month monitoring period. in that context, the deployment of electoral observation missions for the forthcoming elections is foreseen and a first evaluation mission by the commission will indeed take place next week.

the agenda calls for the debate on six motions for resolutions on freedom of expression on the internet.
author. mr president, in our globalised society, the internet is a fast and user-friendly way of communicating between individuals or groups, of doing business, of obtaining information, of creating. the internet has become an open global public space where everyone is, in principle, free to move around and express themselves. the world summit on the information society has placed the fundamental rights of the human person as the foundation of the information society. however, we are not all equal when it comes to freedom of expression on the internet, and some states have taken steps to censor the expression of citizens, journalists and others. worse, reporters without borders has made an alarming assessment of the crackdown on the internet and reports a very high number of internet users imprisoned, especially in china. our resolution enables us to oppose forcefully these violations of freedoms and to condemn the states which practice them. we call on the council and the commission to show the same concern in their international relations and aid and cooperation programmes. but we also want to call for the responsibility of companies, particularly european companies, which, by providing technology or services, are more or less involved in these acts and which should commit themselves to a code of conduct that avoids their participation in censorship, repression and persecution. we cannot advocate free trade while refusing to protect individual freedoms. the athens forum on internet governance, to be held in november, should enable the european union to put the recommendations of this resolution into practice.
member of the commission. mr president, the motions for resolutions on freedom of expression on the internet propose the means to promote access to the internet free of repression by national authorities. these suggestions concentrate on measures to improve internet governance and fight human rights violations. the world summit on the information society held in tunis in november 2005 reaffirmed the links between the development of the information society and respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms, including the freedom of expression and opinion, as well as the freedom to receive and access information. this consensus reached during the summit is a basis for us ‘to prevent and counteract threats, risks and limitations to human rights posed by the misuse of information and communication technologies’ as outlined in the commission’s communication of april 2006 on the summit follow-up. in this communication, the commission ‘encourages the companies concerned to work on a code of conduct on this crucial issue, in close cooperation with ngos’. this code of conduct would constitute an important step towards inspiring these countries to establish respective ethical standards. the promotion of freedom of expression figures highly on the agenda of the community’s corresponding external assistance programmes, in particular the european initiative for democracy and human rights. this will remain unchanged in the coming years under the new financing instrument for democracy and human rights. furthermore, we have a policy of bridging the digital divide between rich and poor countries. the more internet use spreads, the more difficult it becomes for repressive governments to control it, despite the whole panoply of censorship methods. the commission is actively promoting the summit’s recommendations in this area. before concluding, let me add a few more words on internet governance. the tunis agenda called for the establishment of a forum for multi-stakeholder policy dialogue, the internet governance forum, which will first meet at the end of october in athens. europe should play a central role in this process. i am therefore hopeful that the european parliament will take this opportunity to launch this dialogue with the representatives of european civil society before the athens forum.

mr president, commissioner, first of all i would like to express my solidarity with our spanish, greek, italian and other friends who have suffered from these forest fires, and of course i have a thought for the victims, because these fires are ecological tragedies, human tragedies. but there are many things that upset me. when will we stop talking about the forest fires that occurred during the summer every september? on behalf of the alde group. mr president, as head of the european union election observation mission in the democratic republic of congo, i have visited the country on several occasions since the commission, mr commissioner, put me in charge of it last october. there is a whole book to be written about the extraordinary adventure undertaken by the congolese people to establish democratic institutions with the help of the international community and especially the european union. i shall confine my remarks to comments on the next step along this road on sunday 30 july, when the first round of the presidential elections coincides with the parliamentary elections. the day after the first round, on 1 august, i had the pleasure of signing, together with my counterparts from all over the world, from the african union, the francophonie and the carter foundation, a joint declaration which essentially stated how impressed we were - closely with my colleagues mr frattini and mr mccreevy on this issue. these other contract law issues could be related to the other eu contract law acquis or general contract law topics which are directly relevant to the eu acquis. the truth is that the commission has not yet taken a decision on this matter, but it will take a final decision soon. we have taken due note of the european parliament’s opinion on this issue, especially that expressed in the recent resolution. i have also had an opportunity to discuss the issue in the various committees. the commission also intends to seek the council’s position on the remainder of the work on the cfr. the commission intends to use the cfr as a ‘better lawmaking’ tool for achieving clarity when legislating. exactly what legal form to choose in order to best achieve that aim is a key issue, which will need careful consideration. it will be easier to make a decision once there is more certainty over the content of the cfr. then we can examine how best to ensure that the cfr is used as effectively as possible. we have to realise that cfr is work in progress and will take some years to complete. while the commission can take into account the cfr work when drawing up new legislative proposals relating to contract law issues, it would not be useful or necessary to delay future contract law related legislation until all discussions on the cfr have been finalised. meanwhile, the commission has already indicated that it plans to use relevant cfr results in the review of the consumer contract law acquis. as clearly indicated in its communication of october 2004, the cfr as such is not primarily meant to be a legislative instrument applicable directly to legal transactions, but a toolbox to facilitate better lawmaking for legislators. the commission fully understands that parliament wants to be kept informed of and involved in the ongoing work on the cfr and would therefore welcome parliament’s involvement in the cfr process, in particular the creation of the parliament working group. the commission will continue to keep parliament informed of developments in the most appropriate way, in particular through the parliament working group. i would like to conclude by thanking you for parliament’s encouragement and support for our work on this important issue.
the european parliament has a duty to protect the environment. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, a european contract law is certainly likely to promote regulation of the internal market. but such a legal construct must be developed through a transparent and democratic process. the expected benefits for economic operators in terms of legal certainty and reduced transaction costs are closely linked to the clarity, predictability and stability of the rules. a european contract law must be based on the demands of the economic world in order to assess its needs. it should remove inconsistencies in the acquis communautaire on consumer rights, for example in terms of withdrawal periods or information to consumers. the draft texts currently being drawn up seem to be ambiguous, too detailed and do not really meet these objectives. would it not be more realistic, rather than embarking on the utopian path of currently drawing up a european civil code, a legal system, to draw up standard contracts or sectoral rules? however, the answers to the questions raised by this oral question should make it possible to better understand the content of the common reference code. the choice of the legal basis for an instrument dedicated to contract law must follow a political choice on these objectives and not precede it. it is therefore essential that the commission clarifies the objectives of the work that has been financed by the european budget since 2003 and puts the european parliament in a position to give its opinion on concrete proposals. it would be unthinkable to give companies the possibility of applying european contract law, as envisaged in the reflection chamber, in place of national directives and laws without parliament and the council having approved its content on the basis of a very thorough legal and economic impact study.
