in writing. the european parliament votes today on two important fisheries agreements for the indian ocean: one with the republic of seychelles and the other with the republic of comoros. the objectives of these agreements, which are renewable for six and seven years respectively, are: economic, financial, technical and scientific cooperation in the field of fisheries; the fixing of conditions for access by community fishing vessels to seychelles and comoros territorial waters; the establishment of partnerships between undertakings for the purpose of developing, in the common interest, economic activities in the field of fisheries and related activities. a financial contribution will be paid to the seychelles and the comoros in return for the exploitation of their fisheries resources. as an overseas elected representative who is aware of the role of fisheries in the overseas economy, particularly in réunion, i welcome europe's contribution to the establishment of responsible fishing in the indian ocean and the sustainable exploitation of fisheries resources. that is why i voted in favour of both agreements.

more detailed. positive profiling is an initiative that was not born today or yesterday, but a few months ago. this initiative is aimed at identifying accelerated border control procedures at airports and covers two elements: the first, which is reserved for international flights only, does not concern the exchange of data for internal european flights, where we would have insurmountable problems of freedom of movement, schengen area, etc. the system covers international flights from the european union to the european union, via the european union, only for travellers who voluntarily and individually agree to provide their data, especially biometric data, and in return benefit from an automatic identification lane which will obviously take less time for checks. the basis is individual and voluntary, with biometric data. why do we think of such a system? to avoid what has been said about negative profiling, that is, those on ethnic or religious grounds. of course, we cannot accept any such mechanism in this area, but we can imagine, since the council has asked for it, that on a voluntary basis each of us could provide a database which respects confidentiality with his biometric data and in return speed up the boarding procedures. think about frequent travelers, it's a mechanism that we're studying, and we're thinking about putting a proposal in a few months, maybe by the end of the year. i would like to conclude by saying that i will be happy to inform the libe committee of what was said in london on the procedures for strengthening the search for explosives, particularly liquids, on the use of the internet, on positive profiling and all the rest.

in writing. by joining the hague conference on private international law, whose mandate is to work towards the 'progressive unification' of the rules of private international law, parliament is taking a realistic step towards the harmonisation of the legal rules specific to each member state. there are two ways of achieving legal harmonization. the one advocated by the fanatical euro-federalists, which consists in bindingly standardizing the substantive rules of law in each of the twenty-five member states. the second is that it satisfies both the fundamental requirement of legal certainty and effectiveness, which consists in unifying only the rules of conflict of laws and jurisdiction, that is to say, in determining both the competent court and the national law applicable to a legal relationship. in this logic, the states preserve their own legal rules, systems and traditions, but the uncertainties which may arise from the application and confrontation of national laws in different territories of the union are very significantly reduced. we therefore give a favourable opinion on the report and on the european community's accession to the hague conference.

mr president, we are witnessing a somewhat contradictory approach in this parliament today. on the one hand we have a report by mrs wallis, which proposes that we join the hague conference to unify the rules on conflict of laws, which seems to me to be an excellent step. and on the other hand, we have this tendency to want to unify the basic rule of the european contract. i think the first approach is the right one, while the second is much more questionable. as regards the european contract, it seems to me that it would be sufficient to decide, for example, that the applicable law is the law chosen by the parties, and if they have not chosen an applicable law, that the applicable law is the law of the place where the contract was concluded and, finally, if the contract was concluded between parties who are in different places, that the law applicable to the contract is that of the place of its performance. the very simple wording of this rule would suffice to meet the legitimate need for legal certainty without necessarily having to unify the internal law of each member state in a somewhat arbitrary and authoritarian manner.

member of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should first like to thank the two rapporteurs and congratulate them on their extremely diligent work, mrs corbey, rapporteur for the report on the thematic strategy on air pollution, and mr krahmer, rapporteur for the proposal for a directive on air quality and cleaner air in europe. i would also like to thank the committee on the environment, public health and food safety in particular for its efforts so far. air pollution is and will remain one of the most important public health problems. because of this pollution, life expectancy in the european union today is 8.5 months shorter. the quality of life of hundreds of thousands of people is being degraded every day and the natural environment is at risk, despite the significant reductions in emissions in recent years. we must intensify our efforts. the strategy we are proposing sets out the steps we must take in this direction. it sets new, groundbreaking goals for health and the environment. measures on small particulate matter will result in a reduction in expected premature deaths from around 350,000 today to 160,000 in 2020. this will be the result of the combined implementation of the strategy and other measures already agreed. as regards the natural environment, we expect the area of ecosystems threatened by acidification to decline by more than 50% and the area of ecosystems threatened by the presence of excess nitrogen by more than 30%. these are ambitious targets, and their achievement will bring multiple environmental benefits. the strategy must of course be implemented effectively. the commission is committed to proposing measures at european union level to improve air quality. the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat pollution. the air strategy describes some of the relevant community measures. the commission has already put forward a proposal to reduce emissions from passenger cars and vans - often referred to as the euro v proposal - and the committee on the environment has recently adopted its draft report. the euro vi proposal for cars and vans is expected to follow. other proposals will be made for euro vi lorries and buses and the directive on national emission ceilings will also be revised, setting new emission limits for member states. in due course other measures will follow for small-scale combustion and agriculture. all these measures are being prepared today and will of course be evaluated in detail in accordance with the principles of better regulation. one of the main elements of the strategy is the proposed revision of the current legislation on air quality. the proposal maintains the existing limit values for air quality. the official data of the world health organisation clearly confirm that these limit values are necessary. the proposal introduces, for the first time, binding limits for fine particulate matter (pm2.5), i.e. particles with a diameter of less than 2.5 millionths of a meter. the science is unanimous that these particles have serious public health implications. maximum permitted concentration limits are proposed to apply from 2010. the proposal will also oblige member states to start monitoring these fine particles in all european countries. also take measures to reduce the average levels of exposure to particulate matter in the population. the adoption of these proposals should not be delayed. the health effects are very serious and the evidence is overwhelming. in the united states, pm2.5 targets have been in place since 1995. the data contained in the impact study of this proposal demonstrate that the approach to reducing exposure to particulate matter that we propose will benefit more people at a lower cost than the lower limit for pm2.5 proposed by parliament. the commission proposal also gives member states greater flexibility in complying with the existing air quality limit values. uncontrolled natural sources of pollution shall not be taken into account. more time will also be given in cases where member states face severe compliance problems. these extensions of time must be as short as possible in order to protect the health of our fellow citizens and not to injure member states which have made serious and credible efforts to comply. i shall refer very shortly to some of the main amendments proposed by parliament: as regards the possibility of time extensions, the commission proposed an additional five years from the date of entry into force of the limit values, i.e. a lower ceiling until the end of 2009 combined with the possibility of excluding pollution from natural sources. with these facilities the member states will clearly be able to comply with the directive. the committee on the environment has proposed two five-year periods from the entry into force of the new directive. the proposal would delay compliance until 2018 for limit values already agreed in 1999. this cannot be accepted. the new amendment tabled before this plenary session - amendment no 81 - is in the right direction but again cannot be accepted because if we accept the four plus two years from the entry into force of the new directive we will delay compliance until the year 2013 for the pm10 limit values already agreed in 1999. the member states have known these limits since 1999. in accordance with the council and parliament's decision on the sixth environment action programme, the commission has asked the experts of the world health organisation to advise on whether the limit values currently in force for air quality should be changed. their answer was no. the commission cannot therefore accept any weakening of the daily limit value for pm10. amendments nos 46 and 81 increase the number of days allowed for exceeding the limit from 35 to 55. if these amendments were accepted, then on the basis of 2004 data, air pollution measures would no longer be required in cities such as vienna, frankfurt, brno, stuttgart and others. the key question is: how can the health of the citizens be better served? weaken the daily limit value or take measures to deal with the pollution problem? the amendment which weakens the limit values if no new community pollution reduction measures have been taken beforehand cannot also be accepted. it is contrary to the right of initiative of the institutions. it is also not practical because it is impossible to predict the outcome of measures which have not yet been proposed. in this case too, the citizens' right to cleaner air would be undermined. i think i should finish here.

in the current context of globalisation, the complex and multifaceted world of work, which is subject to rapid change, is a source of insecurity and anxiety. the new ways of working, producing, innovating and exchanging require workers to constantly challenge their knowledge and know-how. to reconcile these increasingly difficult economic objectives with our humanistic view of work, there is a broad consensus that lifelong learning, a principle enshrined in most of our national rights, is the right way to go. official injunctions, including european ones, are already numerous. but we must not be content with the slogan. we are still far from having achieved practical application and systematization. lifelong learning is too often either a legal obligation to which companies are subject without any real reflection on the added value of these actions, and without any real long-term policy; or an incantation invoked in an emergency to respond to social difficulties. thus, work must now be done at national and local level to develop effective learning structures and real commitment from employers and employees.

in writing. since the introduction of the euro and the consequent withdrawal of the national currencies of the countries of the union, only one positive thing can be noted: the reduction in counterfeiting. thus, in 2005, the total number of counterfeit euro coins withdrawn from circulation remains well below the total number of counterfeits denominated in the old national currencies before the introduction of the euro. this is due in particular to the good cooperation between the anti-fraud office, the european central bank, europol, interpol and the competent national authorities. but beyond the outright counterfeiting, there is also the recent emergence of new coins that look mistakenly like two-euro coins. since 1 january 2005, turkey has had a new currency, the new turkish lira. the new one-litre coin looks exactly the same and is the same size as the two-euro coin. coincidence or clever counterfeit? you know what ? the problem is that these turkish coins are already circulating in europe, presaging perhaps the announced entry of turkey into europe by our european leaders and eurocrats, in defiance of the will of the people themselves. let us be vigilant, turkey is more than ever at our doorstep!
mr president, we did not vote for mr demetriou's report, although it does improve the council's proposal for a framework decision in a rather substantial way. why didn't we vote for it? because, despite all this, the whole system remains remarkably ambiguous. what exactly does it mean to take account of criminal decisions taken in a member state? is it possible to take them into account in order to avoid the application of the non bis in idem rule and thus avoid unjust double convictions? that would be perfectly natural. but, on the contrary, should they be taken into account when someone is considered guilty of acts which are not considered criminal in his country of origin? for example, will historian david irving, who is unjustly imprisoned in austria today for a crime of opinion, be regarded, when he returns to his country soon, as we hope, as a delinquent and a repeat offender, when he is arguably the greatest british historian in the history of the second world war? these are some of the ambiguities in the text which, in our opinion, justify our reluctance, especially since there is a convention, the 1970 convention. as the report rightly points out, a framework decision cannot unilaterally amend an international convention. this is a problem for countries which are not members of the european union but have ratified the convention. this reservation, which we made after ratification, raises a new problem in international law, which we prefer to settle in accordance with the terms of international conventional law.
in writing. i voted in favour of the excellent report by my colleague panayiotis demetriou on the proposal for a framework decision of the european council on the taking into account of conviction decisions between member states of the european union in new criminal proceedings. the functioning of the single market and the mobility of europeans within the union make it necessary to define the conditions under which a conviction handed down in one member state must be capable of being taken into account in the context of a new criminal proceeding concerning different facts in another member state. it is imperative to establish the principle of mutual recognition of convictions with the associated pooling and exchange of appropriate information. it is a condition, not sufficient, but necessary, for moving towards a european judicial area, since we are convinced that european democracy must be based, in particular, on law and, conversely, that law must be derived from democracy.
in writing. for 2007-13, the progress programme aims to include in a single text all the community programmes on social protection, working conditions, etc. this all-in-one is yet another tool of social uselessness, like the ineffective 'lisbon strategy' for european economic growth. this programme is also clearly ideological. while gender equality and the consideration of the interests of disabled people are highly commendable objectives, the defence of 'people who may be discriminated against at community level on grounds of race or ethnic origin, religion or religious beliefs' can be a means of silencing opposition to the current immigration policy in european countries, which for 30 years has challenged our social protection systems. in addition to its cost, this project strengthens the powers of the euro-brussels bureaucracy, which bears a heavy responsibility for the ruin of many of our industries, the destruction of our countryside and therefore the social regression suffered by the peoples of europe. only a new europe of the homelands, based on national solidarity, will bring about real social progress in our countries.
in writing. i voted in favour of the assent opinion on the strategic guidelines for cohesion, but i would like to stress that the reform of regional policy was carried out in the difficult context of the renewal of the financial perspectives but also in the context of the relaunch of the lisbon strategy, which clearly reoriented its objectives. however, a reorientation towards innovation, the knowledge economy and competitiveness in the former member states alone is not enough to achieve the objectives of territorial cohesion and sustainability, which i believe are a priority. i am particularly sorry that the budgetary allocation to the lisbon objectives and the classification of expenditure have not been submitted to parliament for approval. i also regret that the territorial dimension of cohesion has not been explicitly taken into account as a strategic orientation in its own right. however, for the development of isolated rural areas, this is not enough. i am worried about the fate of these programmes, since we still do not have a clear line of demarcation between erdf and eafrd assistance, which is part of the cap and whose amounts are very limited.
in writing. the community strategic guidelines for 2007-2013 have finally been adopted by the european parliament. i voted in favour of the rapporteur's recommendations, which approve these guidelines. i nevertheless drew the commission's attention to the issue of crossborder cooperation during the debate, which should make it possible to reduce disparities between the union's border areas, provided that disparate allocations of structural funds resulting from the statistical nomenclature do not impede the objective of cohesion and do not increase inequalities. it is essential to ensure conditions for balanced economic, social and territorial development on both sides of the frontiers and to pay particular attention to programmes for crossborder cooperation.
mr president, i should like to explain why, after interesting debates yesterday and the votes today, i voted against the rapkay report. simply because i am forced to see that this is a resounding victory for the liberals. we voted for the deregulation of public services, we voted against a framework directive, we voted against the distinction between services of general economic interest and services of general interest, we voted for the application of competition law to all services of general interest and their precise definition, we voted against the definition of in-house, in other words public administrations, we voted against the clarification of the altmark criteria. in these circumstances, we are considerably behind the previous resolutions, those of mr herzog and mr langen in 2001, and the commission is proposing a new communication at the end of the year. this means that we are leaving whole sections of community law and local public services open to the uncertainties of the court. what do we mean by direct control? what is meant by an intercommunal structure? what is meant by a mixed economy society? what are concessions in relation to market and competition law? we still do not know, and that is why i will continue to advocate transversal texts to ensure subsidiarity. i think that, unfortunately, we are far from being in the right place and that today is a losing battle. i hope this isn't a final defeat.
mr president, we did not approve the rapkay report for a very specific reason: it represents a completely unjustified step backwards from the text of the constitution itself. the text of the draft constitution provided for a european law establishing the principles and conditions for the provision, implementation and financing of services of general economic interest. it was therefore what is known in the present nomenclature as a framework directive. the report not only departs from the substance of the text, but by rejecting amendment no 10 it has formally refused and publicly stated its opposition to the constitutional text. i am therefore concerned about the drift of this house which, by and large, claims to support the constitutional text and which, when something important and even central to public opinion in a number of countries is at stake, backs down without any justification.
in writing. i voted in favour of my colleague bernhard rapkay's report on the european commission's white paper on services of general interest (sig) because it is a balanced report. in particular, it has the courage to point out that it is impossible to define gis in a uniform way in an economic and social environment as heterogeneous as that of the european union and that, in this matter, the principle of subsidiarity should be reaffirmed by leaving it to the member states to set the course for what is or is not in the general interest and to assume directly the consequences of their decisions. after the difficulties in obtaining a political compromise at first reading on the services directive, the debate on gis is far from over. there is an urgent need to legislate at european level on specific sectors, in particular social and health services of general interest, in order to secure them legally. finally, this dossier will be an important element of the competitiveness of the european area to which we must pay attention.
in writing. i voted against mr rapkay's report on the white paper on services of general interest because several amendments which were close to my heart were rejected, including those calling for a framework directive on services of general interest and those calling for clarification of the criteria for distinguishing between gis and sgei and the criteria for granting compensation for public service and in-house (self-production) services. we must not compromise on these crucial points for the future of our public services in our territories and go backwards from what parliament voted in the herzog resolution adopted in 2004 and the langen resolution in 2001, at the very moment when the pes group drew up a proposal for a framework directive on services of general interest that goes even further.
in writing. i voted against mr rapkay's report for the following reasons. firstly, the commission is not asked to propose a framework directive on gis. the regional authorities, mixed-use companies and inter-municipal structures are now under threat because of the risk of litigation in the name of competition law. mr barroso was right when he noted the lack of consensus on a proposal for a framework directive during the debate in plenary. by refusing to define the gis and the specific law applicable to them, the commission leaves the rules of the market and therefore competition law to apply to public services. the time has not come for yet another communication or for new sectoral proposals. we expect the commission to respect the decisions of the european parliament and to evaluate the liberalization policies implemented as soon as possible. we know that the results are far from the stated objectives. this resolution does not consider services of general interest as a fundamental pillar of the european social model or as a means of achieving the social, economic, ecological and territorial cohesion objectives of the union.
in writing. mr rapkay's report on services of general interest, whether economic or not, promises yet another legislative gas factory at european level and new interference by the commission in the budgetary and tax systems of the states and their territorial authorities, all in total violation of the principle of subsidiarity, which is mentioned in abundance by the rapporteur. the european citizens must be constantly reminded that the liberalization of public services, with the consequences we know, is a legal hold-up by the brussels commission on the treaties. the market alone cannot guarantee the quality or the fulfilment of all the missions of these services, whether they are social, spatial planning or of strategic and national interest. public services, whether profitable or not, should be the exclusive responsibility of the states as regards their definition, organisation, designation, number and nature of the entities entrusted with them, and the way they are financed.
in writing. mr rapkay's report on services of general interest (sig) is an attractive report at first sight. the report calls for better protection of public services, better defence of the principle of subsidiarity, democratic respect for national traditions and clarification of the definitions of gis by introducing, in particular, the concept of services of 'non-economic' interest. these good intentions can be deceptive, especially if the draft framework directive seems to have been abandoned. however, many binding rules will compete with the prerogatives of the member states, such as control of the means of financing. the door is therefore open to a future drift towards europeanism. finally, i cannot vote for this text which refers to the constitutional treaty, a constitution which, according to the report, would provide better guarantees for the gis in the face of the current european legislative mess. i would remind you that the european constitution was democratically rejected by the dutch and french peoples. this text, which is half-goat, half-chew, can only be voted against.
in writing. i voted against the rapkay report which does not recognise the need for a framework directive on gis and sgeis, leaving the door open to the continuation of the current deregulation which is calling into question our public services and the access of everyone everywhere to these essential services. a framework directive should guarantee equality between users, equality between citizens and territories, spatial planning and the long-term sustainability of the services provided, as well as a level of quality. it is urgent to put an end to this widespread liberalization which is not satisfactory either for the employees of these activities or for the citizens.
mr president, many of us abstained on the eurlings report for the following reasons. we would have voted for this report because, as i said yesterday, it is the most critical report ever adopted in this parliament on turkey's attitude towards the european union. unfortunately, in its votes the assembly rejected the recognition of the armenian genocide as a precondition for accession and, moreover, despite our vote and that of many of our colleagues, it adopted a provision which implicitly provides for accession as the only outcome of the negotiations. on these two points we disagree. however, we did not want to oppose the efforts made by mr eurlings and the committee on foreign affairs, which sent a very strong signal on behalf of this parliament, which is why we abstained.
mr president, we in the udf very strongly support mr eurlings' report because it contains very strong and important truths. even so, we were forced to abstain. why would you do that? firstly, precisely because this report seems to exclude the idea of a strengthened partnership as an alternative to full membership. but this is unrealistic. and above all because, by rejecting the paragraph on armenia, this parliament is sending an extraordinarily negative signal. i would remind you that in 2004 we voted a resolution saying that we were asking for the recognition of the armenian genocide; in 2005 we voted a resolution saying that we were asking for the recognition of this genocide to be a precondition for accession. today, we forget all that. what's the message? the message of a parliament that changes its mind, that forgets its resolutions. the message is simple, it is to tell the turks: you do not have to hurry to change this point, you can continue to make the very mention of the genocide a crime of opinion, and you will not be asked, in the end, to recognize this genocide. this is an extremely negative message, extremely serious. i regret that it was introduced and that it prevented us from voting on mr eurlings' excellent report.
in writing. the eurlings report takes stock of progress and problems encountered one year after the opening of accession negotiations with turkey. the report also calls for the establishment of a european union-wide network of information and communication networks, including the european information and communication networks, and for the establishment of a european network of information and communication networks. the armenian genocide must be recognized by turkey. however, this recognition cannot be presented as a precondition for accession, if the copenhagen criteria are considered. as for the paragraph on the possibility of special cooperation between the eu and turkey in the event of failure of the negotiations, it is not appropriate at the moment. we are in the process of moving forward and we cannot now be pessimistic about the conclusion of the negotiations. with this vote i want to show the many steps turkey must take to join the european union, but i do not want to create any new barriers to its eventual accession. in my view, turkey's accession to the eu is both an opportunity for turkey and an opportunity for europe.
in writing. if you had not mistakenly described turkey as a european country, which it is not, you would not be in the position today of having to acknowledge a number of truths. today you tell us that religious minorities, especially christians, are being oppressed in turkey. that respect for human rights in general, and women in particular, is not guaranteed. you find that turkey still refuses to recognize cyprus, a member of the union to which it is seeking to join, and frequently provokes border incidents with another member state, greece. you say that turkey is violating one of the fundamental principles of the european union, the free movement of persons. that's just to name a few. and all you have to conclude is: "let's continue the negotiations but be careful, in the end, we can always say no". who can believe this fable? on 3 december you should have listened to the european peoples, the majority of whom are hostile to turkey's entry into europe. you should have offered turkey a privileged partnership which respected our differences, not this political and diplomatic charade which is humiliating for both sides and especially for the turkish people.
in writing. i abstained on this report. the report presented in plenary has the merit of finally facing reality. for a long time parliament had been very angelic on this issue. this report is stronger than the previous ones, but i regret the lack of courage in parliament on the question of the recognition of the armenian genocide. that is why i have decided to abstain on the final vote. i have been opposed to turkey's membership of the european union for many years, but i am calling for a privileged partnership with turkey. more meps are now joining this position, which was still very much in the minority a few years ago. turkey does not recognise one of the member states of the european union, the republic of cyprus, and has occupied it for 30 years! turkey does not recognize the armenian genocide. turkey does not approve of freedom of association, and 97% of its territory is outside europe. europe has a duty to help this country on the road to democracy, but because of its geography, its history and its culture, turkey cannot claim to be part of the political project of the european union.
in writing. mr eurlings' report contained excellent passages, particularly those concerning the armenian genocide which the turkish authorities refuse to admit, the economic blockade imposed on armenia, the refusal to recognise cyprus as a member state of the european union. one of these elements alone should lead to the conclusion that the negotiations for turkey's accession to the european union must be stopped. not only does the rapporteur fail to reach this conclusion, but above all he fails to mention the obvious fact that turkey is not a european country. 95% of its territory is asian; its capital, ankara, is in the heart of asia minor; as christian communities have been eliminated during the 20th century, 99% of its population belongs to the muslim world. turkey has therefore no reason to join the european union. this is a fact which is recognized by the peoples of europe, particularly in france and austria, but not by those who govern us. this morning's vote illustrates this split: not only did the majority of our assembly vote in favour of such an accession, but it rejected paragraph 49 which called for recognition of the armenian genocide, thus submitting to the wishes of turkey.
in writing. although the eurlings report is critical of turkey's accession to the european union, in particular by calling for recognition of the armenian genocide, it does not go so far as to call that accession into question. it is true that the european commission, jacques chirac and the british, the main defenders of the ottoman regime, are there to prevent any deviation or measure that might delay or prevent accession. we have not changed our position in the face of changing circumstances, the fluctuations of the turkish government, which is fighting back and forth with the negotiators of the european commission and the main member states. we are opposed to turkey's membership on a matter of principle. turkey is not a european country and does not meet any of the copenhagen criteria which are supposed to define a country's membership of the european union. the negotiations should move towards the status of privileged partnership by maintaining the visa requirement for turkish nationals as it currently stands. turkey's accession will not be against the peoples of europe. as defenders of the french people, we will be able to protect its interests, which include rejecting turkey's accession to europe.
in writing. i have always felt that turkey's accession to the eu could not be envisaged in the current framework of european integration. i am in favour of a europe of the three circles. the first is a federal nucleus with countries that share ambitious social objectives and the desire for a 'european power' that plays a role on the world stage. the second group includes the 27 countries that are now members of the eu. in view of the difficulties and the need to consolidate the community, any further enlargement must be ruled out. the third is to organise a close and comprehensive partnership with the neighbouring countries, the balkans, the mediterranean and others. i would stress the importance of close partnerships with the mediterranean region, which treats turkey and the maghreb, with which our europe has longstanding and important links, equally. i therefore abstained on all the votes except for the recognition of the armenian genocide which parliament has always defended, and this so that no one could imagine that i had any principle of prevention against turkey. this is another vision of europe.
in writing. we voted against this text, which makes a very unfair reproach to turkey: that of being turkey, that is to say, not being european. what is the point of pressing this country with recommendations and demands: the peoples of europe do not want turkey to join, because it is obvious to them that turkey, and this is not to insult it, is not part of the european family. it has its own culture, its own values, its own sphere of influence. that is the meaning of the amendment we tabled on behalf of the ind/dem group. we must now put an end to the hypocritical and destructive game of accession negotiations, which can only end in a major crisis, since the eventual accession treaty has no chance of being ratified by the peoples. the european parliament has already adopted a resolution on the situation in the former yugoslavia. today we have a thought for our french colleagues caught in the middle of schizophrenia. while they claim to oppose turkey's accession, they vote every year, here and in the french parliament, for pre-accession funds for turkey, and they have welcomed within their own european party, the epp, the observers of the akp, mr erdogan's islamist party.
in writing. i have decided to abstain on the eurlings report, even though it is a hard report. it is true that it marks a turning point in the realisation of the reality of eu-turkey relations, but by implying and confirming, after the rejection of certain amendments, that accession is an end in itself, it remains too one-sided. the undeniable slowdown in reforms in turkey, despite the opening of accession negotiations by the commission, should, on the contrary, strengthen the option of a preferential partnership. the fact that the opening of these negotiations has not accelerated reforms is worrying and our response should be a demand for results and not the idea that accession will happen at all costs. it was therefore necessary to recall that the normalisation of relations with cyprus must be an unconditional precondition for eventual accession. the fact that turkey has still not ratified and implemented the ankara protocol, which is a legal form of recognition that is minimal and just acceptable, is unacceptable. finally, i supported the amendment on the recognition of the armenian genocide as a precondition for eventual accession, because this is not a symbolic point but a moral duty and a historical requirement incumbent on the turkish authorities.

research council, in the people programme, in the capacities programme, and in infrastructure – the things connected with regional development. so it is very hard to compare the money that was devoted today to fp6 with the money that will be used in fp7. what i can tell you is that the funding will be increased considerably in comparison with the existing situation. again, if we compare the funding in europe to that in the united states, we must not forget that the framework programme is 5% of european public funding. therefore, it is obvious, if you compare how much public funding is provided for nanosciences, that it is 30% of that public funding in europe. obviously, we are giving it proportionally much higher attention than the member states are doing. that has to be clearly underlined. secondly, in normal circumstances, two thirds of funding should come from the private sector, where we have to focus our attention. so here one of the things we found out – and it was published in august 2006 – was what the decisive elements are according to the companies doing the research in the area of europe: first, the existence of the market; and second, the knowledge pool , not the wage level. the wage level is almost irrelevant when we talk about knowledge and research and development. these are the areas which need attention. thirdly, concerning the risks, it is true that we do not know everything and it would be hypocritical to say that we do, because it is not true. however, we know a lot, and i agree with all those who said that we need to pay proper attention to that in fp7. extremely important that the way in which we approach questions of risk should be transparent and that we educate people in the proper way. concerning ethics, it is quite clear that we have to maintain the high ethical standards and principles that we have always followed and pay proper attention to that. finally, on the regulatory framework, regulatory issues again form an integral part of the action plan. they are concentrated there and the commission is working in close collaboration with research dgs and dgs active in regulatory aspects, and with external experts, with a view to addressing various uncertainties with regard to potential hazards and exposure, to addressing gaps in knowledge, and to further developing guidelines and methods. the adequacy of existing and future legislation with regard to nanotechnology products is also being examined carefully. to summarise, without any doubt we need a balanced approach, which is transparent, with a high level of care for public health, safety, the environment and consumer protection, but aimed at exploiting the huge potential of nanosciences and nanotechnologies in research and innovation. today’s report was a very good opportunity to underline all these components of our approach and i should like to thank honourable members for their attention to these issues, for the support given to our work and for the concerns they have raised.

member of the commission. mr president, i speak on behalf of my colleague, mr michel, who is unable to be here this morning. i wish to begin by expressing my thanks to the rapporteur, mr hutchinson, and the committee on development for a constructive report on aid effectiveness, a topic of key importance for the eu development policy. improving both the quantity and the quality of our aid is certainly one of the core commitments set out in the european consensus for development, the latter having been endorsed by all member states, the commission and parliament in 2005. the consensus is a crucial document for all of us. first, it opens a new dimension for joint work between the 25 member states and the commission. secondly, it highlights, for the first time in eu history, our collective european vision, principles and objectives that govern our development policy. thirdly, it sets out the comparative advantage of the commission and the objective of redeploying member states’ activities in order to achieve better and highly necessary synergy. as demonstrated during all the debates on the european consensus, the commission should promote the impact of europe in development and push the european aid effectiveness agenda. the european union must be a leading force in international fora dealing with aid effectiveness, in particular in the oecd/dac, where the commission enjoys full statutory membership. a strong eu makes for a strong dac. it is with this in mind that commissioner michel has proposed a package of concrete deliverables on aid effectiveness, which were endorsed by the council in spring 2006. the commission’s approach to aid effectiveness is based on lessons learnt from the field, good practices and expectations from the partner countries. it is rooted in the principles of harmonisation, ownership, alignment and management by results, as in the paris declaration. parliament has made it clear in previous resolutions and again in this report that it supports the commission in its efforts to strengthen the coordination and coherence of both commission and eu actions in the development field. the report highlights three important areas in which progress needs to be achieved in 2007 and i would like to comment on them briefly. first, strengthening complementarity and the division of labour: these issues are crucial for the commission. the eu donor atlas has indeed underlined the gaps and duplications in donor activities which hamper the impact of aid. in order to address these weaknesses, the commission launched a process with member states aimed at adopting operational principles for a better division of labour between eu donors. discussions are currently ongoing and this initiative should be rendered operational with council conclusions in 2007. second, the joint programming of aid: the eu now has at its disposal a joint framework adopted last spring. this framework foresees the drawing-up of common diagnostics and analysis in partner countries, in close partnership with member states involved, to establish common operational solutions. partner countries and civil society play a major and active role in this process. far from being excluded from these discussions, civil society is strongly involved in the country diagnostic set up in order to ensure its full ownership. this approach is fully in line with the approach used in ec programming. thirdly, a few words on an essential tool for improving the division of labour and coordination, that is, cofinancing. in 2007, the commission will bring forward specific proposals on how to strengthen the use of cofinancing as a tool to support the division of labour amongst donors, as well as to assist those member states building their development capacities. parliament has been persistent in its well-founded requests to the commission to ensure coordination among member states in order to strengthen the effectiveness of financing for development. as you can see, the commission has clearly adopted a proactive attitude and will, in close collaboration with member states, use all tools at its disposal to make greater aid effectiveness a reality. i can only advocate that the european parliament uses the joint meeting on development with the national parliaments next october as an opportunity to expand support for these initiatives. indeed, it is important for the eu to ensure that its political ambitions match its financial status as the largest global donor. in this respect, parliament has a crucial role to play in helping member states to accelerate their reforms and make the necessary cultural changes implied by this new joint working dimension. success on this front is of major importance for reaching our development goals, as well as taking the lead on the global development agenda. let us recall that the ultimate objective is to succeed in the fight against poverty. it is only by acting together and by making the best possible use of all the means at our disposal that success can be guaranteed. thanks to the european consensus, we now have all the necessary tools to achieve this goal. we must make sure that these commitments remain high on our political agenda and that we do not miss this real opportunity to turn our ambitious political commitments into reality. it goes beyond politics; it is a matter of collective credibility.

in writing. every day, a growing number of canoes and lifeboats from senegal, mali, mauritania and the gambia are washing up on the canary islands. in total, some 300 000 africans are believed to be entering the eu illegally each year. the european leaders are obliged to wake up to the scale of the phenomenon and are beginning to be moved, without denouncing it, by the disastrous consequences of the criminal schengen agreements and the formidable air appeals of the mass legalisation of the undocumented in spain or italy (more than 1 150 000 foreigners legalised by spain since 1985). at the moment, the european union is only lecturing spain because of its regulations, which are considered too "lax". it is obviously not a question of changing the laws on immigration and asylum, as in the case of switzerland, which, with 68% of the vote, has just voted for a new law on immigration and a tightening of the conditions for access to asylum, thus adopting one of the most restrictive legislation in europe. the time for submission and passivity must end. the solution to stop this overwhelming immigration is now to re-establish borders, zero immigration and stop naturalizations.
in writing. illegal immigration seems to be a concern for european leaders. it's about time! it is true that only since 1995 and the disastrous schengen agreements has the national front ceaselessly warned and denounced the inevitable damage caused by the abolition of internal border controls in the union. it took spain to see the record number of over 25 000 african immigrants disembark in the canary islands since january and the italian coastguard to take over 12 000 immigrants to refugee camps on the small island of lampedusa in southern sicily in nine months for all european governments and our european leaders to become concerned about the irresistible and exponentially increasing migratory surge in europe. europe is exposed as being incapable of managing its maritime and land borders. and it is not the "gadget" of frontex, the eu's external border coordination agency, which shines with its slowness, lack of manpower and resources, that will provide an effective response to immigration-invasion. let us re-establish europe's internal borders and remove the vacuum pumps of immigration, which are first and foremost the regularisation of illegal immigrants. these are the essential preconditions for an immediate halt to this flood of immigration.
in writing. we voted against the two resolutions which were proposed to us. these, with certain nuances, noted the difficulty of controlling the entry and movement of illegal immigrants, without however ever mentioning the fact that this difficulty results precisely from the abolition of national borders. the resolution also takes up the idea, shared by mr sarkozy, of the total abolition of the unanimous vote for justice and home affairs, that is to say, of the sovereignty of the states over their territory. it is also making european integration the solution to the problem it poses. those who today in this parliament, as the epp is doing, are trying to contain immigration are in fact pyromaniacal firemen: we should not have accepted the schengen treaty with the abolition of fixed internal border controls, we should not have accepted the amsterdam treaty, that is to say the com munitization of the bulk of asylum, visa and immigration policies, including the fight against illegal immigration. the doors have been opened to uncontrolled immigration, while the powers of the member states have been taken away and transferred to a union which is necessarily paralysed.
in writing. the massive influx of illegal migrants to the canary islands has reminded public opinion and governments of the serious and complex problems posed by illegal immigration. i would remind my european colleagues that this is not a new phenomenon for french overseas departments, particularly mayotte, french guiana, martinique and guadeloupe, because of their proximity to some of the poorest countries in the world. mayotte is only a few nautical miles from the comoros, and the guyanese border is a territory of equatorial forest that is difficult to control. this is how much the outermost regions, including the canary islands and the dom, would benefit from a common immigration policy. i believe it is essential that the european parliament should focus on five aspects of this future policy: better targeted development aid, the establishment of partnerships with countries of origin, border security and the fight against human trafficking, the strengthening of the return policy, and better integration of legal migrants into the host society. we need clear rules, with concrete and operational priorities. the european union can no longer be satisfied with declarations of intent.

october. we ended up organising the lahti meeting because we wanted to give the heads of state of the union the opportunity to have an open and free debate on two subjects which are important for the future and economic success of the union: innovation and external energy relations. we need a coherent and strong policy both in terms of creating an enabling environment for innovation and in energy matters. this will help to improve the conditions for economic growth and employment in the union. when the union acts concretely for the welfare of the people, we can also expect the union to be more acceptable to the citizens. a coherent common energy policy will also strengthen the union's credibility as an international actor. the commission will prepare the discussions of the meeting of heads of state or government to guide two communications, one on external relations in the energy sector and the other on innovation policy. the notices will be published tomorrow, 12 october. they are not intended to be adopted at the meeting, but they do indicate the issues we want to tackle in the gulf. the informal meeting of heads of state or government in lahti will be preceded by an informal tripartite social summit on friday morning. how europe's labour market of 200 million workers functions and adapts to change is central to europe's future. the social partners therefore play a key role in strengthening europe's competitiveness. russian president vladimir putin has been invited to the gulf for a post-summit dinner. the talks with the president are to focus on the eu-russia strategic partnership, including cooperation on energy issues. mr president, the major challenges facing the union in the field of energy - security of energy supply, climate change, the continuing rise in energy prices and the recent crises - have given impetus to the development of a common eu energy policy. the eu's growing dependence on energy imports is a particular challenge in securing its energy supply. it is estimated that, in the absence of measures, the import dependency will increase from 50% to 70% over the next 20 years. before the finnish presidency, the development of the common energy policy was discussed at the two european council meetings earlier this year. the finnish part of the meeting will focus on external energy relations and will build on the broad energy debate to be held next spring, leading to the adoption of the energy policy action programme. although the focus of the gulf talks will be on external energy relations, it is clear that our external relations objectives cannot be considered as a separate issue. there is a close link between all the priority areas of energy policy identified in the green paper. other areas deal with the internal energy market, solidarity between member states, diversification of energy sources, energy efficiency and renewable energy sources, and energy innovation. external energy policy must achieve a common understanding and vision among member states of the basis of strategy for relations with non-eu countries and of the eu's common external objectives. this means that the member states must be able to commit themselves to a commonly agreed approach to bilateral relations and to speak with one voice in these contacts. by committing to common objectives, the union is also better prepared to face the changes in the world energy market. the gulf energy summit will be an exchange of views on how external energy relations could be developed in the near future. the discussions will focus on three main themes: firstly, the principles underlying the eu-russia energy relationship and the implementation of these principles; secondly, closer relations with strategically important third countries; and thirdly, better data collection as a basis for decision-making on the common energy policy. russia, which accounts for 25% of both oil and gas imports, is the union's most important strategic energy partner. in all strategic partnerships, including with russia, it is important to find a mutual interest in developing the partnership. the eu-russia energy relationship is characterised by a common interest: the eu is dependent on russian energy imports, while russia needs not only long-term, market-price agreements for its energy exports, but also western investment in basic energy production. opening up the market in one way or another is the key factor. the eu heads of state or government's discussions will also build on the discussions with russian president vladimir putin later in the evening, one of the key themes of which will be energy issues. the aim is to convey to russia the eu's commitment to a binding framework for energy agreements that takes into account the interests of both parties, reciprocity and a level playing field. the eu and russia will also be faced with common challenges, such as energy efficiency, which both sides have to overcome. the extension of the principles of the energy common market to the eu's neighbouring regions and the development of relations with strategically important third countries are desirable in terms of security of energy supply. 80% of the world's oil reserves are located in the regions surrounding the union. there are a wide range of instruments for developing relations with third countries, such as the neighbourhood policy action programmes, the energy cooperation agreement, bilateral agreements and regional agreements. energy policy must be one of the pillars of the union's common foreign and security policy. the european union needs sufficient information to pursue a more coherent energy policy. it must also be able to respond to external energy crises and emergencies. the union should also set up a system to increase cooperation between member states and institutions and to improve solidarity on energy issues. the second main topic of the meeting of the heads of state or government is the development of innovation policy. the european research work needs to be better able to be exploited as commercial goods and services. the union must also be able to adopt new technologies as effectively as our competitors. if we continue with current practices, the innovation gap with the union's main trading partners will only increase. in particular, the production of emerging economies is increasingly competing with europe not only in industry but also in the service sectors. china and india are training significantly more highly qualified people for their labour markets than the eu. however, emerging market economies also represent a huge export potential for the union. success can only come from the ability to create new things, that is, from innovation. in an open market, the best commodities thrive. it is impossible to stay on top of the market without continuous investment in research and product development. the union's member states have committed themselves to increasing their investment in research and development in the future, on the basis of decisions already taken in the past. however, it is vital to ensure that europe is able to exploit investments in such a way that research leads to new and better commercially exploitable goods and services. the purpose of the lahti meeting is to highlight issues and challenges where there is a need for joint action by the union. the aim is to create an environment in which innovation is both generated and effectively used. the european parliament has also stressed the importance of innovation policy in its opinions on the lisbon strategy. the creation of an eu-wide ipr strategy is essential to support effective innovation. intellectual property rights are of great importance for the success and competitiveness of enterprises. the key issue is, among other things, the quality of patents, which is the basic principle of a functioning and reliable patent system. as the president, we believe that europe must have a patent system which is cost-effective but which also respects quality, regardless of the alternative on which this system is based. if we can develop the patent system further, companies will be guaranteed substantial savings in the cost of patenting, which will encourage innovation and research in europe. better cooperation between universities and the business world is a prerequisite for the success of innovation policy. the commission will be presenting a proposal next week for a new european institute of technology based on a network model. excellence will be the hallmark of the partnership between science, enterprise and education. the focus will be on promoting innovation. as the presidency, we believe that through the european institute of technology, europe can make more effective use of the opportunities that already exist in business and the scientific community. the cooperation between the private and public sectors must also be improved in order to promote competitiveness. europe has developed so-called european technology platforms, business-oriented strategic research initiatives that are excellent examples of private-public partnerships. the companies have thankfully indicated their willingness to invest in the platforms of their choice, and a corresponding commitment is now required from the public research funder. accelerating the development of european standards in the union would be of great importance for innovation. without a common european standard, many innovations may go unused. what would the european mobile phone market have been like without the gsm standard, for example? the creation of pan-european technical standards for mobile phones made it possible in practice for europe to become a world leader in this field. on the other hand, if purely national standards had been adopted as the basis for the development of mobile phones, the success would not have been as significant and geographically extensive. the rapid establishment of open and compatible standards is one of the keys to the success of enterprises. this also brings clear benefits for consumers. at the same time, it strengthens our competitive position and responds to rapid technological developments, so that technical development solutions developed in europe can genuinely compete with development work carried out elsewhere in the world. mr president, illegal immigration is a problem affecting the whole of the european union. that's why we have to find solutions together. solidarity is best expressed in the europe about half of all researchers are employed by business. in the united states, that figure stands at over 80%. the truth is that europe is falling behind in terms of innovation and research. the status quo is not an option: we need to do more in this matter. we urgently need a strategic approach which focuses on each link in the innovation chain, from the birth of new ideas and knowledge right through to their exploitation and marketing in the economic sphere. the communication which the commission will present at the informal summit in lahti sets out such an approach. it pinpoints the weak links in the chain and puts forward solutions. we need financing, we need the right intellectual property framework to bring the right rewards and we need to tackle obstacles to innovation sector by sector. above all, we need to start with a strong political message of commitment: innovation deserves encouragement, and we need a european approach for it. size matters on this issue. one of the big differences between us and the united states is that we have no pan-european institutions for innovation and research. the united states is much more committed to a real global approach. there are great institutions supporting innovation throughout the united states, not just in one or two states. until now, we had nothing in europe. now we have the european research council and we are proposing the establishment of a european institute of technology. we are proposing a network system to lend a real european dimension and a real european mission to those institutions. that is why we are insisting on this approach. that is the importance of the european institute of technology. it will bring the private and public sectors closer together for cutting-edge research, become a centre of international excellence, bring together the top brains, provide a stream of top class phds and promote spin-offs of innovative small and medium-sized enterprises. in short, it can become a symbol of europe’s ability to work together and innovate. we have been developing the finer details of the eit over recent months and we will bring forward a detailed proposal next week. i am confident that the heads of state and government and the parliamentarians here in the european parliament will look at it in the spirit in which it is designed: yes, it is something a little different, but something which can provide an example of europe taking a fresh direction and finding new ways to work together. one of the fields in which i think we as european leaders can give a mission to a european institute of technology is that of energy and climate change. when we have a problem that we need help to solve, we should ask the best scientists, the best brains on our continent. energy is one of the most important challenges we have today. let me now turn to the issue of energy and let me make it plain: we need to create a truly european energy policy, not 25 energy policies. it is absurd in the 21st century to go on with 25 or 27 energy policies. we need a truly european energy policy. the problems we face – high energy prices, climate change, increasing dependence on imported hydrocarbons – are global and european problems. they need european solutions. national solutions will not be enough. at hampton court last year, european union leaders agreed to develop a common approach. in our green paper of march 2006, the commission defined clear objectives for a european energy policy, long-term sustainability, security of energy supply and economic competitiveness. the member states have endorsed our approach, and the reaction from stakeholders to our green paper has been overwhelmingly positive. the next step is a strategic energy review which the commission will propose at the very beginning of next year. i look forward to reading the european parliament’s report on it. it is obvious that we need coherence between the internal and external aspects of energy policy. we clearly need an effective internal market in energy. having 25 or 27 different energy mini-markets is not the answer to the european energy challenges. however, we must link internal and external policy. our paper for lahti will look at the three external challenges: russia, which i will return to; developing our energy relations with our neighbours; and creating a network to deal with external energy shocks. it is essential to build up energy cooperation with strategically important supply and transit countries. this is already happening with initiatives such as the new energy community treaty and the memorandum of understanding on energy cooperation with ukraine. we need to extend the principles of the internal energy market gradually throughout our neighbourhood. we also need to join the different areas of expertise which exist around europe to create a more effective network to deal with external energy shocks. of course, in the medium term, the best way to cope with energy shocks is through diversity: diversity of energy sources, of country of origin and of country of transit. indeed, we need to mainstream energy to make it a major focus of our relations with partners worldwide. finally, energy efficiency is another crucial element of this strategy. i can announce to you today that next week commissioner piebalgs – the commissioner for energy – and i will propose an ambitious action plan to fulfil our commitment to save 20% of primary energy use by 2020. naturally, with 25% of the oil and gas consumed in the european union coming from russia, energy cooperation with russia is crucial. the president-in-office of the council just explained why it is important. we must have a reinforced energy partnership with russia. such a partnership must be based on reciprocity, transparency, non-discrimination and openness to competition, including a level playing field for upstream and downstream investment. this is the only way to have a stable and secure platform for our energy relationship. the meeting with president putin will be a chance to deliver a clear and hopefully coherent message from european union leaders. we see three long-term objectives in our relations with russia: we want to see a functioning democracy and market economy in which russia lives up to the international commitments it has undertaken; we want to see a broad and strategic eu-russia relationship based on interdependence – russia needs the european union and the european union also needs russia – and we want to enhance our cooperation with russia on international issues. when we talk about effective multilateralism, this is what we mean. we have set our goal of a wide-ranging agreement to follow the current partnership and cooperation agreement. there are mutual benefits to be realised in areas such as investment and market-opening, as well as in energy and energy efficiency. we both have so much to gain from a real partnership. i also take this opportunity to express my deepest sympathy with the family of anna politkovskaya, who was so brutally murdered last week. i want to pay tribute to her relentless pursuit of truth. she was a great defender of freedom of expression in russia. (applause) i sincerely hope that the perpetrators of this heinous crime will be found and brought to justice. another point we are going to address is that of immigration. the massive arrival of illegal immigrants at the frontiers of the european union’s southern member states is a european problem that requires a european solution. in november 2006, the commission presented a communication with a series of practical proposals for the european union to respond to this challenge. on that basis, the european council adopted a global approach to migration, outlining in detail how to respond in its internal and external policies. in less than a year we have seen the start of a lot of practical action: joint operations in the mediterranean and the atlantic under the coordination of the borders agency, frontex; enhanced cooperation among the law-enforcement services of the member states; better coordination of the work of the immigration liaison offices in africa; and dialogue with key african countries of origin and transit, both bilaterally and multilaterally. for the first time, member states are working together in joint operations protecting the european union’s external borders under the coordination of frontex. however, let us be frank: it is not enough; much more is needed to tackle the illegal flows effectively. in order to strengthen the european union’s response capacity, it is of the utmost importance that all member states of the union work together in a spirit of solidarity, not least to assist those member states that are, let us say, in the front line. with a view to the informal european council to be held in lahti on 20 october, i have written personally to the heads of state and government underlining the need for such solidarity. of course, the ideal would be to have already established the community instruments, but we have not got them yet. of course, the ideal would be to have a european migration policy. it is absurd to have 25 or 27 migration policies in an area in which people can move around freely, because decisions taken by one country have a direct effect on the other countries. but before we have a true community method to tackle these issues, we at least expect member states to cooperate well among themselves. (applause) we believe this is also a practical example of european solidarity. we also need to work much more intensively with the countries of origin and transit. the implementation of the action plan agreed in rabat in july is a key priority. the commission will work hard to ensure proper implementation in close partnership with the countries concerned. let us also be frank about this. security matters are not enough. the solution to this problem will come only with our support for sustainable development in africa. by the way, i think we have to engage in a high-level dialogue with african countries. is it not strange that the european union has dialogue with asia and latin america at the level of heads of state and government, but not with africa? is it not about time now for europe to make a commitment to establishing a high-level dialogue with africa? i believe we have the right and the duty to do so. that was the message i took recently to our counterparts in the african union commission in addis ababa. that is why we are also actively engaged – via our cooperation with our african partners – in looking collectively at this issue. in european terms, we also need a european union decision-making process. when there are urgent and serious problems, the european union needs to be able to react appropriately. this means using the bridging clause in article 67 of the treaty. we cannot deny ourselves the means to deliver effective action. to conclude, the informal european council meeting in lahti provides a good opportunity to take stock of the current european union actions in the fields i have outlined and in several other fields as well. we are looking for a renewed commitment from the heads of state and government to deliver solutions to the real and pressing problems of the citizens of the european union, and to deliver a europe of results so that we can have more confidence to solve some of the very important problems in our union. let me give you a final thought. a week ago i was in darfur. amidst the terrible conditions experienced by the people there, i saw something that i resolved to tell my friends back in brussels: in the ngos and other humanitarian organisations, there are so many young europeans, so far from their homes, putting their lives at risk every day to help africans. this is the kind of europe of which i think we should be proud; a europe that is ready to deliver solidarity and help, showing great courage. that is the kind of europe i believe we all want: an open, outward-looking, generous europe. that is the europe we should strive for.
