member of the commission. mr president, the vote at second reading on the services directive will be a milestone in the history of the european parliament, not only because of the importance of this directive for european citizens and businesses, but also because of the leading role parliament has played in the legislative process. it is undeniable that the services directive is an essential element in our efforts to boost the european economy and unleash the potential of the internal market for services. the text which is now on the table will provide real added value to the internal market, cutting red tape, removing barriers and improving legal certainty for business and consumers. it lays solid foundations for a new internal market framework with a positive impact on the freedom of establishment and the creation of new business. this is crucial for fostering entrepreneurship and for promoting growth and jobs. service providers can be confident that they are dealing with fair and transparent authorisation regimes and swift and simple procedures. they will be able to obtain information and complete administrative formalities through points of single contact in any member state and, in addition, in electronic form. this will simplify, accelerate and reduce the cost for the setting up of new business and obviate the need to deal with different levels of authorities. equally, the directive will provide a welcome boost to cross-border service provision. the new provision on the freedom to provide services, which was at the heart of the compromise in first reading, strikes a fair balance between guaranteeing the rights of service providers to free access and free exercise of a service activity whilst allowing member states the right to invoke their most essential requirements in certain clearly defined circumstances. this will definitively improve legal certainty for service providers and consumers. importantly, the directive will be underpinned by obligations on member states to cooperate among and assist each other, in order to ensure that businesses are properly and efficiently supervised across the european union while avoiding duplication of controls. these three elements – simplification of establishment, freedom to provide services and assistance and cooperation between member states – were always at the core of the commission’s drive to open up the services market. the position of the european parliament has been crucial to finding a broad consensus on these issues. in this dossier, the european parliament has shown its maturity and capacity to find well-balanced compromises on very complex issues. at first reading you clearly took the lead and were able to deliver the broad consensus we pursued. getting a consensus in the council was not easy. some member states had serious difficulties in accepting your delicate compromise on the scope of application of the proposal and the freedom to provide services mechanism. in the end, and after a vigorous defence by the commission and the presidency of the compromise reached in parliament, the common position was adopted. it is a common position that respects and reflects parliament’s political compromise, with only minor adjustments introduced mostly to provide greater legal clarity. you are aware that the compromise reflected in the common position is very delicate and fragile. attempts to reopen the text will inevitably give rise to a new debate in the council and put in jeopardy the compromise reached. i call on parliament to recognise that the common position closely reflects parliament’s first reading, and to refrain from seeking further modifications through amendments. the vote in the committee on the internal market and consumer protection on 23 october 2006 demonstrates that this is possible. at this juncture there are no ‘technical’ or ‘minor’ amendments. i am aware that in discussions leading up to the vote in the committee, certain institutional and legal issues have been raised which are of concern to some members of this house. in this context, i would like to make the following statements to address the concerns that some of you have raised. ‘ concerning the screening of national requirements which member states apply to services provided from other member states, the council has requested the commission to provide orientations and analysis and the commission will use its best efforts to abide with this task. this will not give additional powers to the commission which may, pursuant to the treaty, if it considers it necessary, formulate recommendations and deliver opinions on matters dealt with in the treaty. the orientations will merely consist of assistance to member states for the proper implementation of the services directive. they will neither provide legally binding interpretation of the directive, which is the prerogative of the european court of justice, nor will they amend the provisions of the services directive, which is the prerogative of the european parliament and the council. the commission will carry out this task in an open and transparent manner in close cooperation with the other institutions. it will in particular regularly inform the european parliament about the results and the follow-up of its analysis. concerning the need to consider further harmonisation, in the future review of the services directive, the commission will assess whether, in the field of services, further measures are necessary and, if so, what kind of measures are appropriate. the commission will, in particular, examine whether for certain services or certain issues there is a need for additional harmonisation. the commission will thereby take suggestions made by the european parliament, in particular at the first reading of the directive, into consideration. where necessary, and in line with our better regulation approach, the commission will make specific proposals, including proposals for harmonisation, where justified. concerning the impact of the services directive on labour law, the european parliament and the council wanted to avoid that the services directive affects labour law or the rights of the social partners to defend their collective interests. the commission wants to state unambiguously that the services directive does indeed not affect labour law laid down in national legislation and established practices in the member states and that it does not affect collective rights which the social partners enjoy according to national legislation and established practices. the services directive is neutral as to the different models in the member states regarding the role of the social partners and the organisation of how collective interests are defended according to national law and practices. however, community law, and in particular the treaty, continue to apply in this field. concerning the impact of the services directive on criminal law, as is stated in the text, the services directive will not affect member states’ criminal law rules. this means that in general member states will be able to apply their criminal law rules not only to service providers established on their territory but also to service providers from other member states providing services within their territory. this is because criminal law rules, in general, apply to everybody in the same way, irrespective of whether a service is provided. however, member states may not circumvent or prevent the application of the provisions of the services directive by making use of criminal law. concerning the impact of the services directive on social services, social services relating to social housing, childcare and support of families and persons in need are a manifestation of the principle of social cohesion and solidarity in society and are provided by the state, by service providers on behalf of the state or by acknowledged charitable organisations. these services have thus been excluded from the scope of application of the services directive. it is clear that this exclusion also covers services provided by churches and church organisations which serve charitable and benevolent purposes.’ i have arranged for the text of these statements to be handed in to the secretariat for inclusion in the record of this part-session. i hope that these statements help to accommodate the concerns raised by some. the commission hopes that they will facilitate the acceptance of the common position by parliament. before concluding, i note that mrs mccarthy has tabled three amendments on behalf of her committee relating to the new regulatory procedure with scrutiny. these amendments result from the agreement reached between the three institutions last summer on the revision of the comitology procedure and can be accepted by the commission. next week it will be two years since this commission entered office and i became commissioner for the internal market and services. the debate on the services directive has been at the forefront of attention for much of that time. i think we should now move to adopting the directive and start implementing it. i look forward to hearing the view of this house. infringement of social rights, excludes the liberalisation of public services and takes account of the public interest. i can testify to this compromise, since i have been involved in its elaboration mr president, ladies and gentlemen, although much progress has been made in relation to the original text presented by the european commission, the directive on services in the internal market which has been put to our vote today is different from the first reading of the european parliament. i therefore voted against the common position. the services of general economic interest are still covered by the directive, as are some services of general interest. the scope of the exclusion of social services of general interest is also much more limited. the fundamental rights guaranteed by the european charter are now only mentioned in a recital. finally, the text remains very ambiguous as regards the exclusion of labour law. the written statement presented by the european commission provides some of the answers to these questions, which i consider essential, but it has no legal value and, in the event of a dispute being brought before the courts, the court of justice may disregard it. it would have been different if that statement had come from the council, which is a co-legislator with parliament.
in writing. the adoption by the european parliament of the services directive makes it possible to establish the general provisions to facilitate the exercise of the freedom of establishment of providers and the free movement of services whose high quality is guaranteed while avoiding the risk of social dumping included in the original concept of the country of origin principle which has been abolished. its scope has been considerably reduced by excluding, in particular, health services, non-market public services and certain market public services. service activities account for 70% of the eu's gdp and offer considerable growth and employment potential. i would like to point out, in retrospect, how wise it was for the president of the french republic, mr jacques chirac, to stop the original text presented by the prodi commission at the time. this dossier marks the growing influence of the european parliament, for whom it is a major political victory, and it symbolises the concept of the social market economy as expressed in the draft constitutional treaty for europe. the eyes must now be turned to the member states, which have the responsibility to transpose this text into national law in a fair, equitable and sincere manner.
in writing. i voted for the motion for a resolution rejecting the council's common position on services in the internal market. the vote on second reading was on a text which differed from the vote on first reading. there are still too many uncertainties about the application of the principle of country of origin. the text does not clarify the ambiguities that remain regarding the protection of public services and consumers. more seriously, whereas labour law is a matter for national competence, the council has just made compliance with labour law conditional on community decisions, since compliance with labour law will now be subject to the judgments of the court of justice of the european community. the european union is turning its back on its original ambition to create a european area of solidarity. with the downward harmonisation of social, environmental and consumer protection rules, the european social model is being undermined.
in writing. the french socialists refused on wednesday, 15 november, to endorse the report on services in the internal market, in other words the services directive. in fact, despite the very important progress made by the socialist group and the socialist rapporteur, evelyne gebhardt, at first reading - in particular the rejection of the country of origin principle - parliament did not obtain any guarantee from the commission for a draft framework directive on public services. the second reading of a text does not include a final vote on the whole text, so we supported the amendment to reject the text tabled by several groups (gue/ngl and greens/efa). we have also tabled several amendments aimed in particular at ensuring that the freedom of member states to define what they mean by social services of general interest is respected. as bernard poignant, speaking for the french socialists, has said, 'the definition, formulation, organisation and actual financing of services of general interest, whether economic or not, must remain a matter for the member states and their regional and local authorities'.
in writing. i voted for the amendment rejecting the council's common position on the services directive. it is not satisfactory because it introduces more confusion and legal uncertainty and further weakens the amended proposal adopted by the european parliament at first reading, which i voted against. this is particularly the case for labour law and for social and public services excluded from the scope of the services directive. but above all, the council text gives the commission a power of orientation as regards the application of the directive. the concept of country of origin has disappeared from the text in the text amended by the commission, but it has not been replaced by the concept of country of destination or host country. this seems to me to be very damaging, especially since it will be the court of justice of the european communities which will settle any conflicts that may arise. the directive on services of liberal orientation was therefore adopted on 15 november. three years of debate have not been able to avoid an epilogue with dangerous consequences for political and social europe. it is a bad blow to the european construction which hardly needed it.
in writing. despite considerable progress compared with the european commission's initial draft, the text on services in the union proposed today at second reading does not provide sufficient guarantees to avoid any risk of disruption of the european social model. some sensitive social services, such as social housing, family support services or public health services, which were initially excluded from the scope of the future directive at first reading, have thus been reintroduced by the member states. the legal vacuum created by the abolition of the ppo has not been removed, leaving the power to define the future shape of european social policy to the judges of the court of justice and not to the legislator, through the case law that this situation will inevitably generate. in this context, it is clear that the written statement of the commission, which is intended to clarify some of the shortcomings of the text, such as the exclusion of labour law, has no real legal value, which makes its weight and usefulness particularly uncertain. for all these reasons, i voted against the proposal for a directive on services.
in writing. if the new version of the bolkestein directive had not already suffered from serious shortcomings, in particular the fact that it was not fundamentally different from the previous one, there would have been only one reason for rejecting it: the suspicious consensus of the two major groups, the pse and the epp, between themselves, and moreover for accepting the compromise worked out in the council. the real revolution would have consisted, among other things, in explicitly affirming the primacy of the application in the territory of a member state of its national law, in particular its national labour law, its national social, criminal and fiscal laws. that is to say, the principle of the country of destination as opposed to the principle of the country of origin. this would not have prevented providers from another member state from offering services in another country, it would simply have allowed fair competition with national operators. the revolution would have consisted in accepting that the states could impose conditions on access to certain activities, such as the situation of the labour market or reasons for land use planning. they don't have that option. after competition with the rest of the world, competition between firms, europe now devotes itself to competition between european workers, selfemployed or employed, and thus to competition between social systems. it's going into the wall.
in writing. the services directive has just been adopted by a clear majority. it is to the credit of the european parliament. it is a victory for the european union. why would you do that? services account for more than half of the european economy and are the main source of employment. the free provision of services is one of the founding principles of the union and the creation of a genuine internal market in services is essential for economic growth in europe and therefore for job creation. the text voted on today in strasbourg commits us to this, while providing the necessary guarantees on the safeguarding of public services of general interest and on the sustainability of our social acquis and our labour law. by excluding the principle of country of origin, it prohibits social competition and constitutes an effective barrier to social dumping. it removes unjustified protectionist barriers, while allowing member states to apply their national rules where the public interest so warrants. the scope of the text has also been reduced, with the exclusion of sensitive sectors such as the audiovisual sector, health, part of the social services, games and notaries. it is a good compromise that will move europe forward in the interests of its people.
in writing. i voted against this directive because i believe that, despite the improvements achieved in the parliamentary debate and under the pressure of the trade unions and citizens, it remains profoundly liberal. there is no prospect of real harmonization for the benefit of consumers and workers, in contrast to the tremendous deregulation of the services sector in europe, which is mainly for the benefit of businesses. as for public services, while the commission refuses to move forward with the framework directive on services of general interest, the services directive is contributing to the weakening of public services, some of which will suffer the same effects as mere market services. finally, the 'prohibited and to be assessed requirements' of articles 14 and 15 make any public regulation in the services sector impossible, or at least extremely difficult. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full, and i am glad that the commission has taken this step.
in writing. despite some improvements, despite some additional sectors excluded from the scope of application, or rather of nuisance, of the bolkestein directive in its first version, this text, in its new form, remains fundamentally unacceptable. the door remains open to social dumping and unfair competition between workers. it does not in fact solve any of the problems raised by the original directive. it does not exclude public services and does not guarantee the right of states to determine their definition, organisation and financing. it denies the legitimate economic, social or other requirements which those same states may impose on access to an activity, and only allows them to rely on 'overriding reasons of general interest', a vague concept which the luxembourg court will interpret in the most restrictive sense. it makes compliance with the labour law of the state in which the service is provided subject to compliance with community law and in particular with the principle of freedom to provide services laid down in the treaties, which amounts to denying the application of that national law. millions of europeans have said 'no' to this ultra-liberal europe which despises men and peoples and favours the laws of the market, financial interests and sacrosanct competition. hear them before it's too late!
in writing. i voted in favour of the amendment rejecting this directive, which is a step back from the vote at first reading because it leaves open the application of the principle of the country of origin and does not exclude public services - gis, sgei - from this 'free' competition, which will be very destabilised. the european commission explains that the text does not clearly state which law will apply and therefore private international law, which is close to the principle of the country of origin, will apply most of the time. the scope for action by the states in the social field will be extremely limited. despite formal advances, little by little, the liberal reality will prevail with this text and our social model will be called into question.
in writing. in an attempt to win the consent of the french people in the referendum on the european constitution, the supporters of the "yes" vote, particularly the ump, made three promises to the french people: the withdrawal of the bolkestein directive, the lowering of vat for the restoration of the monarchy and the abandonment of the turkish accession project. the french will finally have turkey, bolkestein and an unchanged vat. the compromise we are voting on today is a seemingly watered-down version of the original text, with full powers for the commission and the court of justice to reinstate the original text in the background. how can mr toubon say that by accepting this compromise he wishes to "avoid the worst"? the worst thing would be the absence of a directive, but the absence of a directive is precisely the promise made to the french people in 2005 by the ump and the head of state!
in writing. i voted against the common position in order to be consistent with my vote on the services directive at first reading. the council did not accept all the amendments proposed by the european parliament. the rejection is necessary because the council's common position does not clearly exclude labour law and social services of general interest. that is why i co-signed and voted for three amendments by the french socialist delegation which provide for the clear and complete exclusion of labour law and social services of general interest from the scope of the services directive. it is a question of protecting the fundamental rights of citizens. these should not be governed by the rules of the internal market. the commission's statement, although it clarifies its intention on several points, cannot be sufficient as it has no binding force. i have voted in favour of the amendments seeking to exclude services of general interest from the scope of this directive.

vice-president of the commission. mr president, i wish to begin by thanking the rapporteur, mr herrero-tejedor, for his hard work, the positive tone of this report and the support it gives to the commission’s ideas. however, i must say that i hope his friend is a better journalist than he is an expert on the eu institutions. when the commission adopted the white paper back in february we said that we intended to open a new chapter as regards communication between the european union and its citizens. as we put it, the new communication policy should move from monologue to dialogue. it should put ears on the european union. it should move from institution-centred communication to a citizen-centred approach based on people’s fundamental right to information and to be heard. it should move from brussels-based communication to a decentralised approach and from an accessory tool to a real european policy on an equal footing with other eu policies. in other words, it should be a policy in its own right. this leads me directly to the issue of the legal basis for the communication policy, which is, i agree, an issue here, and a very difficult and controversial one at that. it is a means of giving legitimacy to what we do and creating commitment, and it would set out the principles by which we worked on communication. the commission has proposed a citizens charter, or a code of conduct as we have called it, to which the institutional actors, including member states, could subscribe on a voluntary basis. the report suggests a somewhat different approach, inviting the commission to work on a draft interinstitutional agreement. it also urges the commission to explore the possibility of launching a genuine community programme for information and communication on europe on the basis of article 308 of the ec treaty. the commission is willing, as you recommend, to explore all possibilities for finding a sound basis for joint action, ranging from a citizens charter to a formal legal base. i am more than happy to embrace those ideas, again in order to give legitimacy to what we do. i am glad to see that your report acknowledges the importance of civic education and citizens’ involvement in the decision-making process. it calls on the commission to ensure consultation with the public at an early stage of policy-shaping, and this view is also shared by a broad cross-section of civil society. we shall certainly take action in this regard. we are all more than aware of the crucial role that the media – press, television, radio and the internet – play in contemporary democracy. we all know that a large part of the communication gap has to do with the fact that european affairs are quite marginal and often misrepresented in the media. i would like to be clear on this issue, because you have asked the commission to define with the greatest precision what role it would like to assign to the media. however, the problem cannot be addressed from that angle. the only role the media can have is the one that our democratic tradition has entrusted them with, which is to inform citizens in an independent, pluralistic and critical manner on european issues in the same way as domestic issues. the problem is how to create the conditions for this to happen, and this will be the theme of a stakeholders’ conference that will take place in helsinki in december, as a follow-up to the white paper. another central theme of the white paper is understanding public opinion. our societies are experiencing unprecedented changes due to higher internal mobility, migration and globalisation. public opinion has become more and more complex to define and comprehend. over the last 30 years, the eurobarometer has been a very useful tool for measuring public opinion, perceptions and orientations. however, we feel that much more can be done. i take note of your hesitations as regards our proposal for an observatory for european public opinion, but we can adopt a more pragmatic approach or step-by-step approach to this matter. for example, the idea of setting up networks of experts to exchange best practices and exploit synergies received considerable support during the public consultation. i shall not touch upon the many other issues that you rightly address in your comprehensive report, such as the role of member states, the importance of the regional and local level, the involvement of national parliaments or the responsibilities of political parties, which are all crucial, of course. we fundamentally agree on those issues, and i am very glad that the scope of my mandate allows me to work out concrete proposals to help realise these common aspirations. your report is a milestone in the process we have started with the white paper. it contains strong encouragement to move forward on the basis of ever-closer cooperation between our two institutions. the commission will issue its final report on the white paper next spring. that report will set out a series of concrete proposals, to be followed up by operational plans of action. the way ahead is still long and far from easy, but i am confident that, with your support, we can make a real change in the way europe communicates with its citizens by giving them a real say and by listening to them. an eu communication policy can be a tool to strengthen democracy and i look forward to the debate on it.
the committee on constitutional affairs has tabled a number of amendments to the report. mr president, the committee on constitutional affairs has clearly agreed to a communication policy of its own and welcomes the work of commissioner wallström. it is high time we had such a policy, if we are to believe the eurobarometers which show the discrepancy between our institutions and the expectations of the citizens. the afco committee also welcomes the commission's proposal for a two-way communication, which is very new: the institutions talking to the citizens and the citizens talking to the institutions. the problem is that, after having set out this excellent principle at the beginning of the white paper, we are now trying desperately to find a way for citizens to express their views in practice. that is the great flaw in your proposal, madam commissioner. you may find useful inspiration in the proposals of parliament, in particular the one concerning the creation of a citizen's agora, this consultative body which will enter into a test phase in 2007. our committee is not opposed in principle to a new interinstitutional instrument, charter or code, but it does ask that the guarantees and obligations which this implies be carefully studied. it also recalled that the charter of fundamental rights already defines rights to information and that the prerogatives of parliament, in particular its right to address the citizens freely, must be respected in all cases. it is also necessary to take account of the very particular pace of debate at european level, which is totally disconnected from national agendas. in this connection, we would like to reiterate our wish to have an annual debate on this subject in plenary, here in parliament. as regards new technologies, we are in favour of using them, provided, however, that we do not create a digital divide between citizens who will have access to these new technologies and those who will not. we also believe that we need to prioritise our partnerships between civil society, european political parties and journalists better, while fully respecting their independence, of course. we are even going so far as to make an iconoclastic proposal: the development of a european local administration so that brussels can be closer to the citizens. the unstated point in my report concerns the legal basis. the afco committee did not wish to comment on article 308. in a very close vote, it did not want to refer explicitly to this article, but in another very close vote, thanks to andrew duff it did not formally rule out the use of the same article 308, understand who can... the debate on the legal basis therefore remains very open, even if i personally and tactically agree wholeheartedly with what your rapporteur, mr luis herrero-tejedor, is proposing, and i commend him for his openness and friendliness and for the constructive nature of his work.
on behalf of the pse group. mr president, as rapporteur for the socialists on the draft report on the white paper on european communication policy, i would like to welcome, as mr onesta has done before, the fact that communication is finally being conceived as a two-way process between the institutions and the citizens, and no longer as a simple marketing operation. however, there is still a long way to go before european communication is established to integrate european issues into the very heart of the public sphere at national level. i have said it in committee and i will say it again here: i regret that the white paper continues to overvalue new technologies and undervalue national television. it is well known that national generalist channels remain - as eurobarometer surveys show - the preferred source of information for the inhabitants of the union. and i think that action is needed at this level. the white paper is also strangely silent on the financial means. but we all know that democracy and therefore communication have a cost. as long as the union's multiannual budget is less than that of a european advertising agency, little can be done. i would of course like to congratulate the rapporteur, mr herrero, and tell him that the debate on article 308 is not closed and that my colleague, mrs christa prets, will come back to this issue in a moment. commissioner, whenever the commission talks about communication policy, it is unfortunately when europe is in crisis! and it is only when things are going badly that the commission feels the need to communicate. the question which is put to the commission concerns the very content of its communication. citizens identify the commission as an ultra-liberal body that has no concern at all for protecting european citizens from the strong winds of globalisation. we owe it to the citizens, and to democracy, to offer a better explanation of what is happening in brussels. most european citizens are unaware of the achievements made possible by eu policies and funding. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the liberalisation of electricity, gas, rail and road transport and now the postal services is because the member states wanted it! without the will of the member states, this would not have been achieved. in conclusion, i believe that what we need is not so much a code of conduct for the european institutions on communication with citizens as a code of conduct for the commission to conduct a policy that is more in line with the concerns of our fellow citizens. finally, a short code of conduct must be submitted to the member states so that they can assume their responsibilities and stop once and for all 'nationalizing' european successes and 'communitizing' their national failures. europe will be greatly affected.

in writing. some of mr von wogau's analyses are in line with ours, particularly those concerning the threats to europe's security: terrorism, the vulnerability of our oil supplies, the porosity of our borders... indeed, contrary to the claims of our governments, which have dismantled the defense systems of our nations, the world is more dangerous today than it was before the fall of the berlin wall. the proposals in the report, however, are based on a second delusion, namely, that nations can rely on supranational agencies to ensure their security. but in the face of adversity, a nation is always alone. today the united states spends 3.5% of its gdp on defence, compared with less than 1% for the 25 member states of the european union. of course, european harmonization of defence equipment is necessary, but let us not dissolve our armies into a eurocorps, where orders are given in 21 languages and which, through nato, is under american command. let us strengthen the defence of each of our countries! this effort will be made only by independent nations, conscious of their identity. the first condition is that the europe of brussels, without soul and without frontiers, be replaced by a europe of sovereign nations!
in writing. in seeking to resolve the problems of conflicts of laws and jurisdiction in the field of succession and wills, the european parliament has, for once, avoided interfering with the exclusive competence of the national states. the 50,000 to 100,000 successions with international interests opened each year in the european union do not justify a new approach to the forced unification of substantive law rules, but only of rules of private international law, as well as the creation of a 'european certificate of succession'. we therefore support parliament's second recommendation, which seeks only to harmonise the rules on conflicts of rights and jurisdiction. we believe that this is the only way in which the member states can preserve their own legal systems, customs and traditions. only then will it be possible to coordinate effectively the national legal systems involved in a given succession. in order to prevent possible conflicts of laws in matters of inheritance, it is necessary and sufficient to know in advance in a certain and unquestionable way which law will be applicable.
in writing. i voted in favour of the gomes report on the place of women in economic and political decision-making positions. the political will shown at the beijing summit in 1995 and the existing international conventions have indeed helped to raise awareness of the issue of parity among the public and policy-makers at all levels of society. however, these declarations have not resolved the non-legal obstacles which still prevent women from participating fully in public life. it is necessary for the member states to adopt measures to reconcile social, professional and family life, in line with the conclusions of the barcelona european council and the lisbon strategy. i support the creation of a european institute for gender equality to address the low presence of women in politics and to promote a stronger representation of women in international politics. new avenues for women to be more involved in peace and security issues, including through more equal appointments to the united nations or to the european union's external representations, are therefore urgently needed.
in writing. in germany, liberia, chile and, more recently, in the us congress, the entry of women into key positions has been widely applauded. i would like to join in the applause, but i hope that one day these women's successes will no longer be symbolic but will become a commonplace event. it is no longer enough for a female politician to focus her media discourse on the real or supposed machismo of her opponents, as the sad "example" given by the internal campaign in the french socialist party for the presidential inauguration reveals. we must show more responsibility than demand, since gender equality is now accepted as a logical proposition. the european parliament's ump delegation, which comprises nine women and eight men, is particularly advanced in this respect. i hope that the vocation and motivation of a new generation of women to become involved in politics will be supported. but rather than multiplying the number of regulations that are too stringent and sometimes too radical to favour women, we must have confidence in their ability to assert themselves and to advance their convictions at all levels, local, national or european, as women, of course, but also as elected representatives.
in writing. i would like to congratulate edit bauer on this very high quality report. the unanimous adoption of the report by the libe committee is a testament to this. it is also important to note that the international trafficking of human beings affects between 600 000 and 800 000 men, women and children every year. about 80% of these victims are women and 50% are underage girls. the majority of trafficked victims are subject to commercial sexual exploitation. in order to deal with the increase in trafficking and its increasingly international character, this report proposes a series of integrated measures to be taken at european level which seem to me to be commensurate with the challenges associated with this scourge. above all, it underlines the eu's willingness to follow a human rights and victim-centred approach which i believe is crucial. for these reasons, and because the fight for respect for human dignity deserves our full support, i voted in favour of this text proposing the adoption of a european parliament recommendation to the council on the fight against trafficking in human beings.
in writing. strangely, this report attempts to make a clear distinction between human trafficking and illegal immigration. yet in many cases there is an undeniable similarity, for illegal immigration has become a veritable human trafficking, the most heinous of which is that of sexual exploitation. but who are the real culprits? is it not true that smugglers, drug traffickers, pimps and other slave traders are the ones who profit from a european territory without internal border controls and totally open to migration flows? but it is also the national and european leaders who do nothing serious about illegal entry, mass immigration, fake marriages or worse: who implement an openly "immigrationist" policy. the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat this problem. but the placebo effect will not last long because the real problem, the absence of internal border controls in the european union, remains. without calling into question the free movement of persons who are not union citizens, a veritable dogma established by brussels, illegal immigration will continue to grow irresistibly!
in writing. the report succeeds in making an illusory distinction between trafficking in human beings and illegal immigration. but since the disastrous schengen agreements signed in 1985, which abolished internal border controls in the european union, these two phenomena, which no one doubts are closely linked, have grown exponentially. since europe took over from the member states to create "an area of freedom, security and justice", the profits of the mafia, the pimps and the organised gangs of smugglers have never been so high. these networks are multiplying and thriving by exploiting more and more human beings. in order to find a solution to these human tragedies, the commission and parliament propose that we organise political dialogues between states and various cooperation programmes and plans. what's the point? it is high time to tackle the real causes of human trafficking and illegal immigration: the absence of safe and secure borders in europe. but it is true that it is impossible for our eurocrats to call into question the sacred rule of free movement of persons!
in writing. the figures and estimates of human trafficking are frightening. mrs bauer's report says that 600 000 to 800 000 men, women and children are trafficked internationally every year. exploitation which includes, at a minimum, prostitution but also forced labour or services, slavery or organ harvesting. but what the report does not tell us is that these human tragedies have been growing ever since the destructive schengen agreements abolishing internal border controls were signed in 1985. the european paradise, the 'area of security, freedom and justice' so long awaited and desired by all, is now in all the member states a non-existent, worse, dangerous and conducive to the development of all the mafias and organized criminals. as long as our national and european institutions refuse to see that the origin of the increase in international trafficking is the permeability of borders and as long as all policies to combat trafficking in human beings and illegal immigration require the immediate reintroduction of border controls in europe, one programme after another will have the same effect as a cataplasm on a wooden leg!
in writing. the stated aim of european communication policy is to "counter the effect of the rejection of the constitution [...] and to curb the general increase in euroscepticism". what do you think? information on europe, truncated, distorted, exploited by the media or the national political classes. what's the solution? the beating about the benefits of the european union organized by a brussels "propaganda staffel". the target? the citizens, whose euroscepticism is directly proportional to their ignorance of the paradise prepared for them in brussels and who must be converted to beatific admiration and unconditional support. who are we kidding? you didn't listen, you didn't hear, you didn't understand. it is precisely because they were informed, and they were informed at the source, by reading the text, that the french and dutch citizens rejected the constitution en masse. it is precisely because they live the economic and social disasters of your policy on a daily basis that they are eurosceptic. it is because for once they were asked directly for their opinion that they have taken an interest in europe. and it is because you have a visceral fear of the people that you prefer the skull-blowing to the direct consultation of these citizens whom you consider, in essence, to be idiots. they're giving you a good deal.

prime minister of ireland. mr president, in response to all of the speakers, there is obviously a great divergence of views and opinions, but this parliament, by an enormous majority, did ratify and support the constitution. however, i want to thank all the members for their points of view. it is useful for me as a member of the european council, and having been so involved in the constitution, just to hear those points. i think the exchange from that has been very valuable. it gives me a perspective that i suppose is difficult to get from this remove. as all of those members have said, it is important we listen to the people. it is not always possible to listen to all the people, but in that case you can listen to their elected representatives. this has afforded me the opportunity of explaining the rationale underpinning so many views on the constitution. i have also had an opportunity to give my views. i think that the constitution is a very balanced and fair document. i think it is an equitable document. of course it is made up of compromises. when you are trying to get 25 countries – as it was then – to agree, there have to be compromises in the text. it was not just a quick question of any one person saying ‘this is the position’. things change. as i went around europe there were many issues that were totally different in different countries, that caught the public imagination, that created a lot of difficulties in the media, and then people had to change or deliberate on what wording they could agree on, so it is not perfect insofar as it is just written with no ambiguities whatever, but it has been negotiated. there are those who believe that perhaps it was written in isolation – i think there were some comments about that. i understand that after a few years, but i would remind members of parliament that the convention had a very active group from parliament. they worked very hard. they were the representatives of the people, they were elected by the people, they were answerable to the people and i think the governments are too. you cannot have a constitution that is negotiated by 500 million people. you have to have their representatives doing it, and i think they did a good job on it. so sometimes that is the issue about legitimacy and democracy. i noted the points about fighting for the issues of human rights and values, and that this is what people are about, and not crime and drugs. the people i meet are far more concerned with both issues. they want to see that the rule of law, the rule of courts, the legal system protects everybody equally. however, they also want to see that those who are involved in criminality across borders and those who are engaged in criminal activity are dealt with. so if you are a supporter of human rights, then you are obviously a supporter of the constitution, because the charter for fundamental rights is the first time in europe that we have put all these things into the constitution so i think you should definitely be a strong advocate of the constitution. i think what is necessary for us now is not to try to renegotiate everything. with the german presidency coming up, the chancellor has clearly stated that she will set up a small group of officials to deal with a small group of officials in every country to identify where there are differences or difficulties. in my view, that should count 90% of the constitution out. the focus and the concentration and effort will then be on the remaining 10%. my colleague from ireland, mr de rossa, made a very fair point, one i have made several times, and it happened in the case of ireland and nice. the issue then is to try to get protocols to deal with the issues, that is the sensible thing: not throwing away parts of the constitution that have been agreed upon by parliament, by the council, by 18 countries across europe, but to try to find and accommodate the difficulties and analyse what the difficulties are in those countries which have voted ‘no’, or perhaps others which have reservations. that is not an impossible task. it has been done already in the countries where the constitution was lost. as stated earlier on, there were opinion polls looking into what those issues were and trying to deal with those issues. i think that is possible. if those issues are looked at in the igc or the council, it should be possible. i do not think it should take a long time. i would just ask parliament, and hope – as i will try to do in council – to keep supporting the constitution with the balanced view that we have to deal with a small number of outstanding issues as regards some countries and perhaps as regards countries that have declared their positions recently because of changes in governments. we should try to deal with that. if we can do that, then with the reason and purpose and the whole desire to have a european constitution – if that is what it is called; that is not something i get too excited about – we can move forward collectively to do that. i really believe it is possible. president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the 18th eu-russia summit was held last week in helsinki. as is the established practice, the summit discussed not only the four common eu-russia regions but also wider international issues. the meeting was also accompanied by a nordic dimension summit between the eu, russia, norway and iceland. we had a constructive and wide-ranging discussion on the key issues in eu-russia relations. as regards the forthcoming negotiations on a new eu-russia treaty, we noted that the eu's internal process to obtain a negotiating mandate had continued intensively over the past few weeks. the eu will continue to examine the mandate with a view to opening negotiations as soon as possible. in order to develop concrete cooperation, four meetings of the eu-russia permanent partnership council at ministerial level in the fields of transport, environment, justice and home affairs and in the foreign ministers' configuration were held during the autumn. as regards the common economic area, we noted positive developments in several areas of cooperation. the summit agreed on the payment and waiver of fees for flights over siberia. the eu and russia also noted the strong common interest and mutual dependence in energy relations. the european union has stressed the principles of transparency, predictability, reciprocity and openness in energy markets, investment and transit infrastructure. these principles should also be incorporated in the new eu-russia treaty. the union stressed that the parties should ensure their commitment to the principles of the energy charter. the discussions also covered the growth of trade and investment between the european union and russia, the solution of traffic congestion and the development of an electronic customs system, where we made concrete progress. we noted that the progress of russia's wto accession negotiations would have a significant positive impact on the eu-russia common economic area. negotiations on a deep and comprehensive free trade agreement between the eu and russia can be launched once russia has become a member of the wto. the environmental dialogue, which was strengthened at the eu-russia environmental partnership council in october, lays the foundations for a broad-based cooperation. in the area of justice and home affairs, cooperation has progressed in a number of sectors. we considered it of paramount importance to bring into force as soon as possible the agreements on visa facilitation and the readmission of illegal immigrants signed in may. the european union also called on the authorities of the member states to take all necessary steps to ensure that the situation in chechnya is brought under control and that the situation in chechnya is brought under control. the eu also highlighted the development of the rule of law and freedom of expression in russia and the conditions for independent media, including the investigations into the murder of anna politkovskaya and the case of mikhail khodorkovsky. the eu referred to the human rights consultations held in early november, which provided for a more in-depth discussion of these issues and the wider human rights situation in russia. the eu expressed its commitment to deepening cooperation in the field of human rights and developing human rights consultations. the european union and russia underlined the importance of direct contacts between citizens as the basis for a strategic partnership. this cooperation can be promoted in particular in the fields of education and culture. inter-university cooperation and student exchanges between the union and russia have been strongly emphasised during the autumn and will continue to be promoted in the future. we considered cooperation on international issues to be important for the security and prosperity of europe as a whole. we have seen a positive development in relations on a number of international issues. the eu and russia must develop cooperation in a more concrete way. the european council welcomed the progress made in the implementation of the lisbon strategy and the commission's efforts to achieve a more balanced and more effective implementation of the lisbon strategy. the eu-russia summit was accompanied by the northern dimension summit. the northern dimension summit adopted the new founding documents, political declaration and framework document for the northern dimension. with these decisions, the northern dimension will be renewed from the beginning of next year. the renewed northern dimension is a common policy of the four equal partners, the european union, russia, norway and iceland. the policy of the northern dimension covers a wide geographical area including the baltic sea, north-west russia and the arctic regions. the northern dimension supports the implementation of the four common areas between the eu and russia in this geographical area. in addition, the northern dimension focuses on issues specific to the northern regions, such as the vulnerable environment, indigenous peoples and health. a joint steering group of partners will be established for the northern dimension to accelerate practical cooperation. the existing partnerships in the northern dimension, namely the environmental and social and health partnerships, are to be continued and further developed. the aim is to explore the possibilities of applying the partnership model to the transport and logistics sector and to strengthen cooperation in the field of energy efficiency.
member of the commission. mr president, i am most grateful for the opportunity to inform you about the eu-russia summit, which took place in helsinki. this was the third eu meeting with president putin this year, following the one in sochi in may and the dinner in lahti, which gave us a good opportunity to speak about energy issues. like my colleague, i greatly welcome the fact that commission vice-president barrot and minister levitin were finally able to sign the protocol on siberian overflights. we have been working on this issue for many years and this is an important achievement, bringing an end to a persistent irritant in eu-russia relations. it was also one of our conditions for russia’s wto accession. therefore i warmly welcome this achievement and thank mr barrot for his efforts. immediately before the summit, we had a very good discussion on closer economic integration with eu and russian business leaders. they delivered a message of strong support for the benefits this would bring to the business communities on both sides. later, at the summit, there was a consensus that we should carry forward work on this subject over the coming months. our vision is the creation of a common economic area, essentially operating the same rules and providing for fair trade. on energy, president putin confirmed that the energy charter treaty would not be ratified as it stands, but he also clearly expressed willingness to come to a deal that would respect the interests of both sides and include the principles of the energy treaty, as he said in sochi. he called for reciprocity, including access for russian capital to key strategic industries in the european union. it is unfortunate that it was not possible to announce the opening of negotiations for our new strategic agreement. however, i am confident that the remaining difficulties will be resolved shortly. president barroso made it clear, after the inspection carried out by officials of our food and veterinary office, that we consider that the ban on certain polish exports is not proportionate. he pressed president putin strongly to lift it and, in any case, to agree to tripartite talks between poland, russia and the commission to settle this issue. president putin made it clear that the issue was not polish meat as such, but the transit of meat from other countries through poland to russia. finally, as far as the new agreement is concerned, it was reconfirmed, vitally, that there will be no legal vacuum when the current agreement reaches the end of its initial ten-year period. even though we have not yet started negotiations for an agreement, we can continue and we have a legal basis. another important issue already mentioned tonight is that of the long queues of vehicles waiting to enter russia at eu borders. we agreed to give urgent attention to that. a mission involving the commissioner for taxation and some member states had already taken place at the various borders between russia and the member states. we all noted that the origin of this problem was the growth in trade, namely the increase in trade between the eu and russia, on the one hand, and the overall increase of trade with russia, including transiting, on the other. but the infrastructure is already at maximum capacity and russian procedures are cumbersome. for instance, there are currently seven security procedures, which mr putin has promised to reduce to two. that is very important. for its part, the commission will shortly be making proposals in its report to address some of these customs issues. we also offered to cooperate on a pilot project. the question is whether data can be dealt with on the basis of a computer-based system. there was also a generally positive assessment of cooperation on freedom, security and justice. the russian side said that the agreements on visa facilitation and readmission would be sent for ratification soon. this is very positive, because readmission also helps the european union. i would like to express my appreciation for the parliamentary cooperation committee’s input on kaliningrad. on this matter, russia raised the future of the lithuanian scheme for cost-free visas, aluminium export duties and the treatment of minorities in latvia and estonia. we made it clear that these issues have either already been resolved or, in the case of visas for visitors from kaliningrad to lithuania, can be addressed. on external security, the european union pressed for more cooperation in the common neighbourhood, while russia emphasised non-proliferation and disarmament, particularly with regard to iran and north korea. president barroso outlined progress towards meeting the kananaskis commitments. it was agreed that new ways to cooperate on crisis management should be pursued. we also raised concerns regarding the human rights situation in russia, notably the killing of mrs politkovskaya. president barroso indicated that the perceived lack of due process caused concern in the european union. as requested by the president of parliament and other honourable members, he also raised the case of mikhail khordorkovsky. president putin defended the situation in russia. i will not repeat the comments made by the presidency on foreign policy issues other than to note the importance we attach to cooperation at the united nations on iran, to promote the six-party talks on north korea and to work with russia in the middle east through the quartet. russia asked for an urgent meeting of the quartet, which we hope will take place before christmas. we also need to work intensively to reduce our differences on georgia and kosovo, on which an exchange of views was held. finally, as my colleague said, the special northern dimension summit took place for the first time. it was a success and i welcome russia’s involvement in that overall idea.

romania was not ready in 2004. she has since made considerable efforts; it has implemented an impressive stream of modernising reforms. it was important to emphasize this warmly and, following mr van orden, i too want to welcome romania, as he did bulgaria. in substance, it is a short report which focuses on two points in particular: the date of accession and the accompanying measures and follow-up envisaged by the commission. the report is structured around six main questions. first of all, the report commends the romanian authorities for the great progress made since the beginning of the process. the reform effort undertaken by the government and the incumbent authorities has been extremely important, everyone agrees, so it was necessary to emphasize this in our resolution. the commission then recommended last september that romania should join by 1 january 2007. my report supports this conclusion, which i have been calling my wish for some time. the text also stresses that substantial progress has been made in the areas identified as problematic in the commission's may report. it also recalled that three areas were identified by the commission in september as requiring further progress, namely the reform of the judiciary, the fight against corruption and, to a lesser extent, the absorption of union aid in the agricultural sector, the absorption of the structural funds and the application of the acquis communautaire in certain areas of food security. fifthly, the report supports the commission's proposal to set up accompanying measures to monitor progress in these areas on the basis of a list of identified objectives. such measures were applied during the previous enlargement and this was to the benefit of all parties. the aim is not to stigmatize or isolate the country, but rather to support it in its efforts to consolidate the reforms under way. finally, on the last question, my report urges the romanian government to take all necessary measures and to make full use of the time remaining before accession in order to avoid recourse to safeguard clauses. that, ladies and gentlemen, is the general structure of the report. only five amendments were tabled for the plenary, which i believe reflects the broad consensus that has emerged around this text, the consensus that we have worked towards in the various committees. my group will not give voting instructions for amendments nos 1 and 2 by mrs gibault and mr cavada. these amendments are, however, in line with a written declaration signed by over 400 members, including myself. so, personally, i will vote for them, but my group's position will be expressed through a free vote. my group will support amendment no 5 by the gue/ngl on romania's efforts to join and will vote against amendment no 4 by the same group which is already covered in the report. as regards amendment no 3, my group will abstain. this, ladies and gentlemen, is the fruit of work which i have been doing for less than two years, and which was begun by others, notably mrs nicholson, who was the rapporteur before me. i am happy to hand over the fruits of this work to you, because in the end, over these years, i have always taken the same position. we have a common destiny. romania and bulgaria belong in the european union. you have to move forward, so you have to be friendly but demanding. i believe that the european parliament's position, in line with the commission's position, was the right one because it allowed the necessary reforms to be carried out and because, at the same time, it enabled us to achieve our common objective: the accession of romania and bulgaria on the date set. i think we should welcome this moment as another moment on the road to european reunification. i hope that the consensus we have all worked for will be reflected in an unambiguous vote by the european parliament. i would like the message that will reach romania tomorrow to be clear, if possible expressed massively, audible, positive followed by a warm and sincere welcome. president of the council. the decision-making process on the future financial instruments of the european union during the finnish presidency is coming to an end. we have managed to deal with this matter in a very good spirit and to adopt the bulk of the regulations on new financial instruments. the commission has also been able to take part in the negotiations with the united states, japan and the european union. we have another challenge ahead of us, the adoption of a regulation on the european instrument for democracy and human rights (eidhr). the issue is important both for parliament and for the member states, as it is a matter of promoting the fundamental values enshrined in the treaty on european union. parliament and its members have a special expertise in democracy and human rights issues, which has helped to achieve a good outcome. the draft regulation on a new global human rights instrument has been prepared in a very tight timetable. the member states, along with parliament, have made numerous proposals on the content of the regulation. it is very positive that we have already succeeded in reaching a common position on almost all the issues in these negotiations. the council, for its part, unanimously adopted a compromise text which gives the presidency the mandate to consult parliament in order to find a solution. the presidency's objective is to secure a first reading. the reason for this is clear to all. the current instrument for democracy and human rights expires in a few weeks, at the end of the year. we do not want to see a major break in the european union's support for democracy and human rights. we are obliged to find a solution quickly, not only because of the value of human rights and democracy for us europeans, but also because of the hopes and expectations of human rights and democracy defenders in various countries. the instruments have been prepared in such a way that they form the most functional unit. democracy and human rights activities are also implemented through other instruments, and a specific instrument on democracy and human rights complements this overall approach in specific areas. for this reason too, the adoption of the instrument before the start of the new financial period is highly justified. the council presidency strongly urges parliament to take decisions before the end of the year. the package adopted by the council contains a substantial number of parliament's amendments to the regulation, both as regards the priorities for the content of the aid and parliament's own role in implementing the instrument. a significant feature of the new regulation is that it recognises the importance of democracy work and, as part of this, places a stronger emphasis on the work of parliaments and parliamentarians. the key to our action in third countries is to rely on international human rights conventions and the rights and obligations enshrined in them. the proposed regulation will broaden the eligibility criteria for eu support for different operators. it is good that we are able to take account of the diversity of human rights and democracy activities and to use different means flexibly in different situations. the financial resources of the instrument also appear to be increasing somewhat compared to the current financial period, so that the entry of new players is not necessarily excluded from other players. the key idea behind the creation of the instrument has been to allow support to be given in particular to civil society actors and to allow support to be given in situations where it is done without the explicit consent of the government of the country concerned. it is important that this starting point be maintained until the end and that forms of support for other operators within the regulation are not increased too much. the council's compromise proposal extends the eligibility criteria for support to parliaments and political foundations, in line with the european parliament's proposals. the draft regulation also allows for the eligibility of other operators in specific situations. i think it is a well thought out solution, one which takes account of the wishes and the opposition of the various actors in the european union and is capable of acting. parliament wanted to highlight the specific feature that support under this instrument, which is mainly aimed at civil society actors, can also be granted without the consent of the government of a third country. this principle has been the subject of agreement between the council and parliament from the outset. i believe that we have now also succeeded in finding a way of stating the principle in a more precise and clearer way, taking into account both the treaty of the union and our international treaty obligations. the presidency is prepared to propose the inclusion of the principle in the first recital if agreement on the content of the whole regulation is reached at first reading. parliament also took note of the inclusion in the regulation of the rights of migrants, asylum seekers and internally displaced persons. the text of the regulation takes as a starting point international human rights conventions. it can therefore be considered as already including this point. however, the presidency is prepared to refer this amendment to the council if the regulation as a whole can be adopted at first reading. the council, for its part, is therefore prepared to show even more flexibility in order to find a solution before the end of the year. the flexibility of all parties is a prerequisite for a solution to emerge. the european parliament's committee report proposes that political groups should be included in the scope of the aid. this would include political parties, so that it would also be a matter of financial support for the activities of parties operating in third countries. the democratic parties undoubtedly have an important role to play in strengthening democracy and human rights throughout the world. it is very important that the union's support under this human rights instrument is based on clear principles and is based in principle on internationally agreed human rights principles. the resources of this instrument are far from sufficient to create a general party subsidy, which is granted to all on the same basis, as is the case in many european countries. the selection of individual parties for support would be a very challenging task in terms of finding a clear criteria. this choice should be made in such a way that it does not give the impression that any partisan consideration would override democratic and human rights considerations in the selection of support. it is also clear that in this respect too, an increase in the number of beneficiaries may mean a reduction in the number of others. the main aim of the aid is to target ngos working for democracy and human rights. the presidency's compromise proposal has taken into account, among other things, parliament's proposals to include independent party foundations and national, regional and international parliaments among the beneficiaries. article 9 (2) of the regulation allows for the granting of aid in specific cases to operators other than those referred to in this article. the formulation is largely in line with parliament's wishes and is flexible, allowing for the resolution of problems during the financial period. the requirement to add political groups to the text of the regulation is not acceptable to the council for the reasons mentioned above. this could jeopardise the adoption of the whole regulation at first reading and create a situation in which the european union's action on democracy and human rights would not have a legal basis for the time being. the freezing of all human rights and democracy support in the european union to solve this case would be a very powerful weapon. the council has gone very far in its own way against parliament. it is very important to include and maintain the support of the member states for this set of regulations in order to find a solution. i hope that parliament will be flexible so that we can achieve our main objective together. our main objective is that the european union can continue to support democracy and human rights activities through this new instrument, also next year. in order to ensure the continuity of this support, it is essential to reach a solution to the proposed regulation and to achieve it quickly.
member of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. i wanted to be brief so that we could conclude this debate. this financial instrument is indeed an important cornerstone of this comprehensive reform of the community's external aid system. i am very pleased that in a relatively short time we have succeeded in finding a common text for a regulation on human rights and democracy. i think that this instrument speaks in an exemplary way to the european union's unwavering commitment to democracy and human rights as an essential element of action. we will therefore be in regular dialogue with parliament. in a particularly precarious situation of human rights and democracy, which requires rapid action by the community, i propose that we instrument. the commission's proposal is based on the principle of subsidiarity, which is the basis of the treaty of rome. this is as much about the democratic reform process as it is about the
