the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to thank in particular the secretariat of the committee on transport for its excellent work in preparing and consulting the interested parties on this important matter. this dossier is mainly concerned with the protection of the environment against marine pollution. the report i am presenting to you today concerns the accelerated introduction of double hull requirements or equivalent design standards for single hull tankers. the commission has also proposed that the exemptions which have been in place since 2002 be abolished. after the sinking of the oil tanker prestige in 2002, the commission had decided to accelerate the withdrawal of single-hull oil tankers, in accordance with the december 2002 regulation. the commission also proposed to prohibit, with immediate effect, the transport of heavy petroleum products in single-hull tankers to or from ports of a member state of the european union. at present, international maritime law provides that a vessel flying the flag of a member state may benefit from exemptions from this prohibition, provided that it is sailing outside european ports. commissioner barrot has just mentioned that at a meeting of the international maritime organisation, the italian presidency of the union had declared on behalf of the 15 member states that they would not allow their tankers to use this exemption under rule 13 h. the commission therefore considered that the 2002 regulation should be adapted by deleting the last exemption to rule 13 h and, therefore, prohibiting the transport of heavy petroleum products in single-hull tankers flying the flag of a member state, irrespective of the jurisdiction of the ports, offshore terminals or maritime zone in which those tankers operate. only one european country - greece - had refused to accept the political position of the italian presidency, considering that it was not bound by it. it seems that it wanted to continue to allow its single-hull tankers to sail outside european ports with, of course, heavy oil products on board. finally, during the work of the committee on transport, this objection was not renewed. today the 25 member states of the european union have agreed that no tanker carrying heavy goods will be allowed to fly the flag of a member state if it is a single-hull tanker. in reality, this only confirms what is already respected and applied by the vast majority of member states. the absolute requirement to respect the objective of maximum maritime safety once again prevailed in this case, as did the reduction of the risks of pollution by oil. the risks of pollution are many and can be of various kinds. just five days ago, toxic barrels were drifting between the cotentin and the atlantic in my region. last friday evening, these barrels were blown off the deck of a swiss container ship from antwerp to portugal. while the new double hull legislation is a significant step forward in the prevention of marine pollution, standards must continue to be established to enable tankers and merchant ships to offer the greatest number of guarantees. the motorways of the sea are a solution to congestion, but the safety of ships must not be neglected. it's about the future of our entire planet. mr president, commissioner, i would like to point out that your rapporteur has tabled a technical amendment, which is also supported by the european commission, and which saves us from having to amend a series of references. moreover, this one, of a linguistic nature, concerns only the english version. this amendment does not alter the text on the substance and the finnish presidency has confirmed to us that it does not raise any problems for the council.

madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to make two points on the occasion of this joint debate on energy. firstly, the european union has no competence in energy matters. this is so true that the various reports emphasize that the energy choices of the member states are their exclusive competence. mrs morgan adds an explicit reference to maximum subsidiarity. but everything in these reports contradicts these claims, so prescriptive and directive are they. secondly, the europe of brussels has already shown what it is capable of by usurping the right to conduct an energy policy and liberalizing the electricity and gas markets. with what results? increased prices for consumers, the question of tariff equalization, and therefore of the public service, supply interruptions, concerns about the maintenance, extension and modernization of networks ... today we are witnessing an accelerated concentration of the sector, to the point that the famous competition you keep telling us about is very close to becoming a monopoly of the energy market by a handful of multinational companies. the only difference is that these monopolies will be in the hands of private capital, perhaps not even european, and not public enterprises either. so yes, we are in favour of energy security, energy efficiency, but it is up to sovereign states to manage these strategic matters.

mr president, commissioner, we are discussing this afternoon the question of the european union signing the hague convention on the law applicable to certain rights in securities held with an intermediary. parliament has accepted the union's accession to the hague convention, but it intends to exercise democratic control over each of the sectoral ratifications. the convention in question is of concern to us in more than one way, in particular because it is intended to lead to a revision of a number of directives which we have adopted in this field. i am thinking of the so-called 'collateral', 'finality' and 'liquidation of credit institutions' directives. however, we could easily go back to these guidelines if we were not afraid of three fundamental obstacles. firstly, the ratification of this convention on the law applicable to certain rights in securities leaves such a margin of appreciation for the parties to choose the applicable law that we are very much afraid that the whole mechanism that we have long and meticulously put in place at the european union level to combat money laundering may simply be circumvented. secondly, the recommendations of the financial action task force, the fatf, on the need to be able to identify the owners of securities seem to us to be absolutely incompatible with this hague convention in that, once again, it leaves the parties too much freedom in choosing the applicable law. thirdly, we fear that the entry into force of such a convention will lead to the circumvention of the provisions on market abuse which the union has adopted. once again, without clear identification, we fear that it is possible to circumvent certain obligations established at european level. in this connection, i shall, for the first time, invoke the opinion of the central bank in support of the withdrawal of this proposal. as you know, the european central bank, in its opinion, expressed very serious reservations; in particular, it highlighted the systemic risk and the risk of exponential growth of litigation, which could undermine clear arbitration in the determination of the ranking of collateral. the commission has almost made 'better lawmaking' a leitmotif of its action: you have here a case study in which you could put this principle into practice. that is why we are asking the commission to withdraw its proposal for ratification of the hague convention on the law applicable to certain rights in securities.
the commission's vice-president mr president, madam member, ladies and gentlemen, the commission's 2003 proposal for the signature of the hague convention on securities has reached a dead end. the united states and switzerland signed the convention in july 2006, europe is questioning and the council is divided. the introduction in 1998 of the account location mechanism in the directive on the final nature of the regulation, and later in the directive on the winding-up of credit institutions and the directive on financial guarantee contracts, has helped to ensure legal certainty as regards the law applicable to indirectly held securities. while it is also true that there is no evidence of practical problems in the internal market, the scope of this mechanism is essentially limited to situations where securities act as collateral in the banking sector. determining the place of a securities account in the dematerialized and virtual world in which we now live would require the development of new common regulations, for example, via a standardized numbering of bank accounts. the aim of the negotiations on the hague convention on securities was to create a single, common mechanism applicable at international level. the convention proposes to this end that the parties should be free to choose the law governing the ownership of securities. since all member states had accepted the compromise at that time, the commission proposed in 2003 to sign the convention. since then, several member states have raised new questions about the project. the council then asked the commission for clarification on four specific legal issues. the answer came in the form of a legal impact assessment of the convention, carried out by the commission services and communicated to the council on 3 july. in this study, the commission services considered that the signature of the convention was the simplest solution to have a single rule at international level. the impact assessment also proposed alternatives to signing the convention, including the extension of the account location clause to all uses of securities, not just to uses as collateral. however, to obtain a solution on this basis at international level, further negotiations with third countries would be necessary. at this stage, on the proposal of my colleague in charge of the internal market, we do not believe that an assessment of the economic and financial impact of the convention, as mentioned in the oral question, would help us to find a solution. the member states which negotiated the convention in 2002 and are currently debating it in the council did not consider it necessary to have such a study at the time, nor have they done so since. in accordance with the interinstitutional agreement and in the interest of more efficient legislation, the commission would welcome any additional external analysis of the legal or economic impact which would allow us to move things forward. as i have already said, the matter is blocked in the council, but the commission remains open to all proposals. i would like to say that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter, but it is not yet clear whether it will take a decision on the matter.
the european parliament has a duty to protect the environment. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the hague convention on intermediary securities is intended, as has just been said, to determine the law applicable to property rights arising from the listing of financial securities held by an intermediary. this text is far from unanimous within the european union, which justifies the relevant questions raised by mrs berès. first, the hague convention retains the autonomy of the will of the investor and his intermediary in the designation of the law to which they intend to be attached in the event of a dispute. this is contrary to the law in most european countries, which retains the place of domicile of the securities account as a relevant element in deciding the applicable law. in other words, the choice of law would now be purely contractual, which of course creates legal uncertainty in this area. secondly, and let us not be too euphemistic, given the importance of the american institutions active in this field, there is a risk that the choice of american law will henceforth become the contractual rule, which will inevitably have a number of negative consequences. in terms of activities, on the one hand, the obvious mastery of us law by the overseas players is likely to work in their favour and create a competitive disadvantage for european institutions. in terms of investor protection, on the other hand, if in most european legal systems the investor holding a security has a right over its issuer, in us law he has only a right over his intermediary. hence, there are legitimate concerns in the event of the latter's bankruptcy. finally, the provisions of the convention are likely to defeat - as mrs berès pointed out - anti-money laundering measures because they are based on the principle of territorial cohesion. suspicions must be reported to the competent national authority, i.e. the authority of the country where the intermediary is established. the commission considers that the fact that the bank of greece has not provided the information requested by the commission does not constitute a breach of the principle of legal certainty. the european central bank expressed its concerns, in particular as regards the risk of incompatibility between the prudential and financial stability rules and the provisions of the law chosen by the parties. it also seems difficult to reconcile the principles of most european countries, where the relationship between the investor and the issuer of securities is direct, whereas in the principles of anglo-saxon law there is no direct relationship between the issuer of securities and the investor. you said, commissioner, that accession to the hague convention on securities held by intermediaries was at a standstill: we want it to remain there!

the commission's vice-president mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission, like the other european institutions and like your parliament, is very concerned about the situation in burma. exactly 15 years ago, the european parliament awarded the sakharov prize to aung san suu kyi. we regret that since that date the political process has been completely paralysed in that country. the burmese authorities, like those in other developing countries, are faced with considerable challenges - to ensure national unity, political stability and to accelerate the economic and social development of the country - but this is by no means an obstacle to the establishment of a legitimate civilian government. the current government has repeatedly stated that military rule will be replaced by a legitimate and elected regime, based on the roadmap for burma. but, to date, we are still at the stage of promises. for all of us, international observers and donors, it is unthinkable that a transition to a legitimate and democratically elected regime can take place without dialogue. such a dialogue must bring together government and political actors. it must include the ethnic minorities, who are very numerous in burma, and lead to an end to the fighting in the areas inhabited by these minorities. similarly, a political transition is inconceivable as long as political opponents of the current regime are imprisoned or deprived of their liberty, as is still the case with aung san suu kyi and over a thousand other opponents. the vision of a democratic and prosperous burma also requires respect for human rights. such respect is sorely lacking. despite the existence of a civil society, the exercise of fundamental rights is far from assured: intimidation, arbitrary arrests, imprisonment of civilians for exercising their civil rights, limitations of individual freedoms continue. members of political parties are subject to constant surveillance by the security services. part of the population is exploited by the military for forced labour. of course, the restrictions on the international committee of the red cross, as you have very well said, are intolerable, and there is little sign that the government is committed to remedying this situation. in the face of all this, ladies and gentlemen, what is the european union's position? the universal declaration of human rights and the charter of the international labour organization are our references. the european common position imposes restrictive measures on visas and investments. in trade matters, burma no longer benefits from the preferential trade regime provided for by the generalised system of preferences. however, the very nature of the burmese regime makes the burmese population very vulnerable to poverty and disease. the commission has therefore decided to increase its assistance substantially from 2007, particularly in the areas of health and education. the global fund to fight aids, tuberculosis and malaria, which is placed under the auspices of the united nations and co-financed by the commission, should make it possible to combat these three diseases more effectively. in the particular context of this country, any programme requires vigilance and commitment. the programmes financed by the community, amounting to some eur 24 million, are implemented by un agencies and international ngos. the commission has also set up a programme of decentralised cooperation, which should support civil society. the commission is also by far the largest donor to burmese refugees in thailand. in the context of a critical dialogue with the government, the commission will continue to remind the burmese authorities of their responsibilities. the transition in burma must be done with respect for human rights. the admirable struggle of aung san suu kyi, winner of the european parliament's sakharov prize, reminds us of this every day. mr president, i would like to say on a personal note that i have particularly enjoyed these debates on human rights, particularly the debate on burma. i would like to assure the house that the commission will be extremely vigilant and determined to put an end to the present situation in this country as far as possible.
